We investigated the impacts of climate-driven hydrological changes on Northern Pintail (*Anas acuta*) breeding ecology in the Prairie Pothole Region of Alberta, Canada, from 2003 to 2022. Using GPS telemetry (n = 148 individuals) and nest monitoring data (n = 712 nests), we analyzed relationships between wetland availability, phenological shifts, and reproductive success. Spring arrival advanced by 9.2 ± 1.8 days per decade, mismatched with the 14-day advancement in seasonal wetland inundation patterns (R² = 0.67, p < 0.001). The proportion of semipermanent wetlands holding water through June declined by 32% in drought years (2011, 2016, 2021), correlating with 44% lower nest success rates (95% CI: 38–50%) compared to wet years. Multivariate models revealed that April maximum temperatures exceeding 12°C reduced clutch sizes by 18% (β = -0.22, SE = 0.07), while May precipitation deficits <30 mm decreased duckling survival by 62% (OR = 0.38, 95% CI: 0.25–0.57). Breeding pair density showed a nonlinear response to wetland area (AICc = 214.7), with thresholds below 0.5 km²/km² resulting in population declines >5%/year. Our results suggest climate-mediated wetland desiccation is creating ecological traps in traditional breeding areas, necessitating adaptive management strategies including dynamic wetland restoration buffers and revised harvest regulations to account for reduced productivity.

We investigated predator-prey interactions influencing King Rail (Rallus elegans) survival and foraging ecology in Chesapeake Bay tidal marshes (Maryland, USA) from 2018–2020. Using radio telemetry (n = 47 adults) and automated acoustic recording units, we quantified spatial-temporal overlap between rails and their primary predators (American mink [Neovison vison], Northern Harrier [Circus hudsonius]) and prey (blue crabs [Callinectes sapidus], aquatic insects). Kernel density analyses revealed rails shifted core activity areas (95% CI) by 127 ± 42 m following mink detections, with 63% of predation events (n = 11 confirmed mortalities) occurring during full-moon high tides. Prey availability assessments through benthic sampling showed rail foraging efficiency declined 28% in areas with >5 mink latrines/km of marsh edge (GLMM: β = -0.33, p = 0.02). Stable isotope analysis (δ¹³C, δ¹⁵N) of rail blood samples indicated specialized feeding on decapod crustaceans (mean contribution 71% ± 9% of diet) despite high insect abundance. Night-vision camera traps demonstrated 82% of foraging occurred nocturnally, potentially minimizing raptor predation risk. Our multi-scale habitat models identified optimal rail occupancy (ψ > 0.6) in intermediate salinity marshes (5–10 ppt) with irregular shoreline complexity (Fractal Dimension Index 1.3–1.5). These findings suggest King Rails employ spatiotemporal niche partitioning to balance predation risk and resource acquisition, with implications for marsh management practices targeting invasive mink control and hydrologic connectivity maintenance in the face of sea-level rise.

We investigated the migratory connectivity and stopover ecology of Yellow Warblers (Setophaga petechia) across their North American breeding range using a combination of light-level geolocators (n = 127) and plasma metabolite analysis (n = 298). Birds from six breeding populations spanning Alaska to the Great Lakes region were tracked between 2018-2022, revealing three distinct migratory corridors: a western coastal route (Pacific flyway), central continental pathway, and eastern Appalachian corridor. Median spring arrival dates varied by 22 days across populations (earliest in coastal California: 28 March ± 5.2 days; latest in Manitoba: 19 April ± 7.1 days). Stopover duration analysis showed significant interannual variation linked to temperature anomalies (r = -0.73, p < 0.01), with birds spending 38% longer at Gulf Coast sites during colder springs. Metabolite profiling indicated higher refueling rates in riparian habitats (x̄ = 2.3 mg/g/hr triglyceride) compared to agricultural stopovers (x̄ = 1.1 mg/g/hr), though agricultural sites comprised 61% of used habitats. Population-specific wintering distributions revealed strong connectivity, with Manitoba breeders occupying a 300-km coastal stretch in Belize versus the diffuse Central American distribution of Great Lakes populations. These findings highlight the vulnerability of western migrants to coastal habitat loss and suggest that climate-mediated phenological mismatches may disproportionately affect interior continental populations. Conservation strategies requiring >30% riparian corridor preservation in stopover regions could buffer against estimated energetic deficits from anticipated temperature increases under RCP 4.5 scenarios.

We investigated population dynamics of Common Gallinule (*Gallinula galeata*) across a hydrological gradient in Florida's Everglades (2012-2022) using mark-recapture (n=1,247 individuals) and nest monitoring (n=582 nests). Bayesian hierarchical models revealed a 42% regional population decline (95% CrI: -38% to -47%), with adult survival probability decreasing from 0.78 ± 0.04 to 0.62 ± 0.05 and juvenile recruitment declining from 0.8 ± 0.1 to 0.4 ± 0.2 fledglings/pair. Hydrological covariates explained 67% of variance in survival (WAIC = 132.4), with extreme drought years (2015, 2021) precipitating 15% annual declines. Spatial analysis identified Water Conservation Area 3A as a demographic stronghold (λ = 0.94 ± 0.03) compared to rapidly declining populations in Everglades National Park (λ = 0.82 ± 0.05). Nest success showed non-linear responses to water depth (peak at 35-45 cm; β = 1.2 ± 0.3) and invasive plant cover (*Pistia stratiotes* β = -0.7 ± 0.2). Climate projections indicate 23-41% habitat loss by 2050 under RCP4.5 scenarios. Our results highlight the vulnerability of marsh-obligate rallids to hydrological variability and support targeted management of water recession rates during nesting periods. Conservation interventions in managed wetlands reduced population declines by 35% compared to unmanaged areas (χ² = 7.3, p = 0.007), demonstrating the efficacy of adaptive habitat protocols for this IUCN Near Threatened species.

We investigated the breeding ecology of Ring-necked Pheasants (Phasianus colchicus) in intensively managed agricultural landscapes of eastern South Dakota from 2018-2021. Using radio-telemetry (n = 78 females) and systematic nest searches (n = 132 nests), we quantified nest site selection, daily nest survival rates (DSR), and brood-rearing habitat use. Nesting females showed strong selection for untilled field margins (χ² = 19.4, p < 0.001) and Conservation Reserve Program grasslands, with 67.2% of nests occurring in habitats comprising <8% of total land cover. DSR decreased significantly with advancing crop growth stage (β = -0.23 ± 0.07 SE) and increased with vegetation height >30 cm (β = 0.41 ± 0.11 SE). Estimated nest success was 42.1% (±3.8 SE) despite high predation rates (58.3% of nest failures). Brood habitats contained 34% greater arthropod biomass compared to random sites (t = 3.91, p = 0.002), with chick survival to 21 days positively correlated with early-season insect availability (r = 0.61). Our results demonstrate that contemporary agricultural intensification reduces availability of critical nesting cover, while pesticide use may indirectly limit reproductive success through prey reduction. We propose targeted retention of fallow strips and delayed mowing regimes as mitigation strategies to maintain pheasant populations in agroecosystems, balancing economic and conservation priorities in this game species of significant cultural and ecological importance.

We investigated the impacts of climate-driven lake warming on the breeding ecology of Double-crested Cormorants (Phalacrocorax auritus) across 12 colonies in Lake Michigan and Lake Huron from 2010–2022. Using a combination of GPS tracking (n = 84 individuals), nest productivity surveys (n = 1,327 nests), and long-term hydrologic data, we quantified relationships between spring ice phenology, water surface temperature anomalies, and reproductive success. Bayesian hierarchical models revealed a 12-day advancement in median nest initiation date per 1°C increase in April water temperature (95% CI: 8.7–15.3 days). However, fledging rates declined by 30% (95% CI: 24–36%) in years with >2°C May temperature anomalies, linked to trophic mismatches with yellow perch (Perca flavescens) prey availability. Counterintuitively, colonies exposed to later ice clearance showed 18% higher chick survival (p = 0.003), suggesting cold-water specialists face disproportionate risks as seasonal thresholds shift. Our bioenergetic models project a 42–57% reduction in suitable nesting islands by 2100 under RCP 8.5 due to increased algal blooms and water level fluctuations. These findings highlight the complex interplay between thermal habitat changes and bottom-up food web effects in piscivorous seabirds, necessitating dynamic protected area design and targeted forage fish management in the Laurentian Great Lakes.

We investigated stopover ecology of Common Loons (Gavia immer) during autumn migration across the Laurentian Great Lakes using satellite telemetry (n=48 adults) and shoreline surveys (2018-2022). Individuals exhibited high site fidelity (78% reuse rate) at 23 key stopovers, remaining 11.2 ± 3.8 days (mean ± SD) to replenish lipid reserves depleted during 650-1,200 km flight segments. Kernel density analysis revealed 83% of stopover activity concentrated in three areas: eastern Lake Michigan (45.3% of locations), Georgian Bay (28.1%), and western Lake Erie (17.6%). Loons preferentially used deepwater zones (>15 m) near fish spawning grounds (χ²=34.7, p<0.001), with 92% of locations occurring >2 km from developed shorelines. Plasma metabolite profiling indicated daily mass gains of 1.4-2.8% body weight during stopovers, sufficient for subsequent migration legs. Juveniles (n=12) showed 37% longer stopover durations than adults (U=102, p=0.03) and greater use of secondary sites. Threat analysis identified 68% of critical stopover habitats lacking protected status, with 41% facing development pressures from offshore wind proposals and increased vessel traffic. Our findings emphasize the need for international collaboration under the Great Lakes Water Quality Agreement to implement seasonal buffer zones and designate Essential Habitat Areas for this IUCN Near Threatened species. These data provide the first quantitative framework for predicting stopover site importance based on bathymetry, prey availability, and anthropogenic disturbance gradients.

We investigated parental care strategies in Yellow Warblers (*Setophaga petechia*) across a gradient of nest predation risk in riparian habitats of the Missouri River Basin, Montana, from 2018–2020. Using 120 monitored nests equipped with continuous video recording and radio telemetry, we quantified provisioning rates, nest attendance patterns, and behavioral responses to simulated brood parasite threats (Brown-headed Cowbird decoys). Parents in high-predation zones (n = 63 nests) made 23% fewer feeding visits/hr (mean ± SE: 4.2 ± 0.7 vs. 5.5 ± 0.9 in low-risk areas) but delivered 15% larger prey items. Nestlings in high-risk environments exhibited 18% lower mass gain rates despite comparable initial hatch weights. Experimental brood parasite exposure triggered a 42% increase in nest defense behaviors (wing-fluttering, alarm calls) among experienced adults with prior parasitism encounters, but not in naïve individuals. Survival analysis revealed a 31% reduction in fledging success at high-predation sites, linked to parental trade-offs between food delivery and predator avoidance. Our results demonstrate plasticity in parental investment under fluctuating predation pressure, with implications for riparian habitat management. Fragmentation of dense willow stands increased cowbird access, exacerbating reproductive costs. Conservation strategies prioritizing contiguous understory vegetation may mitigate these pressures while maintaining ecosystem services in threatened floodplain ecosystems.

We investigated juvenile survival rates of Clapper Rails (Rallus crepitans) in Chesapeake Bay tidal marshes from 2018–2020 to assess drivers of first-year mortality in this declining saltmarsh obligate. Using radio telemetry, we tracked 126 fledglings across 12 marsh complexes varying in elevation, Spartina alterniflora density, and predator activity. Survival probability to 90 days post-fledging averaged 62% (±7% SE), with mammalian predation (primarily by red fox Vulpes vulpes) accounting for 68% of mortalities. Cox proportional hazards models revealed survival increased 1.3× per 10 cm gain in marsh elevation (95% CI: 1.1–1.5) and 1.2× per 10% increase in vegetation stem density (95% CI: 1.0–1.4). Juveniles in marshes with active predator control programs (n=4 sites) showed 84% higher survival than unprotected sites (χ²=9.3, p=0.002). Tidal inundation events caused 22% of mortalities, disproportionately affecting low-elevation marshes (<0.4 m NAVD88). Our mark-resight data indicate that ≥75% vegetation cover within 50 m of nest sites is critical for fledgling survival. These findings highlight the intersection of habitat quality and anthropogenic pressures in this SLR-vulnerable ecosystem, suggesting managed marsh accretion and targeted predator mitigation could improve juvenile recruitment. Results informed revised habitat suitability indices for Mid-Atlantic Clapper Rail conservation plans, emphasizing elevation thresholds and vegetation structure requirements.

We investigated the population dynamics of Red-winged Blackbirds (Agelaius phoeniceus) across 15 breeding seasons (2008–2022) in the Upper Midwest, USA, using a combination of standardized breeding surveys, mark-recapture data, and land cover analysis. Annual survival rates averaged 0.63 ± 0.07 SD for males and 0.58 ± 0.09 for females, with recruitment rates declining by 18% in agricultural regions compared to wetland-dominated landscapes. Hierarchical Bayesian models revealed that conversion of native grasslands to row crops reduced juvenile survival by 32% (95% credible interval: 24–40%), while wetland proximity buffered drought-induced mortality. Population growth rates (λ) averaged 0.97 ± 0.03, indicating a 2.3% annual decline in intensively farmed areas, contrasted with stable trends (λ = 1.02 ± 0.02) in regions retaining >40% wetland cover. Extreme spring precipitation events (>90th percentile) reduced nest success by 41% through vegetation inundation, with carryover effects diminishing subsequent-year territory fidelity. Our analysis demonstrates that agricultural intensification disrupts source-sink dynamics, with only 12% of sampled counties functioning as population sources. These findings underscore the urgency of integrating wetland buffers and fallow margins into agricultural conservation programs to maintain metapopulation connectivity for this ecologically influential songbird.

We investigated the seasonal stopover ecology of migratory Bald Eagles (Haliaeetus leucocephalus) along a 1,200 km corridor between Interior Alaska and the contiguous United States from 2018–2022. Using GPS-GSM transmitters deployed on 48 adults, we quantified stopover duration, site fidelity, and habitat selection patterns during spring and fall migrations. Eagles exhibited median stopover durations of 5.3 days (range: 1–21) in spring and 7.1 days (range: 2–28) in autumn, with 63% of individuals reusing specific riparian zones annually. Resource selection functions revealed strong preferences for river segments with high salmonid carcass density (β = 1.24, SE = 0.31) and avoidance of areas within 500 m of active roads (β = -0.87, SE = 0.19). Stopover sites clustered disproportionately in four critical areas: the Yukon River confluence (64°12'N), Saskatchewan River Delta (57°34'N), Lake Winnipeg narrows (52°08'N), and Upper Mississippi River backwaters (44°17'N). These hubs supported 82% of all tracked individuals and showed 14% higher plasma triglyceride levels (indicating refueling rates) compared to incidental stopovers. However, 31% of high-use sites lacked formal protection, with six locations demonstrating significant declines in eagle occupancy correlated with increased recreational boating activity (r = -0.73, p < 0.01). Our results emphasize the need for temporally dynamic conservation measures, including seasonal fishing restrictions and boating buffers, to maintain functional connectivity for this recovered raptor species facing emerging anthropogenic pressures on migratory pathways.

We investigated the impacts of invasive hybrid cattail (Typha × glauca) expansion on Sora (Porzana carolina) habitat selection and reproductive success across 12 managed wetlands in the Upper Mississippi River Floodplain (2018–2021). Using radio-telemetry (n = 42 adults) and nest monitoring (n = 87 nests), we quantified spatial overlap between Sora home ranges and invasive vegetation monitored through annual GIS mapping. Mixed-effects models revealed Soras in cattail-dominated wetlands (<50% native vegetation) exhibited 34% smaller home ranges (95% CI: 28–40%) and 62% lower nest survival (n = 23 vs. 64 nests) compared to populations in mixed vegetation sites. Stable isotope analysis (δ¹⁵N, δ¹³C) of 153 blood samples demonstrated reduced aquatic invertebrate consumption in invaded habitats (p < 0.001), correlating with lower chick growth rates (x̄ = 0.83 g/day vs. 1.12 g/day). Experimental vegetation removal plots (n = 16 ha) showed 127% higher Sora density within two years post-treatment compared to control areas. Our results demonstrate that cattail monocultures alter trophic pathways and constrict breeding habitat, with population-level consequences evidenced by a 22% annual decline in banded individuals at invaded sites. These findings emphasize the need for active wetland management combining invasive species control with native vegetation restoration to support Sora conservation in anthropogenically altered floodplain ecosystems.

We investigated post-fledging survival and drivers of mortality in juvenile Black-crowned Night-Herons (Nycticorax nycticorax) across six breeding colonies in the Chesapeake Bay estuary from 2019 to 2023. Using radio telemetry (n = 142 fledglings), we tracked individuals for 90 days post-fledging, integrating GPS data with weekly prey availability surveys and nest-site quality assessments. First-year survival averaged 58.3% (95% CI: 51.6–64.7%), with predation (primarily by great horned owls, Bubo virginianus) accounting for 62% of mortalities. Cox proportional hazards models revealed that survival increased with higher aquatic prey biomass (HR = 0.72 per 10 g/m² increase, p = 0.003) and nest height >4 m (HR = 0.54, p = 0.018). Juveniles from colonies with >30% urban land cover within 5 km experienced 1.8× higher mortality (p = 0.041) compared to less urbanized sites. Hydrological modeling showed survival probabilities dropped 22% during drought years (2020, 2022) when tidal creek depths fell below 15 cm, reducing access to forage fish. Genetic parentage analysis revealed 37% of surviving juveniles were from parents with ≥3 breeding seasons of experience. These results emphasize the sensitivity of juvenile night-herons to combined anthropogenic pressures, suggesting conservation strategies should prioritize maintaining wetland hydrological regimes, minimizing urban encroachment near colonies, and preserving veteran breeders through predator control programs.

We investigated the migratory connectivity and habitat selection of Swamp Sparrows (*Melospiza georgiana*) in the mid-Atlantic region using miniaturized GPS telemetry. From 2018 to 2020, we deployed 1.2-g nanotags on 48 adult individuals across three tidal marsh complexes in Delaware, Maryland, and Virginia. Movement data revealed two distinct migratory pathways: a coastal route along the Delmarva Peninsula (n = 27) and an inland corridor following the Appalachian foothills (n = 21). Median migration distance was 1,240 km (range: 890–1,580 km), with daily movement averaging 142 ± 38 km during peak migration. Resource selection functions demonstrated strong affinity for emergent wetlands with >60% vegetative cover during stopovers (β = 1.73, SE = 0.41, p < 0.001), though inland migrants increasingly used agricultural ditches in regions with >15% wetland loss since 2000. Survival analysis indicated higher mortality risk during coastal migrations (HR = 2.1, 95% CI: 1.4–3.2), potentially linked to tidal inundation of stopover sites. Our findings highlight the species' reliance on fragmented wetland ecosystems, with 62% of tracked individuals concentrating spring stopovers in just four Chesapeake Bay subestuaries. These results underscore the vulnerability of Swamp Sparrow populations to sea-level rise and marsh degradation, advocating for targeted conservation of inland migratory corridors and elevation-based marsh restoration in priority coastal zones.

We investigated the impacts of invasive common reed (Phragmites australis) expansion on Northern Harrier (Circus hudsonius) foraging ecology across 12 freshwater marshes in the Great Lakes region (Michigan and Ohio, USA) from 2018-2021. Using radio-telemetry (n=47 adults) and prey delivery surveys at 32 nests, we quantified hunting success rates (27.3% vs 41.1%), prey composition, and chick provisioning rates in invaded versus native vegetation communities. Harriers in Phragmites-dominated sites exhibited 38% lower daily hunting efficiency (p<0.001) and shifted prey selection from small mammals (62% biomass in native sites) to passerines (44% biomass) and insects (21% biomass). Nestling growth rates in invaded habitats averaged 15% slower (p=0.023), correlating with reduced protein content of alternative prey. Vegetation structure analyses revealed Phragmites stands reduced prey detection capacity through increased stem density (1,428 vs 892 stems/m²) and visual obstruction. Our results demonstrate invasive plant-mediated trophic cascades impair raptor reproductive success, with modeled population declines exceeding 22% per decade under current Phragmites expansion rates. These findings emphasize the urgency of integrating invasive species control with grassland raptor conservation strategies, particularly in critical breeding habitats along the Mississippi Flyway. Collaborative management trials with state agencies successfully enhanced harrier productivity by 17% through targeted Phragmites removal and native vegetation restoration.

We investigated habitat selection patterns of Caspian Terns (Hydroprogne caspia) across 17 breeding colonies in the Great Lakes region from 2018-2021 using GPS telemetry (n=52 adults) and nest-site characterization. Multivariate analysis revealed strong selection for islands with flat, sparsely vegetated substrates (≤12% vegetation cover) located ≤2 km from deep-water foraging areas (β=1.73, SE=0.29, p<0.001). Terns exhibited significant avoidance of sites within 500 m of human infrastructure (β=-0.94, SE=0.18, p<0.01), contrasting with historical records showing higher anthropogenic tolerance. Nest success varied substantially between colonies (34-82%), with predation rates increasing exponentially as nearest-neighbor nest distance decreased below 1.5 m (R²=0.76). Satellite tracking data showed 73% of foraging trips targeted offshore zones with surface water temperatures between 14-18°C, coinciding with peak alewife (Alosa pseudoharengus) abundance. Annual colony persistence probability declined by 22% for each meter of water level rise observed in Lake Huron (2012-2021 mean), threatening 61% of current nesting sites under projected climate scenarios. Our AIC-weighted model identified three critical thresholds for conservation: maintaining >10 ha of unvegetated nesting habitat per colony, preserving access to fish prey within 3 km, and buffer zones ≥750 m around active colonies. These findings highlight the species' narrowing ecological niche in anthropogenic landscapes and provide quantitative benchmarks for habitat management in freshwater ecosystems.

We investigated intraspecific morphological variation in Sora (Porzana carolina) across three major North American migratory corridors (Mississippi Flyway, Atlantic Flyway, Central Valley, California) using 15 morphometric measurements from 327 live-captured individuals and 214 museum specimens. Multivariate analyses revealed significant clinal variation in bill morphology, with individuals from northern latitudes (60°N) exhibiting 11.2% longer bills (mean ± SD: 24.3 ± 1.8 mm) compared to southern populations (21.8 ± 2.1 mm), potentially reflecting dietary adaptations to varying wetland plant communities. Sexual size dimorphism exceeded 5% for tarsus depth (p < 0.001) and wing chord length (p = 0.002), challenging traditional field sexing criteria. Three distinct plumage morphs were quantified using spectrophotometry (ΔE > 7.6 between groups), showing non-random distribution across hydrologic regimes - melanistic forms predominated (87%) in permanently flooded marshes, while barred morphs dominated seasonal wetlands (63%). Recapture data demonstrated seasonal mass fluctuations up to 18.7% body weight during premigratory fattening, exceeding previous estimates for Rallidae. Mantel tests revealed significant isolation-by-distance patterns (r = 0.41, p = 0.008) in morphological traits across 400-800 km intervals, suggesting limited dispersal between regional populations. These findings highlight the importance of maintaining heterogeneous wetland complexes to preserve morphological diversity in this cryptic marsh specialist, with immediate implications for harvest management and habitat restoration programs targeting specific ecotypes under climate change scenarios.

We investigated the spatial and temporal niche partitioning of Snowy Egrets (Egretta thula) within mixed-species wading bird colonies across coastal Louisiana from 2018–2021. Using GPS telemetry (n = 42 individuals) and systematic foraging observations, we quantified overlap with sympatric species including Tricolored Herons (Egretta tricolor) and White Ibises (Eudocimus albus). Snowy Egrets exhibited 68% spatial overlap in core foraging areas with competitors but demonstrated significant temporal segregation, with 72% of foraging bouts occurring during morning tidal cycles compared to 41% for Tricolored Herons (χ² = 19.3, p < 0.001). Habitat selection models revealed egrets preferentially used shallow (<15 cm) estuarine pools with 30–60% submerged aquatic vegetation cover, while avoiding areas with >1.5 cm sediment turbidity. Breeding success (2.3 ± 0.4 fledglings/nest) was positively correlated with prey density (ρ = 0.67, p = 0.02) in shared foraging zones but declined by 22% in drought years when interspecific competition intensified. DNA metabarcoding of regurgitates (n = 127 samples) showed 54% dietary overlap with Little Blue Herons (Egretta caerulea), primarily driven by Gulf killifish (Fundulus grandis) consumption. Our results highlight the importance of fine-scale temporal partitioning and habitat specialization in maintaining coexistence within wading bird assemblages. Conservation strategies should prioritize maintaining heterogeneous wetland mosaics with staggered hydroperiods to reduce competition during resource-limited periods exacerbated by climate change.

We investigated the migratory ecology of the Virginia Rail (*Rallus limicola*) across the Great Lakes region from 2018–2021 using miniaturized GPS-GSM transmitters (n = 40 adults). Birds captured at breeding sites in Michigan and Ontario exhibited two distinct migration strategies: 72.5% followed a midcontinental flyway through prairie wetlands, while 27.5% migrated along the Atlantic coast. Median autumn migration distance was 1,240 km (range: 680–1,950 km), with coastal migrants making significantly shorter stopovers (x̄ = 3.2 days) compared to inland counterparts (x̄ = 7.8 days; p < 0.01). Unexpectedly, 63% of tracked individuals overwintered in fragmented coastal saltmarshes rather than freshwater habitats, contradicting historical banding records. Spring migration initiation correlated with air temperature thresholds (>5°C sustained) and preceded breeding site arrival by 18–22 days. Kernel density analysis revealed disproportionate reliance on agricultural drainages in Illinois’ Kankakee River watershed during inland migration, areas experiencing 34% wetland loss since 1990. Our data suggest Virginia Rails exhibit greater behavioral plasticity in migration route selection than previously documented, but dependence on rapidly disappearing stopover habitats poses conservation risks. Projected shifts in precipitation patterns may exacerbate mismatches between migration timing and ephemeral wetland availability, necessitating cross-jurisdictional protection of inland corridor sites under climate change scenarios.

We investigated intraspecific morphological variation in American Coots (Fulica americana) across three major North American flyways (Pacific, Central, Mississippi) using 1,237 museum specimens collected between 1980-2015. Multivariate analysis revealed significant latitudinal clines in body size, with mean body mass increasing by 14.2% (F=32.7, p<0.001) and tarsus length by 8.9% (F=21.4, p<0.001) between 32°N and 54°N. Sexual size dimorphism was most pronounced in northern populations (Alaska/Western Canada), where males exceeded females by 18.3% in mass compared to 9.1% in southern populations (Texas/Louisiana). Culmen shape variation followed precipitation gradients, with broader bills (12.1 ± 0.7mm vs 10.8 ± 0.6mm) associated with arid western regions (R²=0.63, p=0.004). Stable isotope analysis (δ¹³C, δ¹⁵N) of wintering coots from the Chesapeake Bay and Sacramento Valley demonstrated 22% greater niche breadth in brackish-water populations, correlated with increased gizzard mass (r=0.41, p=0.02). Temporal analysis showed a 6.4% reduction in mean body size over 35 years (β=-0.18/year, p=0.03) in the Central Flyway, potentially linked to wetland habitat fragmentation. These results challenge the traditional subspecific classification and suggest climate-mediated selection pressures are driving rapid morphological adaptation in this freshwater rail species. Conservation strategies must account for ecotypic variation when managing wetland complexes supporting coot populations.

We investigated the sublethal effects of heavy metal and pesticide contamination on Common Yellowthroat (Geothlypis trichas) populations in the Hackensack Meadowlands (New Jersey, USA), a critical stopover habitat with documented polychlorinated biphenyl (PCB) and mercury contamination. From 2018-2022, we collected blood and feather samples from 143 individuals and analyzed 23 elemental contaminants using inductively coupled plasma mass spectrometry. Mercury concentrations in breast feathers (median = 1.8 µg/g dw) exceeded thresholds for impaired avian reproduction (>1.0 µg/g), while lead levels in blood (3.2 µg/dL) approached acute toxicity benchmarks. Multivariate analyses revealed significant negative correlations between cadmium burden and body condition index (R² = 0.34, p<0.001), as well as reduced clutch sizes (β = -0.21 eggs per log[DDT metabolite] increase) in returning females. Stable isotope (δ¹⁵N) data indicated bioaccumulation patterns differed between wetland-edge territories (x̄ = 8.7‰) and upland habitats (x̄ = 5.9‰, p=0.003). Demographic models projected 23% population decline over five generations under current contamination levels, primarily driven by reduced male survivorship (Φ = 0.61 vs. 0.78 in reference populations). Our findings demonstrate how legacy pollutants interact with modern stressors (e.g., neonicotinoid exposure from adjacent agricultural runoff) to constrain recovery of this declining wetland-associated songbird, advocating for sediment remediation prioritization in urban estuarine ecosystems.

We investigated intraspecific morphological variation in Sora (*Porzana carolina*) across North American wetlands to assess environmental drivers of phenotypic plasticity. From 2018–2022, we captured 312 individuals at 27 sites spanning freshwater marshes, brackish estuaries, and managed impoundments from Chesapeake Bay to Prairie Pothole regions. Standardized morphometric measurements (culmen length, tarsus depth, wing chord) and plumage reflectance spectrometry revealed clinal variation correlated with latitude and habitat type. Northern populations exhibited 6.2% larger mean body mass (p<0.001) and 4.1% longer wings (p=0.003) compared to southern cohorts, aligning with Bergmann’s Rule. Birds in alkaline wetlands (pH >8.5) showed reduced culmen curvature (r²=0.41, p=0.02) and darker ventral plumage (ΔE >3.2 CIELAB units), potentially linked to dietary shifts toward mollusks and submerged vegetation. Multivariate analysis identified three distinct morphotypes corresponding to hydrological regimes: temporary wetlands favored smaller-bodied, shorter-billed individuals, while permanent water sites selected for enhanced swimming morphology. Contrary to expectations, sexual dimorphism was minimal (overlap index >0.89), suggesting weak selection pressure on mating-related traits. These findings highlight Sora’s underappreciated adaptability to heterogeneous wetland conditions, with implications for habitat management under climate change. Targeted conservation of transitional zones supporting phenotypic diversity may buffer against habitat loss, particularly in coastal regions where brackish ecotypes face accelerated sea-level rise threats.

We investigated intraspecific morphological variation in Yellow Warblers (*Setophaga petechia*) across a 1,200 km latitudinal gradient in North America, analyzing 1,843 individuals from 32 populations between Arizona (33°N) and Alaska (65°N). Standardized measurements of wing chord (mean ± SD: 63.2 ± 1.8 mm), tail length (47.5 ± 2.1 mm), bill length (8.1 ± 0.4 mm), and body mass (9.8 ± 1.2 g) revealed significant clinal variation, with Bergmann’s rule adherence in body mass (r² = 0.72, p < 0.001) but countergradient trends in wing:tarsus ratios at higher latitudes. Multivariate analyses identified two distinct morphotypes: southern populations exhibited shorter wings and higher mass-to-wing ratios, while northern birds had elongated primaries and reduced culmen curvature. A novel finding showed urban-breeding individuals were 6.4% lighter (p = 0.003) and exhibited 2.1% shorter rectrices than rural conspecifics, suggesting anthropogenic habitat modification drives subpopulation divergence. Feather δ²H isoscapes indicated northern morphotypes completed pre-alternate molt 11 days earlier than southern birds, potentially linked to phenological adaptation. These results challenge assumptions of uniform selection pressures across the species’ range, with implications for delineating conservation units under climate change. We propose differential management strategies for riparian corridors in urban vs. boreal habitats to preserve adaptive morphological diversity in this declining Neotropical migrant.

We investigated migratory connectivity and winter habitat use in Savannah Sparrows (Passerculus sandwichensis) across their non-breeding range using stable isotope analysis of δ²H, δ¹³C, and δ¹⁵N in rectrix feathers. Feathers were sampled from 162 individuals at four wintering sites spanning the Gulf Coast (Texas to Florida) and compared to a spatially explicit isoscape of δ²H values from 23 breeding populations across North America. Bayesian mixing models revealed distinct isotopic signatures between sparrows originating from prairie grasslands (e.g., Saskatchewan δ²H: -129 ± 14‰) versus coastal meadow breeders (Nova Scotia δ²H: -72 ± 9‰). δ¹³C values (-26.5 to -22.1‰) indicated heavier reliance on C3 plants in northern wintering populations, while southern groups showed increased C4 plant resource use (ANOVA: F₃,158 = 18.7, p < 0.001). Individuals from agriculturally intensive breeding regions exhibited 15N enrichment (+4.2‰) compared to those from native grasslands, suggesting carryover effects of nitrogen fertilizer exposure. Spatial overlap analyses identified high winter site fidelity, with 68% of individuals returning to within 50 km of initial capture locations across years. These findings highlight vulnerability of grassland-associated populations to habitat loss, particularly along the Texas Coastal Bend where 42% of wintering sparrows originated from threatened Canadian mixed-grass prairie ecosystems. Results underscore the need for integrated cross-border conservation strategies addressing both breeding ground agricultural practices and wintering habitat fragmentation.

We investigated stopover ecology of Herring Gulls (Larus argentatus) during autumn migration (2018–2020) across a 1,200-km coastal corridor from Massachusetts to Virginia, USA, using GPS-GSM telemetry and field surveys. Sixty-eight adults captured at breeding colonies were tracked, revealing 83% exhibited ≥1 prolonged stopover (mean duration 6.2 ± 1.8 days) between breeding and wintering areas. Stopover frequency increased significantly south of Delaware Bay (χ² = 14.7, p < 0.001), with 72% of individuals congregating at three primary sites: Cape May, NJ; Chesapeake Bay, MD; and Pamlico Sound, NC. Resource selection functions showed strong preference for marine fishery waste sites (β = 2.1, SE = 0.4) and active harbors (β = 1.6, SE = 0.3) over natural intertidal zones. Birds utilizing anthropogenic food sources gained mass 34% faster (Δmass/day = 4.1 g vs. 3.1 g, t = 3.89, p = 0.002) but exhibited 22% shorter daily foraging flights (kernel utilization distribution 50% area: 1.8 km² vs. 2.3 km²). Plasma metabolite analysis revealed elevated triglyceride levels in gulls at stopovers near landfills compared to coastal sites (F₁,₄₃ = 8.2, p = 0.006), indicating enhanced fat deposition capacity. These findings demonstrate Herring Gulls’ behavioral plasticity in exploiting human-modified landscapes during migration, with critical implications for managing gull population dynamics and mitigating conflicts at waste management facilities along the Atlantic Flyway.

We investigated the effects of legacy pollutants on Marsh Wren (Cistothorus palustris) populations in the Chesapeake Bay estuary, comparing contaminated tidal marshes near industrial sites (n=12) with reference wetlands (n=8). Feather and blood samples from 136 adults and nestlings were analyzed for heavy metals (Pb, Hg, Cd) and organochlorine pesticides using ICP-MS and GC-ECD. Birds in contaminated sites showed significantly higher Pb concentrations (adults: 4.7±1.2 ppm vs 1.3±0.4 ppm; p<0.001) and ΣDDT residues (23.5±6.8 ng/g vs 5.1±2.3 ng/g; p=0.003), with nestlings exhibiting 38% lower plasma protein concentrations (F=9.24, p=0.008). Nest monitoring revealed 22% lower clutch sizes (4.1±0.6 vs 5.2±0.7 eggs; t=3.89, p=0.002) and 41% reduced fledging success in contaminated areas. Stable isotope analysis (δ¹⁵N, δ¹³C) indicated trophic shifts in polluted marshes, with wrens consuming more invasive red-jointed fiddler crabs (Uca minax) versus preferred amphipod prey. Multivariate regression identified sediment PCB concentrations (β=-0.47, p=0.01) and nest height relative to mean high water (β=0.32, p=0.04) as primary predictors of nest abandonment. Our results demonstrate synergistic impacts of historical contamination and sea-level rise on this specialist saltmarsh passerine, emphasizing the need for integrated sediment remediation and adaptive marsh management to maintain viable breeding populations in anthropogenically altered estuaries.

We investigated population dynamics of Ring-necked Pheasants (*Phasianus colchicus*) in Nebraska’s Rainwater Basin from 2017–2022 to assess drivers of regional declines reported since 2005. Using mark-recapture (n = 1,243 banded individuals) and radio-telemetry (n = 87 hens), we quantified survival rates, nest success (May–July), and habitat selection across 12,500 ha of working agricultural landscapes. Annual adult survival averaged 0.62 ± 0.08 SE, with vehicle collisions and mammalian predation accounting for 68% of mortalities. Nest success declined from 42% to 28% during the study period, correlating with reduced grassland cover (-17%) and increased predator activity indices (+39%). Chick survival to 30 days post-hatch varied significantly with early-summer precipitation (β = 0.21, p = 0.03), likely mediating insect prey availability. Spatial analysis revealed pheasants preferentially selected winter wheat–fallow mosaics (selection ratio = 3.1) over continuous corn/soybean systems. Population matrix models indicated λ = 0.91 ± 0.04, with sensitivity analyses identifying chick survival as the most influential vital rate (elasticity = 0.43). Comparison with hunter harvest data (n = 6,287 wings) showed disproportionate declines in second-year recruits, suggesting recruitment bottlenecks. Our results highlight the interacting effects of habitat simplification and climate variability on pheasant demographics, supporting targeted CRP enrollment in riparian corridors and delayed crop residue removal as conservation measures. This study provides mechanistic insights into grassland-obligate population responses to intensive agriculture, with implications for adaptive harvest management in the Great Plains.

We investigated the interspecific interactions and habitat partitioning of the Least Bittern (Ixobrychus exilis) across 34 freshwater marshes in the Great Lakes region from 2018–2020. Using a combination of autonomous recording units (n = 112), vegetation surveys, and nest monitoring (127 nests), we quantified spatial overlap with six sympatric marsh bird species and evaluated nest survival through mixed-effects models. Least Bitterns exhibited strong vertical stratification, selecting tall, dense stands of Typha spp. (mean stem height = 2.3 ± 0.4 m) at significantly higher frequencies (χ² = 18.7, p < 0.001) than competing American Coots (Fulica americana) and Pied-billed Grebes (Podilymbus podiceps), which dominated shorter-emergent vegetation zones. Nest survival declined by 22% for every 10 cm decrease in water depth (β = 0.078, 95% CI: 0.032–0.124), with higher predation rates in marshes shared with invasive Muskrats (Ondatra zibethicus; R² = 0.41). Multispecies occupancy models revealed negative associations with Great Blue Herons (Ardea herodias; ψ = −0.37 ± 0.11) but positive correlations with Sora (Porzana carolina; ψ = 0.28 ± 0.09), suggesting facilitative relationships in prey-rich habitats. Our findings highlight the importance of maintaining vegetation heterogeneity and water-level stability in wetlands facing climate-induced hydroperiod shifts. Targeted removal of invasive predators and creation of deep-water refugia could enhance reproductive success for this IUCN Near Threatened species amid increasing marsh fragmentation.

We investigated the bioacoustic ecology of Sora (Porzana carolina) in the Prairie Pothole Region of North Dakota, USA, to assess vocalization patterns and their relationship to breeding behavior and habitat use. Using autonomous recording units (ARUs) deployed across 12 managed wetland complexes (May–August 2020–2022), we collected 1,200 hours of audio data. Spectrographic analysis identified three distinct call types: advertising "whinny" sequences (dominant frequency: 2.1–3.4 kHz), alarm "keek" notes (4.7–5.8 kHz), and courtship trills. Vocal activity peaked during crepuscular hours (χ² = 34.7, p < 0.001), with 78% of whinny calls occurring within 90 minutes of dawn. Male vocalization rates correlated positively with wetland vegetation density (R² = 0.63, p = 0.008), while female response calls increased with proximity to nesting sites (Mantel test: r = 0.41, p = 0.03). We documented significant intra-seasonal variation, with call complexity declining by 22% during late incubation phases. Playback experiments revealed territorial males exhibited shorter latency times (14.3 ± 3.2 s) to synthetic calls than non-territorial individuals (27.6 ± 6.8 s; t-test: p = 0.004). Our findings suggest hydrological management practices altering water depth thresholds >15 cm disproportionately reduce effective communication distances for low-frequency whinny calls. This study establishes baseline metrics for monitoring Sora populations under climate change scenarios projected to fragment 40% of Prairie Pothole wetlands by 2050, emphasizing the need for bioacoustic indices in marsh bird conservation planning.

We investigated the vocal repertoire and environmental drivers of Pied-billed Grebe (Podilymbus podiceps) acoustic behavior across 12 freshwater wetlands in the upper Midwest, USA, using passive acoustic monitoring during three breeding seasons (2020–2022). Automated recorders collected 4,200 hours of audio, with 18,542 vocalizations analyzed through multivariate spectrogram classification. Males exhibited three context-specific call types: advertising "kowp" calls (87% of detections, mean frequency 1.23 ± 0.15 kHz), aggressive "growl" displays during territory defense (9%), and soft "whinny" duets during pair bonding (4%). Vocal activity peaked 32 minutes post-sunrise (β = 0.78, SE = 0.12, p < 0.001) and showed negative correlation with wind speeds >12 km/h (r = -0.67). Generalized linear mixed models revealed call rates increased 41% during new moon phases compared to full moons (z = 3.92, p < 0.001), potentially mitigating acoustic competition with nocturnal chorusing amphibians. Counterintuitively, territories with higher anthropogenic noise pollution (≥65 dB) showed 28% reduced call complexity (F₂,₉₈ = 5.12, p = 0.008), measured by entropy in 500 Hz bandwidths. These findings demonstrate grebes' acoustic plasticity in dynamic soundscapes while highlighting vulnerability to sensory interference. Our bioacoustic baseline enables non-invasive monitoring of this elusive species, particularly relevant as climate-driven shifts in wetland hydroperiods alter breeding chronologies across their Nearctic range.

We investigated geographic variation in male Marsh Wren (Cistothorus palustris) song structure across 15 tidal marshes along the Mid-Atlantic coast (Chesapeake Bay, USA) and adjacent inland freshwater wetlands (n = 200 males recorded, 2018–2021). Using multivariate analyses of 4,325 song bouts, we quantified regional differences in syllable diversity (Shannon index: H' = 2.1–3.8), trill rates (4.2–6.7 Hz), and frequency modulation (±1.2–3.5 kHz). Coastal populations exhibited significantly higher syllable repertoire sizes (x̄ = 43.7 ± 5.2 vs. 28.1 ± 4.8 in freshwater habitats; PERMANOVA, p < 0.001) and faster trill rates (5.9 vs. 4.8 Hz; p = 0.003), with distinct "coastal" and "inland" dialect clusters identified through NMDS ordination (stress = 0.14). Playback experiments revealed 73% stronger territorial response (n = 40 trials) to local vs. foreign dialects (Wilcoxon signed-rank test, V = 315, p = 0.008), suggesting cultural transmission drives regional divergence. Comparative analysis of historical recordings (1980–2020) from three sites showed a 14% decline in syllable diversity (GLM, β = -0.09 ± 0.03, p = 0.02) concurrent with marsh fragmentation (R² = 0.67). These results demonstrate that tidal marsh specialists maintain complex vocal traditions vulnerable to habitat degradation, with implications for using bioacoustic monitoring to assess coastal ecosystem health under rising sea levels (SLR = 4.9 mm/yr). Conservation strategies should prioritize connectivity of marsh networks exceeding 50 ha to preserve cultural diversity in this acoustically specialized wetland passerine.

We investigated the foraging ecology and migratory connectivity of Northern Gannets (Morus bassanus) using high-resolution GPS-Argos telemetry across three breeding colonies in the North Atlantic (Grand Manan Island, Canada; Grassholm, UK; and Hornøya, Norway). From 2018–2021, 68 adult birds were equipped with solar-powered transmitters, yielding 4,217 tracking days. Kernel density analyses revealed striking intercolony differences in core foraging ranges (50% UD: Grand Manan = 12,300 km² vs. Hornøya = 6,800 km²), with Norwegian birds exhibiting tighter clustering near coastal herring spawning grounds. Dive kinetics showed latitudinal gradients in maximum plunge depth (Grand Manan: 14.3 ± 2.1 m vs. Hornøya: 9.8 ± 1.6 m) correlated with regional differences in prey composition (ANOVA: F₂,₆₅ = 18.9, p < 0.001). Migration pathways revealed 92% of Canadian breeders overwintered in Gulf of Mexico habitats, while European populations showed fidelity to West African waters. Critical stopover sites were identified at oceanic frontal zones along the Mid-Atlantic Ridge, where birds spent 22% of migration periods fattening. Multivariate models indicated sea surface temperature anomalies >1°C reduced provisioning rates by 34% during chick-rearing. Our findings highlight climate-driven prey shifts as a greater threat to North American populations, while European colonies face emerging risks from offshore wind development in feeding hotspots. This pan-Atlantic analysis provides vital baselines for marine spatial planning under the EU Marine Strategy Framework Directive and North American Coastal Bird Joint Ventures.

We investigated the effects of anthropogenic disturbance on Peregrine Falcon (Falco peregrinus) breeding success across 23 nesting territories in coastal California (2018–2022). Using GPS-tracked human activity patterns and continuous nest monitoring, we quantified disturbance thresholds through generalized linear mixed-effects models. Nesting cliffs within 500 m of high-use recreational trails (≥15 visitors/hr) showed 38% lower fledging success (0.62 ± 0.14 fledglings/clutch) compared to low-disturbance sites (0.89 ± 0.11 fledglings/clutch; p < 0.01). Adult falcons exhibited prolonged hunting absences (42% increase in foraging trip duration) when drones or climbers approached within 300 m during incubation. Notably, urban-nesting pairs on skyscrapers demonstrated behavioral plasticity, with 72% shorter response distances to pedestrians (15 m vs. 53 m at natural cliffs) and earlier fledging dates (χ² = 8.3, p = 0.04). However, nestling body condition indices revealed urban juveniles had 12% lower mass-wing chord ratios than rural counterparts (t-test: t = 3.1, p = 0.002), potentially linked to prey shifts from avian to invertebrate biomass. Our findings advocate for seasonal buffer zones (400 m radius) around natural cliff nests and highlight the need to regulate emerging stressors like drone photography near urban eyries. These results emphasize context-dependent conservation strategies for this recovered raptor amid increasing human-wildlife interface pressures.

We investigated the impacts of coastal marsh fragmentation on Virginia Rail (*Rallus limicola*) populations across 23 tidal marshes in the Chesapeake Bay watershed from 2015 to 2022. Using a combination of autonomous recording units (n = 147), nest monitoring, and habitat metrics derived from LIDAR and drone surveys, we assessed relationships between habitat configuration, breeding density, and fledging success. Marshes with >30% edge habitat exhibited 72% lower rail occupancy (β = -1.21, SE = 0.38, p < 0.001) and 54% reduced chick survival compared to contiguous marsh complexes. Sediment accretion rates below 3.8 mm/yr correlated with abandonment of historical nesting sites (R² = 0.67), while invasive *Phragmites australis* cover exceeding 15% reduced invertebrate prey biomass by 41% (t-test, p = 0.013). Counter to expectations, tidal restoration projects increased nest flooding events during storm surges (incidence rate ratio = 2.7, 95% CI: 1.9–3.8). Our multi-state occupancy model revealed a 42% regional population decline since 2009, with dispersal barriers creating genetically isolated subpopulations (FST = 0.12–0.18). These findings challenge assumptions that salt marsh management focusing solely on hydrology can sustain rail populations, emphasizing the need for integrated strategies addressing sediment dynamics, invasive species, and connectivity in coastal resilience planning.

We investigated molt migration patterns in Great Blue Herons (*Ardea herodias*) across three breeding colonies in the Laurentian Great Lakes region (Michigan, USA; Ontario, Canada) from 2018–2021 using GPS-GSM transmitters (n = 47 adults). Individuals exhibited a bimodal migratory strategy, with 68% (n = 32) undertaking post-breeding migrations >800 km to coastal molting sites in the Chesapeake Bay and Santee Delta, while 32% (n = 15) remained near breeding areas. Molt migrants departed earlier (mean ± SD: 23 July ± 4.2 days) than non-migrants (15 August ± 6.7 days), with migration duration averaging 11.3 ± 2.1 days. Stable isotope analysis (δ²H, δ¹³C) of rectrices confirmed distinct molt site fidelity, with 92% of migrants returning to the same estuary annually. Molting sites showed significantly higher aquatic prey biomass (ANOVA, F = 9.45, p < 0.01) compared to breeding wetlands, suggesting resource-driven movements. However, 41% of tracked herons exhibited elevated mercury concentrations (>5 ppm) in molted feathers from industrialized estuaries, posing potential physiological trade-offs. These findings reveal cryptic connectivity between inland breeding populations and coastal ecosystems, emphasizing the need for cross-jurisdictional habitat protection. Our results challenge assumptions of post-breeding site fidelity in Ardeids and highlight vulnerabilities in critical molt staging areas facing sea-level rise and contaminant accumulation.

We investigated the migratory connectivity and stopover ecology of the Sedge Wren (Cistothorus platensis) across its North American range using a combination of light-level geolocators (n = 78) and automated radio telemetry (n = 142) deployed at six breeding sites from Manitoba to New York (2018–2022). Bayesian state-space models revealed two distinct migration corridors: western populations (Alberta to Minnesota) exhibited 62% longer migration distances (x̄ = 3,450 km, SD = 287) than eastern populations (x̄ = 2,130 km, SD = 156), with all birds wintering in Gulf Coast marshes. Stopover duration averaged 18.3 days (95% CI: 14.7–22.1) but increased by 37% at fragmented grassland sites compared to contiguous habitats (p = 0.012). Mantel tests demonstrated weak migratory connectivity (r = 0.19, p = 0.38), with breeding site fidelity uncorrelated to wintering locations. Intraspecific variation in departure timing was strongly influenced by local breeding phenology (R² = 0.71), with northern populations departing 11 days earlier than southern counterparts. Survival analysis indicated 22% higher mortality risk during autumn migration compared to spring (HR = 1.22, p = 0.03), particularly in agricultural landscapes with reduced wetland availability. Our results highlight the importance of conserving high-quality stopover habitats in the Midwest U.S., where 83% of tracked individuals staged for >14 days. These findings challenge assumptions about obligate wetland dependency in this species and suggest grassland restoration programs should prioritize structural vegetation diversity to support declining Sedge Wren populations.

We investigated the effects of accelerating coastal habitat loss on the demography and movement ecology of Savannah Sparrows (Passerculus sandwichensis) across 12 salt marsh complexes in the Gulf of Maine and Chesapeake Bay from 2015–2022. Using GPS tracking (n = 147 individuals), vegetation surveys, and hierarchical Bayesian population models, we quantified relationships between marsh fragmentation metrics and reproductive success, adult survival, and dispersal distances. Sparrows in marshes with >30% tidal creek erosion showed 42% lower nest success (95% CI: 34–51%) compared to intact sites, driven by increased nest flooding and mammalian predation. Adults in degraded habitats exhibited 18% longer dispersal distances (x̄ = 2.7 ± 0.4 km vs. 2.3 ± 0.3 km) and 22% lower annual survival probabilities (φ = 0.51 ± 0.07 vs. 0.65 ± 0.05). Spatial capture-recapture models revealed density declines of 6.8%/year in eroding marshes versus stable populations (<1% decline/year) in protected areas with sediment replenishment projects. Our isotope analysis (δ²H, δ¹³C) demonstrated reduced dietary diversity in fragmented habitats, with arthropod consumption decreasing by 37% in highly eroded sites. These findings highlight the cascading impacts of sea-level rise and anthropogenic hardening of shorelines on a marsh-obligate passerine, emphasizing the need for managed retreat strategies and prioritization of sediment-rich marshes for conservation. The study establishes quantitative thresholds (<15% intertidal vegetation loss, >200 m marsh width) for maintaining viable Savannah Sparrow populations in northeastern North American coastal ecosystems.

We investigated the vocal activity patterns and acoustic variability of Clapper Rails (*Rallus crepitans*) across six Atlantic coastal marsh complexes in Maryland, Virginia, and North Carolina to assess how anthropogenic noise and habitat fragmentation influence their communication. Using autonomous recording units (n = 48), we captured 2,340 call sequences from 132 individuals during the 2022 breeding season. Spectro-temporal features of signature "kek-burr" calls were quantified via dynamic time warping and principal component analysis. Generalized linear mixed models revealed that rail populations in high-traffic zones (≥50 dB background noise) exhibited calls with 15% higher minimum frequencies (p = 0.003) and 22% reduced duration (p = 0.018) compared to those in undisturbed sites. Additionally, fragmented marshes (<50% continuous vegetation cover) showed lower call rates (1.2 ± 0.3 calls/min vs. 2.7 ± 0.5 calls/min; p = 0.009) and reduced individual vocal distinctiveness (MANOVA, F = 6.24, p < 0.001). Satellite telemetry data from 12 tagged birds indicated avoidance of noisy areas during peak vocalization periods. These findings suggest that Clapper Rails adjust vocal behavior to mitigate masking effects, but at potential costs to mate attraction and territory defense. Conservation strategies for this IUCN Near Threatened species should prioritize reducing anthropogenic noise in critical marsh habitats and restoring vegetative connectivity to support acoustic communication.

We investigated the community ecology of Northern Harriers (Circus hudsonius) in the Prairie Pothole Region of North Dakota, USA, from 2016 to 2020, to assess habitat selection, interspecific interactions, and prey dynamics across a gradient of grassland restoration efforts. Using GPS telemetry (n = 32 individuals) and systematic prey surveys, we quantified spatial overlap with sympatric raptors and analyzed microhabitat variables influencing nesting success. Harriers exhibited strong selection for mixed-height prairie vegetation (25–50 cm), avoiding areas dominated by invasive smooth brome (Bromus inermis). Breeding density correlated positively with cyclic vole (Microtus spp.) abundance (r = 0.73, p < 0.01), but negatively with proximity to Red-tailed Hawk (Buteo jamaicensis) nests (β = -0.41 ± 0.12 SE). Resource partitioning occurred temporally, with harriers hunting predominantly at dawn/dusk, while Cooper’s Hawks (Accipiter cooperii) occupied midday periods. Nest survival rates (65%) were highest in parcels with >30% native grass cover, though 18% of failures were attributed to mammalian predation linked to reduced vegetative structure. Our generalized additive models revealed non-linear responses to precipitation gradients, with optimal harrier productivity at 450–550 mm annual rainfall. These findings underscore the importance of maintaining heterogeneous grassland mosaics and controlling invasive grasses to mitigate interspecific competition and climate-mediated prey fluctuations. Conservation strategies prioritizing contiguous native prairie with staggered mowing regimes could enhance resilience of harrier populations amid increasing land-use intensification.

We investigated stopover site selection and duration in migratory American Kestrels (Falco sparverius) across the agricultural landscapes of the Great Lakes region from 2018 to 2022 using GPS telemetry (n = 48 individuals). Birds exhibited mean stopover durations of 2.3 ± 0.7 days during autumn migration, with 68% of individuals reusing sites across multiple years. Resource selection functions revealed strong avoidance of developed areas (β = -1.24, SE = 0.31) and preference for fallow fields (β = 0.87, SE = 0.19) and grasslands adjacent to riparian corridors (β = 0.62, SE = 0.15). Stopover sites with higher small mammal abundance (r² = 0.41, p < 0.001) and lower nocturnal light pollution levels (r² = 0.28, p = 0.003) correlated with shorter refueling periods. Notably, 72% of high-use stopover locations occurred on privately owned lands with no formal conservation status. Our results highlight the critical role of ephemeral agricultural habitats in sustaining migratory raptor populations and suggest current protected area networks inadequately cover key stopover resources. Targeted conservation initiatives promoting heterogeneous farmland mosaics and reducing sensory disturbance could enhance migratory success for this declining species.

We conducted a 2-year telemetry study on male Common Yellowthroats (Geothlypis trichas) in restored prairie wetlands of central Illinois to quantify post-breeding movement ecology and habitat selection. Using miniature radio-transmitters (0.35g nanotags), we tracked 42 adult males from July to September 2021–2022, collecting 1,872 location points across 12 study sites. Kernel density estimation revealed a mean post-breeding home range of 8.7 ± 2.1 ha (95% CI), with individuals preferentially selecting dense sedge meadows (Bhattacharyya's affinity index = 0.81) over adjacent upland grasslands. Dispersal distances from breeding territories to molting locations averaged 1.3 km (± 0.4 km SD), with 22% of individuals moving >2 km to isolated wetland patches. Movement rates peaked during early morning (05:00–08:00 CST), coinciding with insect emergence events. Multivariate analysis showed vegetation structure (β = 0.67, p < 0.001) and water depth (β = -0.23, p = 0.03) as primary predictors of space use, while proximity to woodland edges had no significant effect. Unexpectedly, 14% of tagged individuals exhibited brief (<48 hr) incursions into adjacent agricultural fields during drought periods, suggesting facultative use of suboptimal habitats. These findings challenge assumptions about strict habitat fidelity in this declining Neotropical migrant, highlighting the need for landscape-scale conservation strategies that maintain connectivity between core wetlands and satellite habitat patches within 3 km radii. Our results demonstrate how fine-scale telemetry data can inform targeted management of matrix habitats in fragmented agroecosystems.

We investigated sex-specific parental care strategies in Snowy Egrets (Egretta thula) across three breeding colonies in the coastal wetlands of South Carolina (32°45'N, 79°52'W) during the 2019-2021 nesting seasons. Using a combination of GPS telemetry (n = 32 adults), 350 hours of nest camera recordings, and biweekly chick growth measurements (n = 42 nests), we quantified provisioning rates and division of parental responsibilities. Males contributed 63.2 ± 8.4% of total food deliveries during the critical 10-20 day nestling period (z = 3.12, p = 0.002), though females exhibited significantly longer brooding durations (χ² = 18.7, df = 4, p < 0.001). Logistic regression models revealed tidal cycle timing explained 41% of variance in foraging bout frequency (R² = 0.41, F = 9.87, p < 0.001), with males preferentially foraging during receding tides. Nutritional analysis of 127 regurgitated prey items showed male-delivered prey averaged 23% higher energy content (kcal/g) than female-provisioned items (t = 2.89, df = 125, p = 0.005). Chick survival to fledging correlated strongly with male provisioning rates (r = 0.72, p < 0.001) but not female effort, suggesting potential sex-specific fitness consequences. These results highlight specialized parental roles in Ardeidae species and emphasize the importance of maintaining tidal creek connectivity for this species of conservation concern, particularly given increasing anthropogenic modifications to southeastern US estuarine systems.

We investigated population dynamics of the Clapper Rail (*Rallus crepitans*) in Chesapeake Bay tidal marshes from 2010–2022 using mark-recapture, radio-telemetry, and habitat surveys. Annual survival rates averaged 62% (95% CI: 58–66%) for adults and 34% (95% CI: 28–40%) for juveniles, with stochastic tidal flooding causing 41% of monitored nest failures. Bayesian state-space models revealed a 35% population decline (λ = 0.965, SD ± 0.012) linked to marsh loss (18% habitat reduction since 2000) and invasive red fox (*Vulpes vulpes*) predation, which accounted for 29% of adult mortality. Density-dependent responses were observed in breeding pairs/km² (R² = 0.78, p < 0.001) relative to *Spartina alterniflora* cover thresholds. Multispectral imagery analysis showed that sea-level rise displaced 14% of tagged individuals from low-elevation marshes, with remaining clusters exhibiting reduced body condition (mean mass loss = 8.2g, p = 0.03). Conservation simulations indicate that managed marsh migration corridors and targeted predator control could stabilize populations below a critical threshold of 400 ha of contiguous habitat. These findings underscore the vulnerability of saltmarsh-obligate rails to synergistic anthropogenic pressures, necessitating adaptive management strategies for this IUCN Near Threatened species.

We investigated the impacts of coastal habitat loss on Tricolored Heron (Egretta tricolor) populations across the northern Gulf of Mexico from 2018 to 2022. Using a combination of GPS telemetry (n = 47 individuals), satellite-based land cover analysis, and historical nesting surveys, we quantified relationships between mangrove degradation, submerged aquatic vegetation decline, and heron reproductive success. Habitat loss averaged 32% (± 6.2 SE) in core nesting areas, with Terrebonne Bay, Louisiana, experiencing the most severe reductions (47%). Herons in degraded habitats showed 45% smaller home ranges (p < 0.01), 18% lower foraging efficiency (p = 0.03), and 24% reduced fledging success compared to populations in intact wetlands. Multivariate models revealed that every 10% decrease in preferred nesting habitat correlated with a 7.2% population decline (R² = 0.78, p < 0.001). Survival rates tracked via resightings (n = 1,203 observations) were 67% in fragmented habitats versus 82% in contiguous marsh systems. Our analysis identified hydrological alteration from navigation channels as the primary driver of habitat fragmentation, responsible for 63% of vegetation loss in critical heron colonies. These results underscore the species' vulnerability to coastal squeeze exacerbated by sea-level rise and human infrastructure. We propose targeted restoration of tidal flow regimes and 500-meter protective buffers around known nesting platforms as critical conservation measures for this IUCN Near Threatened species.

We investigated population genomic structure and genetic diversity of Northern Pintail (*Anas acuta*) across continental scales to assess vulnerability to habitat loss and climate change. Using 12,389 SNP markers from 346 individuals sampled at 22 migratory stopover and breeding sites in North America (Alaska to California), Europe (Netherlands, Sweden), and East Asia (Japan, China), we identified three distinct genetic clusters (FST = 0.032-0.057) corresponding to major flyways. Effective population sizes (Ne) ranged from 382 (95% CI: 297-512) in the Pacific Americas Flyway to 1,204 (95% CI: 891-1,654) in the East Asian-Australasian Flyway. Migration rates estimated through Bayesian coalescent simulations revealed asymmetrical gene flow, with 14% annual emigration from drought-impacted Prairie Pothole Region populations to coastal habitats. Heterozygosity (HE = 0.21 ± 0.03) and allelic richness (AR = 1.82 ± 0.12) showed significant declines in populations with >50% wetland conversion since 1980 (Mantel test: r = 0.47, p = 0.008). Mitochondrial haplotype network analysis revealed three deeply divergent clades (π = 0.0017), suggesting historical refugia during Last Glacial Maximum. Our results highlight urgent needs for hemisphere-scale habitat protection in key genetic diversity hotspots like the Yukon-Kuskokwim Delta and Huanghe River floodplain, alongside adaptive management to maintain connectivity between genetically distinct subpopulations under shifting precipitation regimes.

We investigated the impacts of climate-driven hydrological shifts on Horned Grebe (*Podiceps auritus*) breeding success across 22 boreal wetland complexes in Alberta, Canada, from 2003–2023. Using standardized nest surveys, hydrological modeling, and Bayesian survival analysis, we demonstrate a 41% decline in fledging rates (95% CI: 34–48%) coinciding with a 1.7°C mean temperature increase during critical pre-laying periods. Early ice breakup (≥14 days before historical medians) reduced nest initiation synchrony by 63% (R² = 0.82, p<0.001), exposing chicks to higher predation rates during asynchronous peaks in mink (*Neogale vison*) activity. Extreme rainfall events (>30 mm/day) during incubation increased egg abandonment probability by 8.7-fold (OR = 8.69, 95% CI: 4.12–18.34) compared to historical norms. Counterintuitively, wetland area expanded by 19% due to increased precipitation, but emergent vegetation crucial for nest concealment declined by 28% (F₁,₂₀ = 24.7, p<0.001) under warmer water temperatures. Demographic models project a 72% probability of local extirpation for southern subpopulations by 2040 under RCP 6.0 scenarios. Our findings challenge assumptions that waterfowl broadly benefit from wetland expansion, highlighting how thermal mismatches between abiotic habitat availability and biotic requirements threaten specialized species. Conservation strategies must prioritize microhabitat restoration of *Carex* spp. zones and artificial predator exclusion grids to buffer climate-driven trophic disruptions.

We investigated the impacts of invasive European Starlings (Sturnus vulgaris) on American Kestrel (Falco sparverius) nesting ecology across 12 grassland-forest mosaics in Ohio's agricultural landscapes (2018–2022). Using 238 nest box installations monitored weekly during breeding seasons, we quantified competitive interactions through occupancy rates, clutch survival, and prey delivery rates. Kestrel nest occupancy declined by 32% in boxes ≤500 m from active starling nests (GLMM: β = -1.41 ± 0.23 SE, p < 0.001), with starlings physically excluding kestrels from 18% of monitored cavities. Nest cameras revealed starling aggression reduced kestrel prey delivery rates by 41% (Mann-Whitney U = 102, p = 0.008) in shared habitats, disproportionately affecting orthopteran consumption critical for nestling development. Stable isotope analysis (δ¹⁵N, δ¹³C) of fledgling feathers showed 17% lower trophic position in kestrels from starling-impacted territories (ANOVA: F₁,₈₇ = 5.92, p = 0.017), suggesting competition-induced dietary shifts. Unexpectedly, kestrels nesting near starlings exhibited 22% higher blood mercury concentrations (2.1 ± 0.4 ppm vs. 1.7 ± 0.3 ppm), potentially through altered prey selection in contaminated agricultural drainage ditches. Our results demonstrate cascading effects of invasive species on raptor reproductive success and contaminant exposure, supporting targeted nest box designs (23 mm entrance diameter) to exclude starlings while maintaining kestrel accessibility.

We investigated stopover ecology of Sora (Porzana carolina) during autumn migration (2018–2022) across 23 emergent wetlands in the Upper Mississippi River floodplain, USA. Using radio telemetry (n = 127 individuals) and habitat sampling, we quantified stopover duration, site fidelity, and habitat selection relative to vegetation structure, water depth, and invertebrate biomass. Stopover duration averaged 5.2 ± 1.8 days (range: 1–14 days), with 34% of individuals exhibiting multi-day site fidelity (>48 hr occupancy). Generalized linear mixed models revealed strong selection for wetlands with vegetation stem densities >380 stems/m² (β = 2.14, SE = 0.41, p < 0.001) and water depths between 10–25 cm (β = 1.87, SE = 0.33, p < 0.001), avoiding areas with invasive hybrid cattail (Typha × glauca). Invertebrate biomass at used sites (mean = 3.2 ± 0.9 g/m²) exceeded unused sites by 68% (t = 4.11, p = 0.002). Spatial analysis identified 78% of high-use stopover habitats occurring outside protected areas, with 62% subject to agricultural drainage threats. Our results demonstrate that Sora require heterogeneous wetland mosaics with dense emergent vegetation and shallow inundation, contrasting with deeper-water preferences of sympatric rails. These findings highlight the vulnerability of secretive marsh birds to hydrological modification and support targeted restoration of seasonal wetlands through Farm Bill conservation programs.

We investigated Virginia Rail (*Rallus limicola*) population dynamics across a 12-year dataset (2010–2022) from 34 managed wetlands in the Upper Mississippi River floodplain. Using nocturnal call surveys, mark-recapture, and radio telemetry, we assessed breeding density, survival rates, and dispersal patterns in response to hydrologic variability and invasive plant encroachment (*Phalaris arundinacea*). Occupancy modeling revealed a 22% decline in breeding pairs (95% CI: 18–27%) in sites with >40% invasive cover, contrasting with stable populations in native sedge-dominated wetlands. Survival rates (mean Φ = 0.68 ± 0.09 SE) showed strong seasonal sensitivity to early spring flooding events, with 31% mortality during extreme precipitation years (2013, 2019). Displacement distances from natal sites averaged 2.3 km (±1.1 km), but 18% of juveniles dispersed >10 km to colonize restored wetlands. Hierarchical Bayesian models identified water depth variability (CV = 0.35) as the primary driver of reproductive success (β = −1.4, 89% HDI overlap zero), challenging assumptions of flood-tolerant adaptation. Our results highlight vulnerability to precipitation regime shifts under climate change scenarios (RCP 8.5) and advocate for staggered drawdown schedules in managed impoundments. The study provides the first evidence of Allee effects in rail populations below 0.5 pairs/ha, with implications for wetland conservation prioritization in midcontinental migratory corridors.

We investigated trophic niche plasticity in Snowy Egrets (Egretta thula) across coastal gradients in the northern Gulf of Mexico using stable isotope analysis (δ¹³C, δ¹⁵N, δ³⁴S) of primary feathers collected from 127 individuals at 12 breeding colonies between Texas and Florida. Isotopic mixing models revealed significant spatial partitioning in dietary sources, with egrets from Louisiana barrier islands (δ¹³C: -18.3 ± 1.2‰, δ¹⁵N: 12.1 ± 0.8‰) demonstrating greater marine prey reliance compared to Texas coastal prairie populations (δ¹³C: -22.7 ± 1.5‰, δ¹⁵N: 9.4 ± 1.1‰), reflecting differential use of estuarine versus freshwater foraging habitats. Seasonal isotopic shifts (Δδ¹⁵N = 2.3‰) in recaptured individuals indicated prey switching from fish to crustaceans during fall migration. Bayesian ellipsoid analysis showed 34% niche overlap between regions, with Louisiana birds exhibiting 28% broader isotopic niches—a potential adaptation to fragmented marsh habitats. These findings contrast with previous isotopic studies of sympatric herons, suggesting Snowy Egrets’ unique position as dietary generalists in dynamic coastal ecosystems. Population-level isotopic variability correlated strongly with wetland loss rates (R² = 0.71, p < 0.01), highlighting vulnerability to sea-level rise and oil spill impacts. Our results demonstrate how stable isotope ecology can inform habitat connectivity planning for wading birds in anthropogenically altered coastlines, emphasizing the need for watershed-specific conservation strategies to maintain prey resource diversity.

We investigated the cumulative effects of agricultural pesticide and heavy metal contamination on Ring-necked Pheasant (Phasianus colchicus) populations in intensively farmed landscapes of Iowa, USA, from 2018 to 2021. Using liquid chromatography-mass spectrometry and atomic absorption spectroscopy, we analyzed 137 liver tissue samples and 246 egg contents for 32 contaminants, including neonicotinoids, organophosphates, and trace metals. Pheasants exhibited significantly higher hepatic cadmium concentrations (mean 4.7 ± 1.2 μg/g) compared to reference populations in conservation reserve program lands (1.1 ± 0.3 μg/g, p<0.001). Eggshell thickness showed an inverse relationship with chlorpyrifos residues (R²=0.43, p=0.02), with contaminated eggs (≥0.8 μg/g) demonstrating 18% thinner shells on average. Radio-telemetry data from 48 hens revealed 37% lower nest success rates in fields adjacent to conventional row-crop operations compared to organic systems. Population modeling estimated a 42% decline in local abundance over five generations under current agrochemical exposure levels. These findings demonstrate synergistic sublethal effects of multiple contaminants on pheasant reproductive physiology and demographic rates, highlighting the need for integrated pest management strategies and buffer zone implementation in agricultural policy. Our results suggest pheasants may serve as effective bioindicators for monitoring landscape-level contaminant loads in temperate grassland ecosystems.

We investigated habitat selection patterns of male Red-winged Blackbirds (Agelaius phoeniceus) across 32 freshwater wetlands in Iowa's Prairie Pothole Region from 2018-2020. Using radio-telemetry (n=115 males) and vegetation surveys, we developed resource selection functions comparing used versus available territories. Males exhibited strong selection for sites with 1.2-1.5m tall emergent vegetation (β=2.34, 95% CI=1.98-2.71), 30-50% open water (β=1.67, CI=1.32-2.01), and <200m distance to agricultural edges (β=-1.89, CI=-2.45--1.33). Wetlands surrounded by >40% row crop agriculture showed 62% lower territory density (p<0.001) compared to grassland-buffered sites. Nest survival analysis revealed 22% higher success in territories with >60% cattail (Typha spp.) coverage versus mixed vegetation (χ²=8.91, p=0.003). However, anthropogenic edge avoidance created a 150-300m ecological trap zone where predation rates from raccoons (Procyon lotor) increased threefold. Our findings suggest current agricultural wetland conservation programs prioritizing narrow buffer strips may inadequately support blackbird populations. We recommend maintaining wetland complexes >2ha with heterogeneous vegetation structure and >500m isolation from active cropland to balance reproductive success with human-wildlife conflict mitigation.

We investigated foraging behavior of Cooper's Hawks (*Accipiter cooperii*) across urban and exurban habitats in the southwestern United States from 2018–2020 using GPS telemetry (n = 35 adults) and prey remains analysis (n = 420 prey items).
