Hawks in metropolitan Phoenix, Arizona, exhibited significantly shorter hunting bout durations (27 ± 6 min) compared to conspecifics in adjacent Sonoran Desert habitats (49 ± 9 min; p < 0.05). Urban individuals showed preferential selection of introduced Eurasian Collared-Doves (*Streptopelia decaocto*), constituting 43% of identified prey, while exurban hawks primarily targeted native Gambel's Quail (*Callipepla gambelii*; 37%). A novel finding revealed 18% of urban prey items contained detectable anticoagulant rodenticide residues, potentially influencing foraging efficiency through sublethal effects. Habitat utilization metrics derived from kernel density estimates demonstrated 62% of urban foraging occurred within 500 m of riparian corridors, compared to 1.2 km median distance to water sources in desert territories (p = 0.003). Our data suggest behavioral plasticity in hunting strategies buffers against anthropogenic habitat fragmentation but raises concerns about toxicant exposure pathways. These results underscore the importance of maintaining urban green infrastructure and implementing rodenticide regulations to support Accipiter populations in human-modified landscapes. This study provides critical baseline data for monitoring adaptive capacity under expanding urbanization pressures.

Recent population declines of Common Loons (Gavia immer) in northeastern North America have raised concerns about genetic erosion and long-term viability. We analyzed nuclear microsatellites (n=15 loci) and mitochondrial DNA control regions (1,042 bp) across 238 individuals from 12 breeding lakes in the Adirondack Park (New York) and Georgian Bay (Ontario) regions to assess contemporary genetic structure and diversity. Populations exhibited moderate differentiation (FST = 0.08–0.15), with reduced gene flow between regions separated by <200 km. Allelic richness was 23% lower in Adirondack populations (AR = 4.1 ± 0.3 vs. 5.3 ± 0.4 in Georgian Bay), while mitochondrial haplotype diversity showed no significant regional difference (h = 0.72–0.81). Effective population size estimates (Ne) ranged from 38 to 127, falling below thresholds recommended for maintaining evolutionary potential. Bayesian clustering revealed two distinct genetic clusters, with 14% of Adirondack individuals showing mixed ancestry compared to 3% in Georgian Bay, suggesting recent bottlenecks. Mercury contamination (mean blood Hg = 2.8 ppm in Adirondacks vs. 1.2 ppm in Georgian Bay) correlated positively with inbreeding coefficients (r = 0.67, p < 0.01). These findings highlight the urgent need for landscape-scale habitat protection and assisted migration programs to enhance genetic connectivity, particularly for isolated populations facing cumulative stressors from toxic pollutants and shoreline development.

We investigated sex-specific parental care strategies in Red-tailed Hawks (Buteo jamaicensis) across a gradient of habitat fragmentation in agricultural landscapes of central Illinois, USA. Using GPS transmitters (n = 32 adults) and 1,200 hours of video recordings from 25 nests monitored during 2020-2022 breeding seasons, we quantified provisioning rates, nest attendance, and prey delivery composition relative to territory quality. Males contributed 78% of total prey biomass (x̄ = 4.2 kg/week ± 1.1 SD), primarily small mammals (62% of deliveries), while females accounted for 92% of nest guarding time. Parental investment covaried with habitat structure: territories with <40% forest cover within 1 km radius showed 34% higher male foraging effort (p = 0.013) and 22% lower nestling survival rates (p = 0.041) compared to more forested areas. Plasma corticosterone levels in nestlings from high-foraging-effort territories averaged 18.7 ng/ml (±3.2) versus 12.1 ng/ml (±2.8) in low-effort sites (p = 0.007), indicating nutritional stress. Contrary to expectations, female nest departure frequency increased with prey abundance (r = 0.61, p < 0.001), suggesting compensatory behaviors in resource-rich environments. Our findings demonstrate that anthropogenic landscape modification alters parental role specialization in this generalist raptor, with cascading effects on offspring condition. Conservation strategies maintaining ≥60 ha contiguous forest patches may buffer against energetic trade-offs imposed by fragmented habitats, critical for sustaining breeding populations amid expanding agricultural intensification.

We present a 15-year demographic study (2008–2023) of Osprey populations across five major Chesapeake Bay tributaries, analyzing survival rates, breeding success, and age-specific mortality using mark-recapture data from 1,243 banded individuals. Bayesian hierarchical models revealed spatial heterogeneity in adult survival probabilities (0.76–0.89 annually), with lowest rates in urbanized watersheds experiencing elevated mercury concentrations (+38% vs. rural sites). First-year survival averaged 0.52 (±0.07 SE), influenced by hurricane frequency (β = -0.21, p<0.01) and wintering ground deforestation in South America (β = -0.17, p=0.03). Breeding pairs showed high nest fidelity (87% reuse rates), but productivity declined from 1.8 to 1.3 fledglings/nest over the study period, correlated with dissolved oxygen levels (ρ = 0.62) and menhaden (Brevoortia tyrannus) biomass reductions. Population matrix projections indicated source-sink dynamics, with three tributaries acting as net exporters (λ = 1.12–1.21) and two urban-adjacent populations declining (λ = 0.93–0.97). Our results highlight the species' sensitivity to cross-continental environmental stressors and propose targeted management of coastal prey fish stocks and mercury emission controls to stabilize metapopulation viability. This study establishes quantitative benchmarks for assessing Osprey recovery under the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service's 2025 raptor conservation framework.

We assessed the genetic structure and diversity of the threatened King Rail (*Rallus elegans*) across its North American range to inform conservation strategies for this rapidly declining marsh obligate. Using 12 microsatellite loci and mitochondrial DNA sequences (ND2, 1,042 bp) from 143 individuals sampled in coastal and inland wetlands (Chesapeake Bay, Gulf Coast, Mississippi Alluvial Valley), we identified three genetically distinct clusters (FST = 0.11–0.18) corresponding to major watershed boundaries. Coastal populations exhibited 27% lower allelic richness (mean Ar = 3.1 vs. 4.3) and higher inbreeding coefficients (FIS = 0.15 vs. 0.08) compared to inland groups, likely reflecting habitat fragmentation from saltwater intrusion and urbanization. Effective population sizes were critically low (<50) in four of eight sampled subpopulations. Mitochondrial haplotypes revealed a historic population expansion (~12,000 YBP) followed by recent contraction, with contemporary genetic diversity metrics 40% below Pleistocene-era levels. Our results suggest that anthropogenic barriers disrupt gene flow between watersheds, exacerbating genetic erosion in coastal zones vulnerable to sea-level rise. We recommend prioritizing wetland connectivity projects in the Mississippi Alluvial Valley, which hosts the most genetically diverse population, and initiating genetic rescue trials to bolster coastal subpopulations. This study underscores the urgency of integrating hydrological management with genetic monitoring to prevent weiter losses of adaptive potential in this IUCN Near Threatened species.

We investigated juvenile survival rates of Horned Grebes (Podiceps auritus) across their Pacific Flyway migration route from Alaskan breeding grounds (61°N) to California wintering sites (38°N) during 2018–2021. Using radio telemetry (n = 85 juveniles) and capture-recapture modeling, we quantified fledging-to-winter survival probabilities while assessing environmental and physiological covariates. First-year survival averaged 62% (±6% SE), with 78% of mortality occurring during autumn migration. Survival probabilities showed strong positive correlations with post-fledging body mass (β = 0.43, p < 0.001) and negative associations with late hatch dates (β = −0.29, p = 0.03). Satellite tracking revealed critical bottlenecks at coastal British Columbia staging areas, where 43% of tracked individuals experienced delayed departure due to marine heatwave conditions in 2019, resulting in 22% lower survival compared to baseline years. Blood plasma analysis indicated elevated corticosterone levels in juveniles from oil-impacted wetland habitats (χ² = 8.7, p = 0.003), correlating with 35% reduced first-month survival. Unexpectedly, mortality rates doubled during severe atmospheric river events in California wintering areas (HR = 2.1, 95% CI 1.4–3.2), contrasting with historical patterns of migration-phase dominance in population bottlenecks. Our results highlight climate-mediated shifts in juvenile survival drivers, emphasizing the need for coordinated habitat protection across hemispheric migration stages and revised population models incorporating non-linear storm mortality effects.

We investigated stopover ecology of Savannah Sparrows (*Passerculus sandwichensis*) during spring migration across the Gulf Coast and Upper Mississippi River Valley from 2018–2021. Using radio telemetry (n = 342 individuals) and plasma metabolite analysis, we quantified stopover duration, habitat selection, and fuel deposition rates in response to land-use gradients. Sparrows exhibited strong affinity for herbaceous wetlands (β = 1.24, SE = 0.31) and Conservation Reserve Program grasslands (β = 0.89, SE = 0.27), avoiding agricultural fields (β = -1.57, SE = 0.42). Stopover duration averaged 2.3 ± 0.6 days, with fuel deposition rates 38% higher in floodplain habitats compared to upland sites (t = 4.12, p < 0.001). Structural equation modeling revealed vegetation density (λ = 0.71) and invertebrate biomass (λ = 0.65) as primary drivers of body condition indices. However, 22% of tracked individuals shifted sites due to disturbance events, increasing daily energy expenditure by 15–18%. Our results demonstrate that managed wetlands and riparian corridors provide critical stopover resources, but habitat fragmentation reduces functional connectivity. Conservation plans prioritizing >40% native vegetation cover within 1 km of wetland complexes could enhance refueling efficiency for this declining grassland specialist (population trend: -2.7% annually since 1970). These findings underscore the need to integrate stopover habitat metrics into full life-cycle models for migratory songbirds.

We investigated the daily energy expenditure (DEE) of Northern Pintails (*Anas acuta*) during winter staging in California's Central Valley using a combination of telemetry-derived activity budgets and doubly labeled water measurements. From 2018-2020, 42 adult pintails (24 males, 18 females) were equipped with tri-axial accelerometers and GPS transmitters to quantify time-activity patterns across three managed wetland complexes. Concurrently, plasma samples analyzed via isotope-ratio mass spectrometry provided field metabolic rates. Results revealed significant spatial (F₂,₃₈ = 9.17, p < 0.001) and temporal (F₄,₃₆ = 5.43, p = 0.002) variation in DEE, ranging from 987 ± 134 kJ/day in flooded rice fields to 1,532 ± 189 kJ/day in seasonal wetlands. Nighttime foraging accounted for 63% of total energy expenditure, with flight costs (12.8 kJ/km) representing 22% of daily budgets during periods of roost-to-feeding site movements >5 km. Lean body mass declined by 8.3% (±1.2%) between December and February despite ad libitum food availability, suggesting trade-offs between energy conservation and predator avoidance behaviors. Our mechanistic model demonstrates that reducing anthropogenic disturbance during crepuscular periods could decrease daily energy demands by 17-24%, potentially improving pre-migration body condition. These findings highlight the critical role of habitat configuration in waterfowl energy budgets, with implications for wetland management strategies aimed at supporting pintail populations that have declined 56% in the Pacific Flyway since 1999.

We investigated the migratory ecology of the Brown Pelican (*Pelecanus occidentalis*) across five breeding colonies in the Gulf of Mexico and Eastern Pacific (2018–2020) using satellite telemetry (n = 50 individuals) and stable isotope analysis (δ²H, δ¹³C) of feather samples. Pelicans exhibited divergent migratory strategies: 72% of Gulf populations were short-distance migrants overwintering along the Yucatán Peninsula, while 89% of Eastern Pacific breeders undertook longer migrations (mean ± SD: 1,240 ± 170 km) to coastal Ecuador. Migration timing correlated strongly with sea surface temperature anomalies (SSTa; *r* = −0.63, *p* < 0.01), with delayed southward movements during positive SSTa phases. Wind support during migration significantly influenced route selection (*F* = 8.3, *p* = 0.005), with pelicans favoring coastal updrafts to reduce energetic expenditure. Foraging efficiency at stopover sites declined by 23% in regions with high commercial fishing activity, as evidenced by GPS-derived dive frequency and prey capture rates. Survivorship analysis revealed higher annual mortality in long-distance migrants (14%) versus resident populations (7%), linked to habitat loss in key estuarine wintering areas. These findings underscore the vulnerability of Brown Pelicans to climate-driven shifts in marine productivity and coastal development. We recommend dynamic marine protected area designations along migratory corridors and prioritized restoration of mangrove roosting sites in the Gulf of California and Campeche Bank to buffer against anthropogenic stressors.

We investigated the impacts of coastal habitat degradation on Pied-billed Grebe (Podilymbus podiceps) populations across 12 major estuaries in the Gulf of Mexico and southeastern U.S. Atlantic coast from 2015-2022. Using satellite telemetry (n=87 individuals) and systematic breeding surveys, we documented a 42% decline in grebe density (95% CI: 37-47%) coinciding with a 1.8% annual loss of brackish wetland habitats critical for nesting and foraging. Multivariate analyses revealed significant correlations between reduced reproductive success (χ²=19.3, df=4, p<0.001) and increased salinity intrusion from sea-level rise (R²=0.71), as well as diminished aquatic invertebrate prey biomass in areas adjacent to coastal development. Ground-truthing using UAV imagery showed 63% of historical grebe territories now exhibit fragmented vegetation structure unsuitable for nest concealment. Survival models incorporating GPS tracking data identified wintering habitat fidelity as a vulnerability factor, with individuals returning to degraded sites experiencing 22% lower annual survival rates (p=0.013). Our findings challenge previous assumptions about this species' adaptability to anthropogenic change, revealing threshold effects when >40% of marsh vegetation is replaced by open water or invasive Phragmites. These results underscore the need for prioritized protection of remaining coastal lagoons and implementation of managed wetland hydrology to buffer against saltwater intrusion under climate change scenarios.

We investigated the impacts of invasive blue catfish (*Ictalurus furcatus*) on Osprey (*Pandion haliaetus*) foraging ecology in Chesapeake Bay, Maryland, from 2018 to 2022. Using GPS telemetry (n = 32 adults) and regurgitated pellet analysis (n = 417 samples), we quantified dietary shifts in Ospreys nesting in tributaries with high invasive catfish densities (>5 individuals/100 m² via electrofishing surveys) versus reference sites. Ospreys in invaded systems exhibited a 42% reduction in preferred native prey (American shad *Alosa sapidissima*, white perch *Morone americana*) consumption (PERMANOVA, *F* = 9.31, *p* < 0.001), replacing 58% of their diet with invasive catfish. Stable isotope analysis (δ¹⁵N, δ¹³C) revealed significantly higher trophic positions in Ospreys from invaded habitats (ANOVA, *F* = 7.89, *p* = 0.006), correlating with a 27% decline in fledging success (GLM, β = -0.33, *p* = 0.02). Nest monitoring showed that catfish-dominated diets reduced chick survival probabilities by 19% due to higher rates of siblicide and parental abandonment. These findings highlight cascading effects of aquatic invasive species on apex avian predators, emphasizing the need for integrated fisheries management to mitigate subsidized predation on novel prey with lower nutritional value.

We investigated the effects of human recreational activities on Brown Pelican (Pelecanus occidentalis) behavior and reproductive success across 12 breeding colonies in the Gulf of Mexico (Texas to Florida) from 2018 to 2021. Using GPS telemetry (n = 54 adults) and 1,200 hours of behavioral observations, we quantified flight initiation distances, nest attendance rates, and foraging efficiency in relation to vessel traffic, beach visitation, and coastal development. Pelicans exposed to >5 watercraft encounters/hour exhibited a 37% reduction in prey capture rates (95% CI: 22-49%) compared to control sites. Nest abandonment probability increased exponentially when human presence occurred within 50 m (OR = 4.2, p < 0.001), with a 19% decline in fledging success at disturbed sites (mean = 0.68 chicks/nest vs. 0.84 at protected colonies). Multivariate GLMMs revealed that weekend tourist numbers explained 41% of variance in adult stress hormone levels (corticosterone R² = 0.41, p = 0.003). Our results demonstrate that current buffer zones (30 m) inadequately protect nesting pelicans, supporting the need for seasonal closures of critical foraging habitats within 1 km of rookeries during breeding seasons. These findings highlight the urgency of adaptive management strategies to mitigate cumulative anthropogenic impacts on coastal seabird populations.

We investigated the movement ecology of Sora (Porzana carolina) across their annual cycle using GPS-GSM telemetry units deployed on 45 adults captured in freshwater emergent wetlands of the Prairie Pothole Region (2019-2021). Birds exhibited bimodal departure timing from breeding areas, with 62% migrating between August 15-September 10 (x̄ = 496 km migration distance) and 38% delaying departure until September 20-October 5 (x̄ = 723 km). Wintering sites in the Lower Mississippi Alluvial Valley (n=27) and Gulf Coast marshes (n=18) showed 68% interannual site fidelity, significantly higher than previously documented (χ²=4.32, p=0.038). Breeding ground home ranges averaged 12.5 ± 3.2 ha (95% kernel density estimate), with 73% of locations occurring in sedge-dominated habitats <30 cm water depth. Unexpectedly, 22% of tracked individuals used flooded agricultural fields during fall staging, spending 18.6 ± 2.4 days in these anthropogenic habitats prior to migration. Mortality risk increased 2.7-fold (Cox proportional hazards model, z=3.11, p=0.002) for birds traversing urbanized regions of the Midwest, with collision infrastructure accounting for 41% of deaths. Our results highlight previously unrecognized plasticity in migration phenology and habitat selection, suggesting conservation strategies targeting wetland complexes with heterogeneous hydrological regimes may enhance resilience to climate-mediated habitat shifts. The high vulnerability during migratory passages underscores the need for coordinated flyway-scale protection of stopover resources in agricultural landscapes.

We investigated predator-prey dynamics of American Coots (Fulica americana) in Nebraska's Rainwater Basin wetlands from 2018–2021, analyzing how anti-predator behaviors influence reproductive success amid varying carnivore densities. Using GPS-tracked brood movements (n = 127 nests) and camera trap data from 45 wetland complexes, we quantified coot responses to native predators (mink [Neogale vison], coyotes [Canis latrans]) and invasive raccoons (Procyon lotor). Chick survival probability (MARK models) decreased by 32% in wetlands with raccoon densities >2.1/km² (95% CI: 1.8–2.4) compared to predator-controlled areas. Coots nesting in bulrush (Schoenoplectus spp.)-dominated habitats exhibited 2.7× higher fledging rates (logistic regression: β = 1.32, SE = 0.41) than those in open-water zones, with vigilance time increasing 18% per additional terrestrial predator species detected (linear mixed model: F₁,₈₇ = 6.24, p = 0.014). Unexpectedly, nocturnal foraging declined by 42% during full moon phases (ANOVA: F₂,₁₃₄ = 9.87, p < 0.001), correlating with increased raccoon activity peaks. Our results demonstrate invasive mesopredators disproportionately impact coot populations compared to historical predator guilds, with habitat structure mediating survival outcomes. Management strategies prioritizing dense emergent vegetation and invasive carnivore control could increase seasonal survival rates by 19–27% (population viability analysis: λ = 0.91 vs. 1.18 scenarios), critical for maintaining this keystone species in dynamic wetland ecosystems.

We investigated nest site selection patterns of Cooper's Hawks (Accipiter cooperii) across an urban gradient in metropolitan Phoenix, Arizona, from 2018 to 2022. Using GPS telemetry (n = 32 adults) and nest monitoring (n = 62 nests), we quantified habitat characteristics at three spatial scales (nest tree, 100m radius, and 1km radius) and compared used versus available sites through conditional logistic regression. Nesting hawks showed strong selection for mature non-native Eucalyptus spp. (OR = 4.2, 95% CI = 2.8-6.3) and Aleppo pine (OR = 3.1, CI = 1.9-5.0) over native desert vegetation, with 87% of nests occurring in ornamental trees ≤50m from residential structures. Canopy cover ≥60% within 100m (AIC weight = 0.79) and distance to nearest building ≤25m (AIC weight = 0.67) emerged as the strongest predictors of nest site occupancy. Urban nests exhibited 18% higher fledging success (mean = 2.8 young/nest) compared to natural desert interface sites (mean = 2.3 young/nest), though urban nestling survival rates declined by 12% when ambient temperatures exceeded 40°C. Our results demonstrate unexpected adaptation to anthropogenic landscapes, with implications for conservation planning in arid regions experiencing rapid urbanization. Retention of mature ornamental trees and strategic placement of artificial nesting platforms could enhance breeding habitat suitability in areas where native vegetation restoration proves impractical.

We analyzed demographic parameters of Brown Pelican (*Pelecanus occidentalis*) populations across six breeding colonies in the northern Gulf of Mexico from 2015–2023 to assess drivers of recent regional population declines. Using mark-resight data from 1,243 banded individuals and Cormack-Jolly-Seber models, we estimated annual adult survival at 0.78 (95% CI: 0.72–0.83), showing a 12% decline since 2010. Nest monitoring revealed productivity dropped from 1.2 fledglings per pair in 2015 to 0.7 in 2023, strongly correlated with reduced menhaden (*Brevoortia patronus*) abundance (*r* = 0.89, *p* < 0.01). Bayesian integrated population models identified mercury contamination (mean eggshell [Hg] = 3.1 ppm ± 0.4 SE) and increased storm frequency as primary mortality drivers for juveniles. However, colonies near estuarine nurseries maintained stable growth rates (λ = 1.04), suggesting habitat connectivity buffers climate impacts. Our matrix projections indicate a 34% population reduction by 2035 under current trends, highlighting the need for fisheries management reforms and mercury emission controls. These results contrast with stable Atlantic coast populations, emphasizing regional vulnerability to anthropogenic stressors in Gulf ecosystems.

We investigated the postbreeding molt migration strategies of Laughing Gulls (Leucophaeus atricilla) across the Gulf of Mexico using a combination of GPS telemetry (n = 48 individuals), stable isotope analysis of primary feathers, and molt progression assessments. Between 2018 and 2022, 73% of tracked adults exhibited a distinct two-stage migration, departing breeding colonies in coastal Texas to undergo primary feather replacement at transitional molting sites in the Laguna Madre (Mexico) before completing migration to wintering areas in the Yucatán Peninsula. Juveniles followed asynchronous routes, with 62% delaying southward migration until completing partial body molt. Molt duration averaged 28 ± 5 days for adults, synchronizing with peak abundance of blue crab (Callinectes sapidus) megalopae—a critical protein source for feather regeneration. Isotopic δ²H values revealed that 89% of adults molted in hypersaline lagoons distinct from breeding habitats, suggesting specialized resource partitioning during this vulnerable life stage. Comparison with historical banding data (1980–2010) showed a 22% reduction in molt site fidelity, correlating with wetland loss in critical Mexican stopover regions (R² = 0.81, p < 0.001). These findings challenge the traditional paradigm of direct breeding-to-wintering migrations in Larids, emphasizing the need for international protection of ephemeral molting habitats. The study demonstrates how molt migration plasticity mediates energetic trade-offs in seabirds facing rapid coastal ecosystem change.

We investigated the genetic structure and diversity of Mallard (Anas platyrhynchos) populations across North America and East Asia to assess conservation vulnerabilities in the context of habitat fragmentation and hybridization threats. Using microsatellite analysis (15 loci) and mitochondrial DNA sequencing (ND2 gene) from 300 individuals across 12 migratory flyways, we identified significant population structuring (FST = 0.083, p < 0.001) between eastern Asian and North American lineages, with admixed zones in Alaska's Yukon-Kuskokwim Delta. Bayesian clustering revealed reduced genetic diversity (He = 0.614 vs. 0.721) in East Asian populations, potentially linked to wetland loss in China's Yangtze River floodplain. Hybridization rates with domestic ducks (Anas platyrhynchos domesticus) exceeded 8% in agricultural regions of California's Central Valley and Hokkaido, Japan, raising concerns about genetic introgression. Effective population sizes (Ne) estimates ranged from 1,200 (95% CI: 850–1,600) in stable prairie pothole regions to 340 (95% CI: 210–510) in fragmented coastal wetlands. Our results emphasize the need for distinct conservation strategies: North American populations require wetland connectivity maintenance, while East Asian groups necessitate urgent genetic rescue interventions. Hybridization monitoring and domestic waterfowl management regulations should be prioritized in agricultural landscapes to preserve adaptive potential in wild populations under climate change scenarios.

We investigated the bioacoustic signatures and contextual use of vocalizations in Forster’s Terns (*Sterna forsteri*) across three breeding colonies in Lake Manitoba, Canada, from 2018–2020. Using autonomous recording units (ARUs) and behavioral observations, we captured 512 high-quality vocalizations from 42 breeding pairs during courtship, chick provisioning, and predator-defense contexts. Spectral analysis revealed distinct call types: a high-pitched, harmonic-rich "kitter" call (mean frequency: 3.2 ± 0.4 kHz) during courtship, and a lower-frequency, broadband "chatter" call (2.1 ± 0.3 kHz) during nest defense. Generalized linear mixed models showed wind speed (β = 0.37, *p* < 0.01) and proximity to neighboring nests (β = −0.22, *p* = 0.03) significantly influenced call rate and amplitude modulation. Playback experiments demonstrated that chick-provisioning calls containing rapid frequency modulations (>5 Hz/ms) elicited stronger parental response times (14.2 s vs. 22.7 s for control calls, *p* < 0.001), suggesting acoustic features encode urgency. However, anthropogenic noise from nearby agricultural machinery (>65 dB) reduced call discrimination efficiency by 38% in experimental trials. These findings highlight the vulnerability of Forster’s Tern communication to environmental stressors, with implications for wetland management strategies that prioritize buffer zones to mitigate acoustic interference in critical breeding habitats. Bioacoustic monitoring is proposed as a non-invasive tool to assess colony health amid increasing anthropogenic pressures on prairie wetland ecosystems.

We examined the impacts of climate change on Brown Pelican (Pelecanus occidentalis) breeding success across six colonies in the Gulf of Mexico (2015–2022) and Pacific Coast (2016–2023), integrating satellite telemetry, nest monitoring, and oceanographic data. Multivariate models revealed a 37% decline in fledging rates at Gulf colonies (p < 0.001) correlated with a 1.2°C rise in sea surface temperature (SST) anomalies, which reduced anchovy (Engraulis spp.) biomass by 42% in pelican foraging zones. Pacific colonies showed greater resilience, with only 12% fledging decline (p = 0.03), attributed to 18% higher prey diversity in cooler upwelling zones. Extreme weather events caused complete breeding failure at three Gulf sites during record hurricane seasons (2017, 2020), with 92% nest loss during Hurricane Harvey. Isotopic analysis of blood samples (n = 348 adults) indicated a 29% reduction in δ15N values since 2000 (p = 0.004), signaling nutritional stress from shifting prey composition. Rising sea levels submerged 14% of preferred nesting islets in the Gulf of California, forcing pelicans to suboptimal mainland sites with 2.8× higher predation rates. Our findings emphasize the need for dynamic marine protected areas adjusted to SST gradients and artificial nesting platform deployment in vulnerable regions. Climate-driven prey depletion and habitat loss pose systemic risks to this recently delisted species, warranting reevaluation of conservation status under accelerating environmental change.

We investigated population genetic structure and diversity of Ring-necked Ducks (Aythya collaris) across their North American range to assess connectivity among breeding and wintering grounds and identify potential conservation priorities. Utilizing 12 microsatellite loci and mitochondrial control region sequencing (n = 278 individuals from 22 sites), we found moderate differentiation between eastern (Atlantic Flyway) and western (Mississippi and Central Flyways) breeding populations (FST = 0.083, p < 0.001). Migration rates estimated via Bayesian assignment tests revealed asymmetrical dispersal, with 14% of western migrants moving eastward versus 6% reverse movement. Effective population size (Ne) estimates were lowest in the Atlantic Flyway (Ne = 1,200; 95% CI: 980–1,450), correlating with wetland loss rates quantified through 30-year Landsat trend analysis (R² = 0.63, p = 0.002). Wintering populations in the southern United States showed elevated inbreeding coefficients (FIS = 0.11 ± 0.03) compared to boreal breeding sites (FIS = 0.04 ± 0.01), potentially reflecting habitat fragmentation in agricultural-dominated wintering landscapes. Three evolutionarily significant units were identified through multivariate clustering, highlighting the need for distinct management strategies in the Prairie Pothole Region, Boreal Forest, and Appalachian Highlands. Our results emphasize the importance of maintaining connectivity between Canadian breeding wetlands and southeastern wintering areas while addressing genetic bottlenecks through wetland restoration initiatives targeting regions with <40% remaining natural habitat.

We investigated long-term demographic trends in a recovering Peregrine Falcon (*Falco peregrinus*) population across the Pacific Northwest (USA) and British Columbia (Canada) from 2010–2022. Using mark-recapture data from 317 banded individuals and nest monitoring at 124 territories, we applied Cormack-Jolly-Seber models to estimate annual adult survival (0.82 ± 0.04 SE) and recruitment rates. Urban populations exhibited 18% higher fledgling survival than rural cohorts (χ² = 6.7, p = 0.01), likely driven by anthropogenic food subsidies from invasive rock pigeons (*Columba livia*). However, rural nesting pairs produced 2.1 ± 0.3 fledglings annually compared to 1.4 ± 0.2 in urban habitats (t = 3.45, p < 0.001), with cliff nests showing higher structural stability than artificial platforms (87% vs. 63% success rates). A population matrix model revealed a lambda of 1.12, indicating sustained growth, but sensitivity analyses identified adult survival as the most influential parameter (elasticity = 0.71). Climate covariates explained 34% of interannual variation in productivity, with warmer springs reducing prey delivery rates in boreal forest territories (R² = 0.28). Our findings highlight a spatial dichotomy in demographic drivers, emphasizing the need for habitat-specific management strategies. While urban adaptation buffers against natural prey fluctuations, reliance on anthropogenic structures and invasive prey species poses novel conservation challenges as climate change intensifies.

We investigated predator-prey dynamics influencing Marsh Wren (Cistothorus palustris) reproductive success across 12 tidal freshwater marshes in the Chesapeake Bay watershed from 2018–2020. Using 150 monitored nests equipped with camera traps, we quantified predation rates (34% of all nest failures) and identified marsh rice rat (Oryzomys palustris; 41%) and northern water snake (Nerodia sipedon; 21%) as primary nest predators. Nest survival analysis revealed significant spatial variation, with edge nests ≤5 m from open water showing 2.3× higher daily predation probability (95% CI: 1.7–3.1) than interior nests. Vegetation structure mediated predation risk, with nests in dense cattail (Typha spp.) stands (>85% vertical cover) exhibiting 58% lower predation rates compared to mixed vegetation patches. Experimental manipulation of 30 nests demonstrated artificial clutch survival decreased by 72% when surrounding vegetation density was reduced below 70% coverage. Stable isotope analysis (δ¹⁵N, δ¹³C) of adult wren blood samples indicated prey composition shifts during nesting, with Odonata consumption increasing from 18% to 42% of diet biomass to meet elevated protein demands. Our results suggest hydrological management practices that maintain ≥1.2 m water depths during nesting seasons could reduce terrestrial predator access while supporting aquatic invertebrate prey populations. These findings highlight the need for mosaic vegetation management in coastal wetlands to balance predator exclusion and foraging resource availability for this declining species (35% regional population decrease since 2000).

We investigated the breeding biology of Red-tailed Hawks (Buteo jamaicensis) across a 5-year period (2018–2022) in the mixed hardwood forests of southern Ontario, Canada, addressing knowledge gaps in reproductive success drivers for this apex predator. Using motion-activated cameras and nest monitoring (n = 127 nests), we quantified clutch size (2.3 ± 0.5 eggs), hatching success (78.4%), and fledging rates (1.7 ± 0.8 young/successful nest). Nestling mortality peaked at 14–21 days post-hatching (32% of losses), primarily due to sibling aggression exacerbated by prey shortages during drought years (r = -0.71, p < 0.05). Breeding pairs in forest fragments <100 ha produced 23% fewer fledglings than those in contiguous habitats (p = 0.012), with elevated abandonment rates (18% vs. 7%) linked to human disturbance within 500 m buffers. A novel Cox proportional hazards model revealed that nest survival declined by 40% for every 10% increase in impervious surface within territories. Contrary to previous studies, urban-adjacent pairs exhibited earlier egg-laying (mean ± SD: 2 April ± 6 days vs. 10 April ± 8 days, p < 0.001) but lower chick provisioning rates. Our results underscore the sensitivity of Red-tailed Hawks to landscape-scale habitat degradation, emphasizing the need for forest conservation buffers and mitigation of anthropogenic noise in critical breeding areas to sustain viable populations under increasing development pressures.

We investigated parental care strategies in Redheads (*Aythya americana*) across six wetland complexes in the Prairie Pothole Region (2018–2021) to assess how brood parasitism influences maternal investment and offspring survival. Using radio-telemetry and nest cameras, we monitored 120 females (60 parasitic, 60 non-parasitic) and their broods, quantifying provisioning rates, nest attendance, and duckling growth. Parasitic females initiated nests 12 ± 3 days later than non-parasitic counterparts (p < 0.001) and showed 27% lower nest attendance during incubation. Duckling survival to fledging differed significantly between groups, with parasitically reared young exhibiting 18% lower survival (95% CI: 12–24%) under natural predation pressure. Stable isotope analysis of egg membranes revealed parasitic females allocated 15% less protein to eggs (δ15N = 8.7‰ ± 0.4 vs. 10.1‰ ± 0.3, p = 0.012), correlating with reduced duckling body condition indices (r = 0.43, p = 0.03). However, parasitic females demonstrated higher post-breeding survival (82% vs. 68%, HR = 0.62, p = 0.04), suggesting a trade-off between current reproductive effort and future survivorship. These findings challenge assumptions of equivalent fitness outcomes in alternative reproductive tactics and underscore the need for wetland management strategies that maintain heterogeneous vegetation densities to support diverse nesting strategies in this IUCN Near-Threatened species.

We investigated post-fledging survival of Savannah Sparrow (Passerculus sandwichensis) juveniles across a 3-year study (2018–2020) in Saskatchewan’s mixed-grass prairie, using a combination of radio telemetry (n = 217 individuals) and mark-recapture methods. Daily survival rates averaged 0.963 ± 0.007 SE during the critical 60-day post-independence period, yielding a cumulative survival probability of 0.35. Cox proportional hazards models revealed predation (accounting for 68% of mortality events, primarily by mustelids and raptors) and late-season precipitation extremes as dominant mortality drivers. Juveniles in pastures with >40% native grass cover exhibited 1.7× higher survival (HR = 0.59, 95% CI: 0.43–0.81) compared to those in reseeded hayfields, mediated through reduced predator detection probabilities in structurally complex vegetation. An anomalous 2019 drought year reduced survival by 22% relative to baseline levels, with carryover effects decreasing first-year breeding site fidelity (r = 0.71, p < 0.01). Our results demonstrate that conversion of heterogeneous native grasslands to homogeneous agricultural landscapes imposes fitness costs on this declining grassland obligate. Targeted retention of >30 cm vegetation height within 200 m of nest sites could enhance juvenile recruitment by 18–24%, providing a scalable management strategy to mitigate habitat fragmentation impacts. These findings underscore the importance of incorporating post-fledging dynamics into population viability models for temperate grassland songbirds.

We investigated the foraging ecology and habitat selection of Double-crested Cormorants (Phalacrocorax auritus) across 12 managed wetlands in the Upper Mississippi River watershed (2018–2022) to evaluate their response to hydrological variability and implications for multi-species conservation. Using GPS telemetry (n = 54 individuals) and prey sampling, we found cormorants preferentially targeted shallow (<1.2 m) ephemeral pools during drawdown events, where fish biomass (primarily Lepomis macrochirus and Pimephales promelas) was 3.8× higher than in permanently flooded areas. Nesting success (0.82 ± 0.11 fledglings/pair) correlated inversely with spring water-level fluctuations (R² = 0.67, p < 0.001), with rapid 15+ cm/week increases causing 42% nest abandonment. Stable isotope analysis (δ¹⁵N, δ¹³C) revealed 68% dietary overlap with Great Egrets (Ardea alba), though cormorants showed greater reliance on invasive Cyprinus carpio in deeper basins. Hydrological modeling indicated that current water management protocols optimized for waterfowl reduce potential cormorant carrying capacity by 31–39% during critical pre-fledging periods. We recommend phased drawdowns and structural habitat heterogeneity to balance cormorant conservation with fisheries management goals while minimizing conflicts with recreational anglers. These findings underscore the need for adaptive wetland management frameworks addressing competing demands of piscivorous birds under increasing climate-driven hydrological uncertainty.

We investigated the genetic structure and diversity of Ring-necked Pheasant (*Phasianus colchicus*) populations across fragmented agricultural landscapes in the Upper Midwest, USA, and Shaanxi Province, China, using 12 microsatellite loci. Over 200 individuals from 12 populations (6 native, 6 introduced) were analyzed to assess inbreeding coefficients (F<sub>IS</sub>), allelic richness, and population differentiation (F<sub>ST</sub>). Native Chinese populations exhibited higher genetic diversity (mean H<sub>e</sub> = 0.73 ± 0.08 vs. 0.58 ± 0.11 in US populations) but showed significant isolation-by-distance (Mantel test, *r* = 0.62, *p* = 0.002). US populations displayed elevated inbreeding (mean F<sub>IS</sub> = 0.15 vs. 0.04 in China) and reduced effective population sizes (N<sub>e</sub> < 100 in 83% of sampled sites). Genomic clustering analyses revealed three distinct genetic clusters in China versus a single admixed lineage in the US. Landscape genetic models identified crop heterogeneity and hedgerow density as primary predictors of gene flow in fragmented habitats (*R*<sup>2</sup> = 0.42). Our results highlight contrasting conservation priorities: maintaining connected grassland-cropland mosaics in native ranges versus targeted translocations to mitigate inbreeding in introduced populations. These findings provide a genomic foundation for adaptive management of this economically important game species under accelerating land-use change.

We investigated habitat selection patterns of Red-tailed Hawks (Buteo jamaicensis) across a 15,000 km² gradient in the Appalachian Mountains from 2018-2021 using GPS telemetry (n = 32 adults) and 1,200 ground-based vegetation surveys. Resource selection functions revealed strong avoidance of high-elevation conifer forests (β = -1.24, SE = 0.31, p < 0.001) and agricultural areas (β = -0.87, SE = 0.28, p = 0.002), with preference for mixed deciduous-coniferous edges within 500 m of open foraging areas (β = 1.56, SE = 0.42, p < 0.001). Hawks selected nest sites with greater canopy openness (25-40%) compared to random locations (Mann-Whitney U = 12,340, p < 0.01) and showed 73% higher hunting success in regenerating timber harvest zones versus mature stands. Seasonal shifts occurred in winter, with 58% of tracked individuals moving to lower elevations (<800 m) exhibiting 22% larger home ranges (x̄ = 18.7 km² vs 15.3 km²). Our multiscale analysis (25 m to 5 km radii) identified critical thresholds in habitat configuration, with reproductive success declining sharply when forest fragmentation exceeded 35% within 2 km territories (logistic regression, OR = 0.62, 95% CI 0.41-0.83). These findings highlight the importance of maintaining heterogeneous forest mosaics for this apex predator, with direct implications for sustainable forestry practices and ridge-top development policies in eastern North America.

We investigated the post-breeding migration ecology of Horned Grebes (Podiceps auritus) using satellite telemetry across three key breeding populations in Churchill, Manitoba (Canada), Yukon Delta National Wildlife Refuge (Alaska, USA), and southern Greenland. Forty-five adult grebes were fitted with 5-g solar-powered satellite transmitters during the 2020-2022 breeding seasons, yielding 8,723 location fixes. Migration routes revealed significant intraspecific variability, with Alaska populations exhibiting transcontinental movements averaging 6,215 ± 342 km to wintering areas in the Sea of Japan, while eastern Arctic populations primarily used Atlantic flyways (4,890 ± 410 km) to coastal Europe. Stopover duration at key staging sites (Great Lakes, Baltic Sea) averaged 8.2 ± 2.1 days, with 73% of individuals showing high site fidelity to specific wetlands. Accelerometer data indicated elevated energy expenditure (1.8× basal metabolic rate) during lake transitions compared to coastal wintering periods. Multivariate analyses identified chlorophyll-a concentrations (proxy for prey availability) and wind patterns as primary drivers of migration timing (R² = 0.67, p < 0.001). Population-specific conservation vulnerabilities were identified, with 62% of Alaska-tracked individuals encountering proposed offshore wind farm zones during migration. These results highlight the importance of maintaining nutrient-rich stopover habitats and implementing dynamic marine spatial planning to address climate-driven shifts in grebe migration phenology.

We examined molt migration patterns in Ruffed Grouse (Bonasa umbellus) across the northern hardwood forests of Michigan’s Upper Peninsula from 2018–2021 using GPS telemetry (n = 142 adults) and stable isotope analysis of primary feathers. Our study revealed a previously undocumented 35.6 ± 12.8 km (mean ± SD) post-breeding movement toward early-successional aspen (Populus tremuloides) stands, with 78% of tracked individuals abandoning breeding territories between late July and early September. Resource selection functions demonstrated strong selection for 15–20 year-old clearcuts during wing feather replacement (β = 2.41, SE = 0.67, p < 0.001), coinciding with peak protein content in aspen catkins (18.3% crude protein vs. 9.7% in mature stands). Survival analysis revealed elevated predation risk during molt migration (weekly hazard ratio = 1.72 compared to sedentary periods), particularly from avian predators in fragmented landscapes. Counterintuitively, individuals undertaking longer migrations exhibited 23% higher post-molt body condition indices (t = 4.12, df = 89, p < 0.001), suggesting nutritional benefits outweigh predation costs. These findings challenge assumptions of Ruffed Grouse as non-migratory and highlight the critical role of dynamic forest mosaics in maintaining plumage quality and population resilience. Our results provide mechanistic insights into regional population declines, where homogenized timber harvest practices have reduced availability of transitional successional habitats essential for sequential molt.

We investigated intra-specific morphological variation in Northern Gannets (*Morus bassanus*) across their North Atlantic breeding range to assess environmentally driven phenotypic plasticity. Morphometric data (n=1,568 adults) were collected from six major colonies spanning 15° latitude (Bonaventure Island, Canada to Helgoland, Germany) during peak breeding seasons (2016-2021). Standardized measurements included culmen length (127.3±4.1 mm), wing chord (486.7±12.8 mm), and tarsus depth (21.4±1.3 mm), with multivariate analysis revealing significant clinal variation (PERMANOVA, p<0.001). Birds from higher latitudes showed 6.2% greater body mass (3,410±210 g vs 3,210±190 g) and 4.7% longer wings compared to southern populations, aligning with Bergmann's rule. Sexual dimorphism accounted for 18% of variance (PCA), with males exceeding females in bill depth (Δ=1.8 mm, p=0.003) and wing loading (Δ=12.4 N/m², p<0.001). Stable isotope analysis (δ¹⁵N, δ¹³C) of breast feathers indicated trophic niche partitioning mediates morphological differences, with 14% wider isotopic niches in western Atlantic populations. Comparison with historical specimens (1920-1950) revealed a 3.1% reduction in culmen length over 90 years (ANCOVA, p=0.02), potentially linked to shifting prey size distributions from ocean warming. These results underscore the importance of colony-specific conservation strategies, particularly for rapidly warming Gulf of Maine colonies where morphological mismatches may reduce diving efficiency.

We investigated factors influencing breeding territory selection and community-level interactions in male Common Yellowthroats (Geothlypis trichas) across 18 riparian sites in the Connecticut River Valley (2018-2019). Using standardized point counts, mist-netting, and nest monitoring (n = 127 territories), we developed generalized linear mixed models to assess relationships between territory density, vegetation structure, nest predator abundance, and interspecific competitor presence. Territory density showed strongest correlation with dense shrub-layer complexity (β = 0.67 ± 0.12 SE, p < 0.001), particularly native dogwood (Cornus spp.) and willow (Salix spp.) coverage exceeding 60%. Sites with higher corvid (Corvus brachyrhynchos) and raccoon (Procyon lotor) activity supported 34% fewer territories (χ² = 8.91, p = 0.003), while presence of ecologically similar Yellow Warblers (Setophaga petechia) reduced territory establishment probability by 22% (OR = 0.78, 95% CI: 0.65-0.94). Multi-model inference (ΔAICc < 2) identified three competing hypotheses: 1) predator-mediated habitat selection overriding competitor effects, 2) synergistic interactions between vegetative structure and avian community composition, and 3) spatial autocorrelation of abiotic factors influencing multiple guilds simultaneously. Our results suggest Common Yellowthroat conservation requires integrated management addressing both habitat restoration (maintaining 3-5m tall dense shrub layers) and multi-trophic interactions, particularly controlling mesopredators and monitoring competing secondary cavity-nesting species. This community ecology approach highlights the importance of cross-guild dynamics in shaping habitat suitability for declining migratory songbirds.

We investigated nest site selection patterns in Sedge Wrens (Cistothorus platensis) across 24 restored wet meadow complexes in northern Indiana and southern Michigan from 2018-2021. Using systematic vegetation surveys and nest monitoring (n=147 nests), we compared microhabitat characteristics at occupied nest sites (n=62) versus randomly selected unoccupied sites. Nesting territories exhibited 34% greater vegetation density (F=12.7, p<0.001) and 22% taller vertical structure (F=8.9, p=0.003) compared to unused areas, with dominant species including prairie cordgrass (Spartina pectinata) and bluejoint (Calamagrostis canadensis). Logistic regression models identified water depth (β=0.42±0.11 SE) and distance to open water (β=-0.57±0.09 SE) as significant predictors of nest placement (AICc weight=0.87), with optimal sites occurring in shallow flooded zones (5-15 cm depth) within 50 m of permanent water features. Nest survival analysis revealed 28% higher daily survival rates in areas with intermediate vegetation height (40-60 cm) versus shorter (<30 cm) or taller (>80 cm) stands (χ²=7.3, p=0.026). Post-breeding habitat sampling demonstrated rapid vegetation succession reduced suitable nesting areas by 42% annually, emphasizing the need for rotational disturbance regimes. Our findings challenge assumptions about this species' habitat flexibility and suggest current restoration practices prioritizing uniform vegetation structure may inadequately support breeding populations. Targeted management incorporating hydrological variability and patch-scale heterogeneity could enhance reproductive success in fragmented agricultural landscapes.

We investigated juvenile survival rates in Common Loons (*Gavia immer*) across 35 lakes in northern Minnesota from 2018 to 2022 using satellite telemetry and mark-resight techniques. Forty-seven fledglings were equipped with solar-powered GPS transmitters to track dispersal patterns, mortality events, and environmental drivers of survival. First-year survival averaged 62% (±7% SE), with 78% of mortalities occurring within 90 days post-fledging. Cox proportional hazards models revealed that chicks from lakes with higher pH (≥6.8) exhibited 2.3-fold greater survival probability than those in low-pH systems (≤5.2), likely due to enhanced prey (yellow perch *Perca flavescens*) biomass. Body mass at fledging significantly predicted survival, with individuals above the median (2.1 kg) showing 30% higher survival rates. Unexpectedly, 22% of mortalities were attributed to mercury exposure (≥4.3 µg/g in blood), despite levels below established toxic thresholds. Avian cholera outbreaks during autumn migration accounted for 17% of fatalities, highlighting emerging disease risks. Our findings emphasize the vulnerability of juvenile loons to anthropogenic lake acidification and bioaccumulative contaminants, urging revised conservation strategies that prioritize watershed buffering capacity and mercury emission controls in breeding territories. This study provides the first quantitative framework for predicting recruitment bottlenecks in this climate-sensitive indicator species.

We investigated the effects of nest predator dynamics on Yellow Warbler (Setophaga petechia) reproductive success across a 250 km² riparian corridor in the Missouri River floodplain, USA. From 2018–2021, we monitored 132 nests using motion-activated cameras and conducted weekly point-count surveys of avian predators (Corvus brachyrhynchos, Cyanocitta cristata) and mesocarnivores (Procyon lotor, Mustela frenata). Nest survival probability decreased by 42% (Cox proportional hazards model: HR = 1.87, p < 0.001) in territories with predator activity exceeding 0.75 detections/hour. Counterintuitively, warbler nest density showed a nonlinear relationship with predation risk, peaking at intermediate densities (2.3 nests/ha) where predator functional responses plateaued. Vegetation structure mediated outcomes: nests in areas with >60% canopy cover and <30% understory density experienced 30% higher fledging success (χ² = 9.41, p = 0.002) despite comparable predator abundance. Stable isotope analysis (δ¹⁵N) of 57 feather samples revealed that surviving nestlings had significantly higher trophic position (mean ± SE: 8.2 ± 0.4‰) compared to depredated counterparts (6.9 ± 0.3‰; t = 3.12, p = 0.003), suggesting maternal allocation of nutrient-rich prey during incubation. Our findings challenge assumptions about linear density-dependent predation in passerines and highlight the importance of fine-scale habitat heterogeneity in mitigating anthropogenic fragmentation impacts. Conservation strategies should prioritize maintaining structural diversity in riparian buffers rather than solely focusing on predator control measures.

We investigated post-fledging survival and habitat-use patterns of juvenile Green Herons (*Butorides virescens*) in the Atchafalaya Basin, Louisiana, from 2018 to 2021. Using radio telemetry (n = 87 individuals) and mark-recapture surveys, we quantified survival rates across three critical life stages: weeks 1–2 post-fledging (45.7% survival), weeks 3–6 (78.2%), and dispersal onset (62.4%). Mortality risk peaked during the first week post-fledging, with predation by raccoons (*Procyon lotor*) and Great Horned Owls (*Bubo virginianus*) accounting for 68% of confirmed deaths. Habitat selection models revealed juveniles preferentially used forested wetlands with ≥30% submerged aquatic vegetation (β = 1.24, SE = 0.38), avoiding open-water areas (β = −0.92, SE = 0.27). Survival increased with proximity to parental nests (HR = 0.72 per 100 m, 95% CI: 0.61–0.85) and in years with higher summer water levels (ρ = 0.63, p = 0.04). First-year survival averaged 31.5% (SE ± 4.2), 18% lower than previous estimates from Midwestern populations. Our findings emphasize the vulnerability of fledglings to rapid hydrological fluctuations in managed floodplains and highlight the importance of maintaining contiguous riparian corridors. Conservation strategies targeting wetland water-level stability and mesopredator control could improve recruitment in this declining wading bird species, particularly under climate change scenarios projecting increased drought frequency in the southeastern United States.

We investigated the postbreeding movements and molt strategies of Bufflehead (Bucephala albeola) across western North America using satellite telemetry (n = 65 individuals) and stable isotope analysis of flight feathers from museum specimens (n = 142). Between 2016–2020, tracked birds breeding in Alberta (55°N) and Alaska (63°N) revealed a bimodal migration strategy, with 72% undergoing remigial molt at brackish estuaries in the Salish Sea (48°N) before wintering in coastal California, while 28% delayed molt until reaching hypersaline lagoons in Baja California (26°N). Molt duration averaged 32 ± 4 days, with males initiating flight feather replacement 11 days earlier than females (p < 0.01). Isotopic δ²H values confirmed that 89% of males exhibited leapfrog migration to northern molting sites, compared to 63% of females. Birds using northern molting habitats showed 23% higher plasma corticosterone levels during flightless periods (p = 0.03), suggesting increased energetic demands in cooler environments. Molt-site fidelity was strong (84% interannual return rate), but 17% of tracked individuals shifted molt locations following El Niño events. Coastal development has reduced historical molting habitat by 41% in the Puget Sound region since 1950, with current sites supporting densities of 8.2 birds/ha—exceeding carrying capacity during drought years. These findings highlight the need for cross-jurisdictional protection of both northern and southern molt corridors, particularly given rising temperatures altering the phenological mismatch between flightless periods and peak predator activity.

We investigated molt migration patterns in Eastern Wild Turkeys (Meleagris gallopavo silvestris) across the Ozark Highlands ecoregion of Missouri using GPS transmitters deployed on 45 adult individuals (23 males, 22 females) from 2018 to 2022. Movement analysis revealed that 78% of tracked birds undertook distinct post-breeding migrations averaging 58.3 ± 12.1 km (range: 22–134 km) to concentrated molting areas characterized by riparian corridors and mature oak-hickory forests. Molt timing showed strong synchronization with rising summer temperatures, commencing 7–14 days earlier in males than females. Body condition indices measured via serum metabolites indicated significant energetic stress during primary feather replacement (p < 0.01), with males expending 18% more daily energy than females during this period (t = 3.45, df = 21, p = 0.002). Juvenile dispersal overlapped spatially with adult molt migration routes, creating localized population densities up to 3.2× higher than breeding territories. Habitat modeling identified vulnerability of key molting sites to oak decline (24% projected loss by 2040) and fragmentation from expanding hardwood timber harvests. Our results challenge assumptions of Wild Turkey sedentarism and suggest current hunting season frameworks may inadvertently pressure molting populations. We propose landscape-scale conservation strategies prioritizing connectivity between nesting areas and calcium-rich molting habitats critical for feather regeneration.

We investigated the effects of coastal habitat degradation on Laughing Gull (*Leucophaeus atricilla*) breeding success across 12 barrier islands in the Gulf Coast of Louisiana, USA, from 2015 to 2022. Using a combination of GPS tracking, nest monitoring (n = 347 nests), and habitat suitability modeling, we assessed how rapid marsh erosion and beachfront urbanization influenced colony site fidelity, clutch survival, and chick recruitment. Annual nest density declined by 42% (95% CI: 34–51%) in natural marsh habitats, while anthropogenic rooftop nesting increased 18-fold, comprising 31% of all monitored nests by 2022. Rooftop nests exhibited 26% lower fledging success compared to natural sites (χ² = 14.3, p < 0.001), with thermal stress and predation by rats identified as primary drivers. Radio telemetry data revealed that adults nesting in fragmented marshes expended 37% more daily energy (p = 0.008) foraging in disturbed estuaries compared to intact habitats. Multivariate models highlighted tidal inundation frequency (β = -0.71, SE = 0.12) and proximity to oil infrastructure (β = -0.53, SE = 0.09) as the strongest predictors of colony abandonment. Our findings underscore the urgent need for managed retreat strategies that prioritize high-elevation nesting berms and predator-free artificial platforms to mitigate compounding pressures from sea-level rise and industrial coastal development.

We investigated seasonal variation in field metabolic rates (FMR) of American Coots (Fulica americana) at Mono Lake, California, using doubly labeled water (DLW) techniques. Thirty-two adult coots were captured and instrumented during winter (December–February) and breeding seasons (May–July) from 2018–2020. Mean FMR increased by 62% during winter (4.8 kJ g⁻¹ d⁻¹ ± 0.7 SE) compared to breeding season values (3.0 kJ g⁻¹ d⁻¹ ± 0.4), with energy expenditure peaks correlating with subfreezing ambient temperatures (<-5°C) and reduced food availability. Energetic costs of daily diving activity (12.3 ± 2.1 dives/hr) accounted for 38% of total winter energy budgets, while breeding-season costs were dominated by nest construction (17% of FMR) and chick provisioning. Alkaline water conditions (pH 9.8) elevated preening frequency by 22% compared to populations in neutral wetlands, adding an estimated 410 kJ/d to thermoregulatory costs. Linear mixed-effects models revealed significant interactions between water temperature, dive depth, and body mass (R² = 0.74, p < 0.001), with lean individuals exhibiting 18% higher mass-specific metabolic rates than heavier conspecifics during cold stress events. These results demonstrate how extreme habitat conditions amplify energy demands in freshwater rails, suggesting climate-induced changes in wetland salinity and temperature regimes may disproportionately impact coot populations at physiological thresholds. Management strategies should prioritize maintaining vegetated thermal refugia and minimizing human disturbance during winter to reduce compounding energetic stressors.

We investigated the competitive interactions between invasive Amur honeysuckle (Lonicera maackii) and Ring-necked Pheasant (Phasianus colchicus) populations across 32 agricultural landscapes in Ohio and Iowa. Using a combination of vegetation surveys (n=1,240 plots), nest monitoring (n=127 active nests), and GPS telemetry data from 54 adult pheasants, we quantified how this woody invasive shrub alters brood-rearing habitat selection and reproductive success. Pheasants in honeysuckle-dominated areas exhibited 37% lower nest success (95% CI: 29-44%) compared to native grassland sites, with chick survival to 8 weeks post-hatch declining from 62% to 41% in invaded habitats. Resource selection functions revealed significant avoidance of honeysuckle thickets during brood-rearing periods (β = -1.82, SE=0.31), despite 68% reduction in preferred native forb cover. Experimental removal plots demonstrated 2.3× higher arthropod biomass – critical chick food – in restored native vegetation versus invaded areas (t=4.17, p<0.001). Landscape-level analysis using CircuitScape revealed 19% increased connectivity barriers for pheasant movement in watersheds with >40% honeysuckle coverage. Our findings challenge assumptions that woody invasives provide universal wildlife benefits, demonstrating trophic mismatches between pheasant life-history requirements and invasive-dominated ecosystems. These results inform adaptive management strategies balancing invasive species control with native habitat restoration in working agricultural lands.

We investigated habitat selection patterns of Ring-billed Gulls (Larus delawarensis) across the Laurentian Great Lakes region from 2018–2021 using GPS loggers deployed on 68 adult individuals during the breeding season. Resource selection functions revealed strong selection for anthropogenic habitats, with gulls disproportionately utilizing landfills (β = 2.17 ± 0.41, p < 0.001) and agricultural fields (β = 1.83 ± 0.33, p < 0.001) over natural wetlands. Daily movement radii averaged 23.6 ± 7.2 km from colony sites, with 78% of foraging locations occurring within 10 km of urban centers. Compositional analysis demonstrated seasonal shifts in habitat use, with landfill dependence increasing from 42% of locations during incubation to 68% during chick-rearing (χ² = 19.3, p = 0.003). Unexpectedly, gulls nesting on natural offshore islands (<5% vegetation cover) showed 34% higher foraging success rates than those on managed coastal sites, potentially linked to reduced human disturbance. Thermal imaging revealed that urban-nesting individuals maintained lower nighttime body temperatures (ΔT = 1.2°C) compared to rural counterparts, suggesting behavioral adaptations to heat island effects. Our findings highlight the species' ecological plasticity in exploiting human-modified landscapes, with critical implications for managing gull-human conflicts through landfill operation policies and alternative habitat creation. These results challenge traditional assumptions about Larid habitat requirements and emphasize the need for dynamic conservation strategies addressing synurbization processes in aquatic birds.

We investigated the breeding biology of Black-crowned Night-Herons (Nycticorax nycticorax) across six urban and natural colonies in the Lake Michigan Basin (2018–2021) to assess how anthropogenic landscapes influence reproductive success. Using weekly nest monitoring (n = 120 nests) and motion-activated cameras, we quantified clutch size (3.2 ± 0.4 eggs/nest), hatching success (78.3%), and fledging rates (1.8 ± 0.6 chicks/successful nest) relative to habitat variables. Urban colonies exhibited 22% higher nest density (0.7 nests/ha vs. 0.5 nests/ha) but 15% lower fledging success compared to natural wetlands. Nest survival analysis revealed proximity to artificial lighting (β = -0.41, SE = 0.12) and pedestrian traffic (β = -0.33, SE = 0.09) as significant predictors of abandonment. Counterintuitively, urban nests located <50 m from water treatment facilities showed 30% higher hatching success due to stable prey availability (χ² = 7.2, p = 0.007), though this advantage disappeared post-hatching. Multimodel inference identified nest height (ΔAICc = 2.1) and early-season initiation date (ΔAICc = 3.4) as primary drivers of reproductive output, outweighing colony type. Our findings challenge assumptions about urban habitats as ecological traps for Ardeids, demonstrating their conditional value as breeding sites when specific resource thresholds are met. These results inform adaptive management strategies for balancing urban development with waterbird conservation in the Laurentian Great Lakes region.

We investigated the foraging ecology of Tricolored Herons (Egretta tricolor) across tidal cycles in estuarine habitats of the Upper Texas Coast (29°30'N, 94°50'W) from 2019 to 2021. Using focal-animal observations (n = 228 individuals) synchronized with water depth measurements, we quantified prey capture rates, strike success, and microhabitat selection. Herons exhibited tidal state specialization, achieving highest foraging efficiency (1.2 ± 0.3 prey/min) during ebbing tides when water depths ranged 15-25 cm. Multivariate analysis revealed significant partitioning between daytime (visual hunting: 89% of prey attempts) and crepuscular periods (tactile foraging: 72% attempts), with twilight activity concentrated in submerged Spartina alterniflora zones. Stable isotope analysis (δ¹⁵N, δ¹³C) of regurgitated pellets (n = 147) showed dietary dominance by cyprinodontiformes (62% biomass) and palaemonidae crustaceans (28%), with niche breadth narrowing 34% during winter months. Anthropogenic disturbance events (boat traffic ≤50 m) reduced foraging time budgets by 41% (GLMM: β = -0.67, p < 0.001) and increased vigilance behavior frequency. Our results demonstrate tidal and diel patterns in resource exploitation strategies, highlighting vulnerability to coastal development pressures that alter hydrologic regimes. Management strategies maintaining heterogeneous intertidal zones with minimal human disturbance could enhance carrying capacity for this state-threatened species under accelerating sea-level rise scenarios.

We investigated molt migration patterns in Northern Gannets (Morus bassanus) using GPS-accelerometer tags deployed on 45 breeding adults from Bonaventure Island, Canada (n=22) and Grassholm, UK (n=23) between 2019–2022. Tracking data revealed a bimodal migratory strategy post-breeding, with 68% of individuals undertaking long-distance migrations (>1,500 km) to discrete molting areas in the Grand Banks (western Atlantic) and Bay of Biscay (eastern Atlantic), while 32% remained within 300 km of breeding colonies. Molt duration averaged 54 ± 7 days, with migratory individuals delaying primary feather replacement until reaching destination zones characterized by sea surface temperatures of 13–17°C and mesoscale eddy activity (p<0.01). Stable isotope analysis (δ13C, δ15N) of shed primaries confirmed that migratory molters derived 73% of their protein from distinct pelagic food webs during plumage regeneration. Energetic modeling revealed migratory molters expended 18–22% more daily energy (1,850–2,100 kJ/day) than resident counterparts, potentially compensated by higher sardine (Sardina pilchardus) and capelin (Mallotus villosus) consumption rates in target habitats. Our results demonstrate that molting site fidelity emerges by age 4 (McFadden’s R2=0.41, p=0.003), creating conservation vulnerabilities as 84% of migratory molting areas overlap with commercial fishing grounds and proposed offshore wind development zones. These findings highlight the need for dynamic marine spatial planning that accounts for cryptic annual cycle phases in pelagic seabirds.

We investigated habitat selection patterns of Green Herons (Butorides virescens) across a gradient of freshwater wetlands in the Lower Mississippi Alluvial Valley from 2018 to 2021. Using radio telemetry (n = 32 adults) and systematic nest surveys (n = 147 sites), we quantified microhabitat characteristics and landscape-scale variables through generalized linear mixed models. Individuals showed strong selection for forested wetlands with 60-80% canopy cover (β = 2.14, SE = 0.47, p < 0.001), shallow water depths (15-30 cm; β = 1.89, SE = 0.32), and proximity to submerged aquatic vegetation (≤5 m; β = 1.02, SE = 0.28). Nest sites exhibited 75% greater woody stem density (12.3 ± 2.1 stems/m² vs. 7.0 ± 1.8 in random sites) and 2.5× higher prey fish density (ANOVA F₁,₂₉₂ = 18.7, p < 0.001). Contrary to previous assumptions, herons avoided agricultural ditches despite prey availability, with 83% of foraging locations occurring in natural oxbows and sloughs. Multivariate analysis revealed water-level stability (CV < 25%) as the strongest predictor of territory retention (Wald χ² = 14.3, p = 0.002). Our findings highlight vulnerability to altered hydrologic regimes, with 62% of high-quality habitats projected to experience increased flooding frequency under climate scenarios. Conservation strategies emphasizing riparian buffer maintenance and artificial wetland creation should prioritize structural complexity over open-water configurations to support this understudied ardeid.

We investigated how Yellow Warbler (Setophaga petechia) breeding success and territory selection interact with avian community structure in riparian corridors of the Upper Mississippi River watershed. From 2018–2021, we monitored 214 nests across 12 study sites (40–120 ha each) and quantified vegetation structure, brood parasitism rates by Brown-headed Cowbirds (Molothrus ater), and predator activity using camera traps and radio telemetry. Nest survival probability (34.7% ± 5.2 SE) showed strong negative correlations with cowbird abundance (R² = 0.62, p<0.001) and corvid activity (R² = 0.41, p=0.03), but positive associations with shrub layer complexity (NDVI > 0.65). Generalized linear mixed models revealed warbler territories with >40% shrub cover experienced 2.8× higher nest predation by raccoons (Procyon lotor) compared to open habitats (β = 1.12, p=0.04), while areas with intermediate vegetation density (25–35%) showed optimal balance between predator avoidance and food availability. Community occupancy modeling demonstrated significant spatial segregation from competing Neotropical migrants, with 72% reduction in warbler density within 150 m of Prothonotary Warbler (Protonotaria citrea) territories. Our results highlight how fine-scale habitat partitioning mediates interspecific interactions in dynamic floodplain ecosystems, suggesting managed riparian buffers should maintain vegetation stratification gradients rather than uniform dense shrub layers to support Yellow Warbler conservation while balancing predator and parasite pressures.

We investigated the spatial ecology and survival dynamics of Wild Turkey (Meleagris gallopavo) populations in the fragmented hardwood forests of Missouri’s Ozark Mountains using GPS telemetry. Between 2018–2021, 45 adult birds (27 females, 18 males) were fitted with solar-powered transmitters recording locations every 2 hours. Movement analysis revealed significant seasonal differences (ANOVA, F₃,₄₁ = 12.7, p < 0.001), with males exhibiting 38% greater daily displacement during spring breeding (1.2 ± 0.3 km/day) compared to fall (0.7 ± 0.2 km/day). Home ranges averaged 485 ha (95% kernel density estimate) but contracted to 112 ha during nesting periods. Survival rates showed strong spatial dependence, with individuals occupying managed timber stands with ≥40% canopy closure experiencing 80% annual survival versus 52% in open-canopy areas (Cox proportional hazards, HR = 2.9, p = 0.004). Predation accounted for 67% of mortality (n = 19 deaths), predominantly from coyotes (Canis latrans, 58%) during roosting hours (2200–0500). Accelerometer data revealed distinct behavioral shifts post-predator encounters, including prolonged immobility (≥90 minutes) and altered foraging patterns. Our results demonstrate that current forestry practices promoting intermediate canopy coverage enhance turkey survival while meeting timber production goals. However, habitat use-mortality tradeoffs suggest landscape-scale management must balance early-successional foraging patches with mature forest refugia to mitigate mesocarnivore impacts. These findings directly inform adaptive harvest regulations and habitat conservation strategies across the species’ eastern range.

We investigated population dynamics of Marsh Wrens (*Cistothorus palustris*) across 24 tidal freshwater marshes in the Chesapeake Bay estuary from 2013–2023, analyzing drivers of interannual variability and long-term declines. Using mark-recapture data (n = 2,147 banded individuals) and territory mapping, we documented a 34% population reduction, with site-level declines strongly correlated with salinity intrusion (β = -0.78, p < 0.001) and invasive *Phragmites australis* coverage (β = -0.63, p = 0.004). Cormack-Jolly-Seber models revealed reduced annual survival rates (0.42 ± 0.05 SE) in high-salinity marshes compared to freshwater sites (0.61 ± 0.04 SE). Nest monitoring showed 22% lower fledging success in *Phragmites*-dominated habitats versus native cattail stands, driven by increased nest predation (χ² = 15.3, p < 0.001). Precipitation levels during May–June explained 41% of interannual variation in juvenile recruitment (R² = 0.41, p = 0.02). Spatial capture-recapture analysis revealed 58% smaller home ranges in fragmented marshes (0.83 ± 0.12 ha) compared to contiguous wetlands (1.98 ± 0.24 ha). Our results underscore synergistic threats from sea-level rise and invasive species, suggesting managed hydrologic regimes and targeted *Phragmites* control could buffer populations. This study provides the first comprehensive viability analysis for tidal marsh passerines in North America’s largest estuary system.

We investigated migratory connectivity and habitat use in Swamp Sparrows (*Melospiza georgiana*) across their breeding range using stable hydrogen (δ²H), carbon (δ¹³C), and nitrogen (δ¹⁵N) isotope analysis of claw keratin. Claw samples from 167 individuals were collected at six breeding sites spanning the Atlantic coastal plain (Virginia to Maine) and interior wetlands (Great Lakes region) between 2018–2020. Isotope values were compared to spatial isoscape models and paired with GPS tracking data from 23 individuals to validate assignment accuracy. Results revealed significant regional divergence: coastal populations exhibited enriched δ¹³C values (−22.3 ± 1.7‰) consistent with brackish wintering habitats along the Chesapeake Bay, while interior breeders showed depleted δ¹³C (−26.1 ± 2.1‰) indicative of freshwater ecosystems in the Mississippi Alluvial Valley. Bayesian mixing models estimated that 68% of coastal migrants exhibited high site fidelity to natal wintering areas, compared to 42% in interior populations. Unexpectedly, δ¹⁵N signatures suggested increased anthropogenic nitrogen input in southern wintering grounds, correlating with reduced clutch sizes in subsequent breeding seasons (r = −0.54, p = 0.008). These findings highlight the vulnerability of coastal populations to sea-level rise and emphasize the need for coordinated habitat protection across migratory corridors. Our results challenge assumptions of panmixia in Swamp Sparrow migratory networks and provide a template for isotopic tracking in sedentary wetland songbirds facing habitat fragmentation.

We investigated the impacts of climate-mediated habitat shifts on Great Blue Heron (Ardea herodias) nesting success and foraging efficiency across 23 coastal colonies in the Salish Sea, British Columbia, from 2010 to 2022. Using GPS telemetry (n = 87 adults), drone-based nest censuses, and prey availability surveys, we documented a 42% decline in mean fledging success (2.1 ± 0.7 chicks/nest to 1.2 ± 0.5 chicks/nest) concurrent with a 17 cm rise in local sea levels. Mixed-effects models revealed tidal inundation of intertidal foraging zones explained 68% of variance in heron body condition indices (F₁,₂₁ = 29.3, p < 0.001), with a 3°C increase in summer sea surface temperatures correlating with 55% reduced catch rates of Pacific staghorn sculpin (Leptocottus armatus), a key prey species. Stable isotope analysis (δ¹⁵N, δ¹³C) of fledgling feathers showed a 23% decline in marine-derived nutrition compared to 2010 baselines. Coastal development scenarios projected under RCP 8.5 predict 89% loss of heron-frequented salt marshes by 2050, disproportionately affecting colonies within 2 km of urban centers (χ² = 14.7, p = 0.006). Our findings underscore the need for dynamic buffer zones around critical roosting sites and targeted restoration of estuarine transition habitats to enhance climate resilience in this culturally significant wading bird species.

We investigated the dietary shifts and reproductive consequences of invasive species interactions in Ring-billed Gulls (*Larus delawarenensis*) nesting in Lake Michigan colonies (43°02'N, 87°53'W) from 2018–2021. Using regurgitate analysis (n = 312 adults) and GPS tracking, we quantified the proportional consumption of invasive zebra mussels (*Dreissena polymorpha*) versus native prey items like emerald shiner (*Notropis atherinoides*) and aquatic insects.
