Gulls in colonies with high zebra mussel density (≥1,500 individuals/m²) derived 43.7 ± 8.2% of their diet from mussels—a 29% increase over pre-invasion historical data—while foraging effort increased by 18% (p < 0.05). Stable isotope analysis (δ¹⁵N, δ¹³C) revealed reduced trophic positioning in mussel-dependent individuals, correlating with 22% lower chick fledging success (R² = 0.67, p = 0.003) due to lower protein content in mussels compared to fish prey. Spatial overlap with invasive round goby (*Neogobius melanostomus*) altered nesting site selection, with 37% of gulls abandoning traditional rocky substrates for anthropogenic structures. Our results demonstrate how invasive species synergistically reshape gull foraging ecology, with cascading effects on reproductive output. Conservation strategies for this generalist species must now account for indirect nutritional limitations imposed by aquatic invaders, challenging traditional paradigms of gull population management in urbanized coastal ecosystems.

We investigated juvenile survival rates and drivers of mortality in Great Blue Herons (Ardea herodias) across six breeding colonies in the Chesapeake Bay estuary from 2018–2021. Using radio telemetry, we monitored 127 fledglings post-independence, tracking dispersal patterns and survival outcomes over 12 months. First-year survival averaged 42.1% (95% CI: 34.8–49.7%), with mortality peaking during initial coastal migrations (September–November) and winter months. Cox proportional hazards models identified storm frequency (HR = 1.87 per event, p < 0.001), urbanization of foraging sites (HR = 1.52, p = 0.003), and bald eagle (Haliaeetus leucocephalus) predation pressure (HR = 1.29, p = 0.04) as significant mortality predictors. Juveniles selecting oligohaline tributaries with submerged aquatic vegetation exhibited 38% higher survival than those utilizing urbanized shorelines. Stable isotope analysis (δ13C, δ15N) revealed surviving individuals consumed proportionally more mummichog (Fundulus heteroclitus) and fewer invasive blue catfish (Ictalurus furcatus), suggesting prey selectivity influences fitness. Survival rates showed strong interannual variation, ranging from 31.2% (2019, record hurricane season) to 51.6% (2021, mild winter). Our results underscore the importance of preserving fringe wetlands as transitional habitats and mitigating coastal development near heronries. These findings provide a framework for predictive population models under climate change scenarios and inform targeted conservation strategies for this ecologically pivotal wading bird species.

We investigated climate-driven hydrological shifts impacting Virginia Rail (*Rallus limicola*) populations across 12 Midwestern U.S. wetlands from 2010–2022. Using automated recording units (ARUs) and capture-recapture modeling, we documented a 42% decline in breeding site occupancy (95% CI: 37–47%) correlated with decreasing early-season water depths (r = 0.78, p < 0.001). Extreme precipitation variability reduced nest success rates from 58% (2010–2015) to 31% (2016–2022), with flooding events destroying 23% of monitored nests during peak incubation periods. Hydrological modeling projected 68–84% loss of suitable ephemeral wetlands under RCP 8.5 scenarios by 2050, disproportionately affecting northern breeding ranges in Minnesota and Wisconsin. Counterintuitively, adult survival increased 15% (p = 0.03) during drought years, suggesting trade-offs between habitat quality and predator avoidance in shrinking wetlands. Our stable isotope analysis (δ²H, δ¹³C) revealed shifts in foraging strategies, with rails increasingly utilizing invasive *Phalaris arundinacea* habitats despite lower invertebrate prey biomass. These findings challenge assumptions about rail resilience to environmental change and highlight threshold effects in wetland-dependent species. We propose dynamic water-level management and creation of artificial hummock microhabitats as climate adaptation strategies, emphasizing the need to preserve hydrological connectivity in agricultural landscapes where 73% of remaining rail habitat occurs.

We investigated migratory connectivity and habitat use in the Sedge Wren (Cistothorus platensis) across its North American range using stable isotope analysis of δ²H and δ¹³C in flight feathers. Feather samples from 150 individuals were collected at breeding sites (Manitoba, Ontario, Iowa) and wintering grounds (Texas, Mexico) between 2018–2021. Isotopic values were compared to precipitation-based isoscapes and regional vegetation baselines using discriminant function analysis and Bayesian mixing models. Results revealed weak migratory connectivity, with only 25% of breeding populations showing isotopic signatures matching predicted wintering latitudes. δ²H values ranged from -120‰ to -60‰ (mean = -85.3 ± 12.7‰), indicating substantial variation in molt locations. δ¹³C values (-28.4‰ to -22.1‰) suggested winter dietary shifts from C3-dominated prairie habitats to C4-influenced coastal marshes. Three distinct isotopic clusters emerged, corresponding to (1) northern breeders wintering in Tamaulipas mangrove systems, (2) central populations using Veracruz agricultural wetlands, and (3) a diffuse group with no clear geographic patterning. This contrasts with previous assumptions of strict longitudinal migration in this species. Conservation implications highlight the need to preserve heterogeneous wetland networks across multiple ecoregions rather than prioritizing discrete stopover sites. Our findings demonstrate how cryptic variation in habitat specialization, revealed through isotope tracers, necessitates refined management strategies for this declining grassland-obligate species (+2.1% annual population decline, Partners in Flight 2022). The study further establishes δ¹³C as a critical marker for tracking anthropogenic impacts on trophic pathways in rapidly changing agricultural wetlands.

We investigated the impacts of coastal habitat degradation on Least Bittern (Ixobrychus exilis) populations across 12 tidal marsh complexes in the Chesapeake Bay watershed from 2015–2020. Using a combination of GPS telemetry (n=47 individuals), habitat suitability modeling, and high-resolution land cover analysis, we documented a 32% reduction in preferred high marsh habitat dominated by _Schoenoplectus americanus_ and _Spartina patens_. Marsh fragmentation increased by 41% in areas experiencing >3 mm/yr relative sea-level rise, with bitterns in these zones exhibiting significantly longer inter-patch movement distances (x̄=1.7 km vs. 0.8 km in stable marshes; p<0.001). Nest survival probability declined from 0.68 to 0.42 in habitats with >15% invasive _Phragmites australis_ coverage. Multivariate analyses revealed salinity intrusion (>5 ppt) and anthropogenic shoreline hardening explained 63% of observed population declines. Remarkably, 22% of tracked individuals shifted to anthropogenic habitats, primarily drainage ditches in abandoned agricultural fields, though these sites showed 58% lower fledging success than natural marshes. Our results demonstrate nonlinear thresholds in bittern resilience, with critical habitat loss occurring when >35% of marsh platform converts to open water or transitional upland. These findings underscore the urgency of prioritizing sediment replenishment in drowning sub-estuaries and maintaining freshwater inputs to remaining bittern strongholds like the Blackwater River complex. Managed wetlands designed with microtopographic heterogeneity could partially offset losses, but must be paired with upland buffer zones to mitigate predation pressures amplified by habitat compression.

We investigated intraspecific morphological variation in Sora (Porzana carolina) across six North American breeding populations (2018-2022), analyzing 200 specimens from freshwater wetlands in the Mississippi Flyway, Chesapeake Bay, and Prairie Pothole Region. Morphometric measurements (culmen length, tarsus diameter, wing chord) and body mass data revealed significant latitudinal clines, with northern populations (Minnesota, Manitoba) exhibiting 8.7% larger mean wing chords (F = 14.3, p < 0.001) and 6.2% higher mass-volume ratios compared to southern cohorts (Louisiana, Texas). Sexual dimorphism followed reversed patterns from typical rallids, with females exceeding male mass by 11.4% (95% CI: 9.8-13.1%) in post-breeding adults. Multivariate analysis (MANOVA) identified three distinct morphotypes corresponding to hydrological regimes: temporary floodplain populations showed reduced tarsus robustness (x̄ = 3.1 ± 0.2 mm vs. 3.9 ± 0.3 mm in permanent marsh groups, p = 0.004). Stable isotope analysis (δ¹³C, δ¹⁵N) of rectrices correlated culmen dimensions with aquatic vs. terrestrial foraging strategies (R² = 0.47). These results challenge assumptions of uniform allometric growth in marsh specialists and suggest climate-driven habitat fragmentation may disproportionately affect northern morphotypes adapted to seasonal ice dynamics. We recommend incorporating ecotype-specific criteria into wetland restoration designs to maintain adaptive morphological diversity in this IUCN Near Threatened species.

We investigated intraspecific morphological variation in Sora (Porzana carolina) across 12 freshwater emergent wetlands in the Prairie Pothole Region of North Dakota, USA, from 2018 to 2021. Using mist-netting and morphological measurements (n = 356 adults), we quantified sexual dimorphism and geographic variation in body mass, bill length, tarsus length, and wing chord. Multivariate analysis revealed significant sexual size dimorphism (p < 0.001), with males exhibiting 8.3% greater body mass (mean ± SD: 92.5 ± 14.2 g vs 85.4 ± 12.7 g) and 5.1% longer wing chords than females. Principal component analysis segregated populations along a moisture gradient, with birds from permanent wetlands showing 6.2% shorter tarsi (23.4 ± 1.1 mm) and 4.7% deeper bills (18.9 ± 0.9 mm) compared to seasonal wetland counterparts. Seasonal morphometric shifts were observed, with post-breeding adults averaging 7.1% higher body mass than pre-breeding individuals (p = 0.003). Unexpectedly, we found a positive correlation between bill length and δ¹³C values from feather analysis (r = 0.42, p = 0.012), suggesting trophic specialization linked to bill morphology. These results demonstrate previously undocumented phenotypic plasticity in Soras, with implications for wetland conservation strategies. Habitat fragmentation models suggest that loss of intermediate-depth wetlands may disproportionately affect populations with specialized morphotypes, potentially reducing adaptive capacity under climate change scenarios. Our findings highlight the need for maintaining wetland complexes with diverse hydroperiods to preserve morphological diversity in this cryptic rallid species.

We investigated the impacts of wetland management practices on Common Loon (Gavia immer) breeding success and habitat selection across 24 managed wetlands in the Laurentian Great Lakes region (2018–2022). Using GPS telemetry (n = 47 adults) and weekly nest monitoring, we quantified relationships between water chemistry, shoreline development, and loon reproductive output. Multivariate analyses revealed that wetlands with pH < 6.2 supported 63% fewer fledged chicks than neutral sites (p = 0.017), correlating with reduced prey fish biomass (r = 0.78, p < 0.001). Loons exhibited strong avoidance of shorelines with >15% artificial structures (OR = 0.32, 95% CI: 0.18–0.54), yet 38% of managed sites exceeded this threshold. Mercury concentrations in blood samples (n = 112) averaged 3.2 ppm (SD ±1.1), with 22% of adults exceeding toxicity thresholds associated with reduced chick provisioning rates. Hydrological stabilization measures increased loon occupancy probability by 41% (ΔAICc = 2.3) compared to unmanaged fluctuating wetlands. Our results demonstrate that current acidification mitigation strategies insufficiently address loon dietary requirements, while shoreline hardening practices directly reduce breeding habitat availability. We recommend revising wetland management protocols to prioritize buffer zones ≥50 m, mercury mitigation in watersheds, and dynamic water-level regimes that mimic natural flood pulses. These findings have critical implications for sustaining loon populations under increasing anthropogenic pressure across northern temperate wetlands.

We investigated the impacts of contaminant exposure on Black-crowned Night-Heron (Nycticorax nycticorax) populations within urbanized wetlands of the Great Lakes Basin (2018-2022). Blood and egg samples from 127 adults and 234 nests across six colonies revealed elevated concentrations of polychlorinated biphenyls (PCBs: 2.3-18.7 μg/g wet weight), mercury (0.85-4.2 μg/g), and perfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS: 34-288 ng/g). Hepatic cytochrome P450 enzyme activity in adults showed strong positive correlations with PCB burden (R²=0.67, p<0.001). Nesting success declined significantly with increasing egg contaminant loads, with a 45% reduction in hatching rates between quartiles of lowest versus highest PCB exposure (χ²=23.8, p=0.001). Stable isotope analysis (δ¹⁵N, δ¹³C) demonstrated biomagnification factors of 3.1-5.8 for mercury through the herons' aquatic food web. Contaminant loads exceeded toxicity thresholds for avian reproduction in 38% of sampled individuals, with colonies near industrial point sources showing 2.3× higher mean PCB concentrations than reference sites. Our findings suggest chronic exposure to legacy pollutants and emerging contaminants may be driving the species' 6.2% annual population decline in the study region, highlighting the need for targeted sediment remediation in critical foraging habitats. This study provides novel evidence linking sublethal contaminant exposure to demographic impacts in a cryptic urban-adapted Ardeid species.

We investigated stopover site selection and duration in Eastern Wild Turkeys (*Meleagris gallopavo*) across a 12,000 km² forest-agriculture matrix in the Ozark Highlands, Arkansas, using GPS telemetry data from 78 individuals (2018–2022). Contrary to expectations of nomadic winter movements, resource selection functions revealed turkeys exhibited limited stopover behavior during seasonal range shifts (<3% of locations at potential stopover sites). Individuals traversed fragmented landscapes rapidly (mean movement rate: 1.2 km/day ± 0.4 SD) with high fidelity to core winter and breeding ranges (mean overlap: 82%). Stopover events (≥48 hr in a 1 km² area) occurred primarily at ecotones between mixed hardwood forests and agricultural clearings, but showed no consistent association with food availability metrics (acorn abundance: *p* = 0.34; insect biomass: *p* = 0.21). Multivariate analysis identified proximity to roost trees (≤200 m; *p* < 0.01) and reduced coyote (*Canis latrans*) density (*p* = 0.02) as primary predictors of transient habitat use. Results challenge assumptions of facultative migration strategies in galliforms and suggest turkeys prioritize predator avoidance over foraging optimization during dispersal. These findings underscore the importance of maintaining contiguous forest corridors with dense canopy cover, rather than prioritizing small-scale stopover habitats, in regional management plans for this culturally significant game species.

We investigated the effects of heavy metal contamination on Yellow Warbler (Setophaga petechia) populations across a gradient of riparian habitats in southern Ontario’s lower Great Lakes basin. From 2018–2022, we sampled blood mercury (Hg) and lead (Pb) concentrations in 342 adult warblers and monitored reproductive success at 167 nests within three watersheds exposed to agricultural runoff and legacy industrial pollution. Birds in contaminated sites exhibited 45% higher blood Hg (mean ± SE: 1.27 ± 0.14 μg/g) compared to reference populations (0.88 ± 0.09 μg/g), with Pb levels exceeding toxicity thresholds (>20 μg/dL) in 18% of individuals near former smelting zones. Nesting success declined by 32% in high-pollution areas, with clutch sizes reduced by 12% (4.1 vs. 4.6 eggs) and fledgling counts 27% lower than reference sites. Multivariate models revealed Hg exposure explained 41% of variance in fledging success after controlling for habitat quality and invertebrate prey availability. Stable isotope analysis (δ¹⁵N, δ¹³C) confirmed trophic transfer of contaminants through aquatic-emergent insects constituting >60% of nestling diets. Longitudinal data showed a 15% annual decline in male territory occupancy within contaminated floodplains, contrasted with stable reference populations. Our findings demonstrate sublethal pollution effects disproportionately impacting riparian songbirds through dietary pathways, with implications for wetland remediation strategies and bioindicator frameworks under Canada’s Environmental Protection Act. Mitigation efforts targeting sediment-bound contaminants may enhance resilience in this declining Neotropical migrant population.

We assessed population genomic structure and genetic diversity across 12 major breeding colonies of Northern Gannets (Morus bassanus) spanning the North Atlantic to evaluate vulnerability to emerging environmental pressures. Using restriction site-associated DNA sequencing (RAD-seq), we genotyped 3,893 single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) from 214 individuals collected between 2015-2022. Analysis revealed low but significant differentiation among colonies (FST = 0.012, p < 0.001), with subtle isolation-by-distance patterns explaining 34% of genetic variance (Mantel test r = 0.58). Colonies in the eastern Atlantic (Norway, UK, Iceland) showed 18% lower heterozygosity (He = 0.21 ± 0.03) compared to western Atlantic populations (He = 0.26 ± 0.02), potentially reflecting historical founder effects during post-glacial expansion. Temporal comparisons at Bass Rock (UK, n = 48) revealed a 9% decline in effective population size (Ne) from 2015 (Ne = 1,240) to 2022 (Ne = 1,128), coinciding with mass mortality events from avian influenza. Migration rate estimates using BayesAss indicated asymmetric dispersal, with 4.7% annual emigration from Gulf of St. Lawrence colonies to European sites versus 1.2% reverse flow. These findings suggest that while panmixia persists at broad scales, recent climate-driven prey shifts and disease outbreaks may be exacerbating genetic erosion in key populations. We advocate integrating genomic monitoring with international habitat protection measures to maintain adaptive potential in this central-place forager facing rapid marine ecosystem changes.

We investigated the spatial ecology and habitat selection of Marsh Wrens (Cistothorus palustris) in fragmented wetland ecosystems of California's Sacramento-San Joaquin Delta using miniaturized radio-transmitters (0.45 g) deployed on 30 adults (15 males, 15 females) during the 2018-2020 breeding seasons. Movement data revealed significantly larger home ranges in males (2.8 ± 0.6 ha) compared to females (1.2 ± 0.3 ha; p < 0.001), with maximum daily displacements of 1.2 km during territory establishment. Resource selection functions indicated strong preference for areas with 60-80% emergent vegetation cover (β = 1.34, SE = 0.21) and avoidance of open water features >5 m wide (β = -0.89, SE = 0.15). Survival analysis demonstrated 28% lower overwinter site fidelity in populations occupying invasive hybrid cordgrass (Spartina alterniflora × foliosa) habitats compared to native tule (Schoenoplectus acutus) stands. Telemetry data revealed a critical 14-day post-fledging period where juvenile dispersal success correlated positively with contiguous vegetation corridors (r = 0.72, p = 0.003). These findings highlight the species' vulnerability to habitat fragmentation and suggest current tidal marsh restoration targets underestimate microhabitat structural requirements. Management strategies prioritizing <50 m spacing between vegetated patches and maintaining water depths <30 cm during nesting could enhance reproductive success in anthropogenically altered estuaries.

We investigated the vocal repertoire and environmental drivers of acoustic variation in Double-crested Cormorants (*Phalacrocorax auritus*) across five breeding colonies in the Great Lakes region (Lake Erie and Lake Ontario, 2018–2021). Using autonomous recorders (400 hours) deployed within 50 m of nesting aggregations, we quantified 2,150 adult vocalizations with Raven Pro 1.6, measuring frequency modulation, duration, and amplitude. Three distinct call types were identified: territorial "growls" (mean frequency 0.85 ± 0.12 kHz), nest-directed "grunts" (1.32 ± 0.18 kHz), and alarm "hisses" (broadband 2–5 kHz). Generalized linear mixed models revealed wind speed (β = -0.27, *p* = 0.003) and colony density (β = 0.41, *p* < 0.001) as primary predictors of call frequency plasticity. High-density colonies exhibited 18% greater vocal complexity than low-density sites, with call redundancy decreasing during peak courtship periods. Playback experiments demonstrated 73% response rates to conspecific territorial calls versus 22% to heterospecific controls. However, anthropogenic noise from commercial shipping routes overlapping two colonies reduced acoustic active space by 40% (95% CI: 32–48%), as modeled via sound propagation analyses. These results highlight vocal adaptability to social and environmental conditions but suggest cumulative stressors may disrupt intra-colony communication. We recommend expanding acoustic buffer zones beyond current 500-m protections to mitigate auditory masking in this IUCN Least Concern species, particularly along migratory corridors with intensifying vessel traffic.

We investigated intraspecific morphological variation in Great Blue Herons (Ardea herodias) across a latitudinal gradient spanning 1,200 km of North America’s Atlantic coast. From 2018–2021, 387 adult individuals were captured at six estuarine sites between Maine (43.8°N) and Virginia (37.2°N), with standardized measurements of body mass, culmen length, tarsus diameter, and wing chord recorded. Multivariate analysis revealed significant clinal variation, with northern populations exhibiting 12.3% greater mean body mass (1,982 ± 167 g vs. 1,765 ± 142 g; p < 0.001) and 7.1% longer wing chords (472 ± 18 mm vs. 441 ± 15 mm; p = 0.003) compared to southern cohorts. Sexual dimorphism accounted for 22% of variance in structural measurements (males: 14% larger in linear dimensions; p = 0.012), but did not explain geographic trends. Stable isotope analysis (δ¹⁵N, δ¹³C) of breast feathers indicated dietary specialization in northern birds, with higher trophic positioning correlated with increased body size (r = 0.67, p = 0.028). Coastal development intensity, quantified through GIS land-use analysis, showed inverse relationships with heron morphometrics at breeding sites (R² = 0.81 for culmen length vs. wetland loss). These results demonstrate previously undocumented phenotypic plasticity in a widespread wading bird, suggesting local adaptation to latitudinal gradients in prey availability and anthropogenic habitat modification. Conservation strategies for A. herodias may require regional differentiation to address evolving pressures on coastal morphotypes.

We investigated molt migration patterns in Sora (Porzana carolina) across their North American breeding range using GPS telemetry (n=42 adults) and stable hydrogen isotope analysis of flight feathers (δ²Hf) from 327 individuals. Birds captured at Upper Midwest breeding sites (Minnesota, Wisconsin; 2018-2021) exhibited a bimodal migration strategy, with 68% undertaking directed movements to coastal Louisiana and Texas tidal marshes before initiating primary feather molt. Remaining individuals delayed migration up to 28 days (±5.3 SE) while undergoing body molt in northern palustrine wetlands, prioritizing fattening rates (0.52 g/day ±0.11) over predator avoidance. Molt duration varied significantly between cohorts (coastal: 34.7 days ±2.1 vs. northern: 41.9 days ±3.4; p<0.01), with coastal molters showing 23% higher post-molt survival based on mark-recapture data. Isotope signatures revealed 19% of wintering populations in Central America originated from northern molt sites, challenging assumptions about molt-related habitat specialization. Motus tower detections confirmed rapid nocturnal migration bursts (mean 382 km/night ±89) between molt sites and wintering areas. Our results demonstrate facultative molt strategies mediated by wetland productivity gradients, with coastal marsh molters achieving higher pre-migration body condition indices (x̄=2.84 g/mm ±0.21 vs. 2.37 ±0.19). Conservation prioritization should address hydrological threats to coastal molting habitats, where 82% of tracked individuals showed high site fidelity despite sea level rise impacts. These findings redefine Sora as a molt-migration specialist among Rallidae, with energy allocation trade-offs influencing continental-scale population dynamics.

We investigated population dynamics of Common Yellowthroat (*Geothlypis trichas*) across a 12-year period (2010–2022) in the Midwestern United States, analyzing breeding success, survival rates, and habitat-mediated drivers of decline. Using mark-recapture data from 1,243 individuals at 27 wetland-associated sites in Iowa, Illinois, and Indiana, we integrated Breeding Bird Survey trends with intensive field surveys to quantify annual survival (φ = 0.52 ± 0.07 SE), recruitment rates (γ = 0.31 ± 0.05 SE), and territory fidelity. Multistate models revealed a 38% decline in adult survival correlated with wetland fragmentation (β = -0.19, 95% CI: -0.27 to -0.11), while recruitment decreased by 22% in areas with <30% riparian shrub cover. Nest monitoring (n = 612) showed brood parasitism by Brown-headed Cowbirds (*Molothrus ater*) reduced fledging success by 43% in edge habitats versus core wetlands. Climate covariates explained 18% of interannual variability, with extreme spring precipitation events lowering juvenile dispersal distances (radio-telemetry data: n = 187, mean = 1.7 ± 0.3 km vs. 3.1 ± 0.4 km in dry years). Agricultural encroachment within 500 m of breeding sites increased extinction risk for local populations (hazard ratio = 2.4, p < 0.001). Our results emphasize the vulnerability of this Neotropical migrant to synergistic pressures, advocating for wetland buffer zones ≥100 m and targeted restoration of emergent vegetation to stabilize metapopulation dynamics. Bayesian hierarchical models project a 29% range contraction by 2050 without adaptive management, highlighting urgent conservation needs for riparian songbirds in working landscapes.

Recent population fluctuations of Ring-billed Gulls (Larus delawarensis) in the Laurentian Great Lakes region prompted a 12-year study (2010–2021) examining demographic drivers and environmental correlates. Using a combination of aerial colony surveys, resightings of 4,582 color-banded individuals, and GPS tracking of 87 adults, we quantified regional population declines of 32% (95% CI: 28–36%) concurrent with reduced annual adult survival (0.89 to 0.82) and clutch sizes (2.7 to 2.1 eggs/nest). Multistate models revealed differential site fidelity between males and females, with dispersing individuals preferentially selecting urban habitats over traditional island colonies. Paradoxically, urban-nesting gulls exhibited 18% lower fledging success than island-nesting counterparts despite higher anthropogenic food availability. Isotopic analysis (δ¹⁵N, δ¹³C) of 347 eggshell membranes demonstrated significant trophic shifts linked to declines in historically critical prey fish species (rainbow smelt Osmerus mordax, 73% biomass reduction), forcing increased reliance on terrestrial food sources. Breeding phenology advanced by 9.2 days since 1990, creating mismatches with remaining aquatic prey availability. Our results challenge assumptions about urban adaptivity in Larids, demonstrating that apparent habitat generalists may face complex constraints from interacting nutritional, climatic, and competitive pressures. Conservation strategies must address both coastal zone management and urban waste policies to prevent continued population erosion in this ecologically pivotal species.

We investigated habitat selection patterns of Redhead ducks (*Aythya americana*) across their annual cycle in the Prairie Pothole Region (PPR) of North Dakota and wintering grounds in Laguna Madre, Texas, from 2018 to 2021. Using GPS transmitters deployed on 75 female Redheads, we quantified habitat use relative to wetland characteristics, vegetation cover, and anthropogenic disturbance. Resource selection functions (RSFs) revealed strong selection for permanent wetlands with emergent vegetation during breeding (β = 1.24, SE = 0.18, p < 0.001), avoiding cropland-dominated areas (β = -0.89, SE = 0.21, p = 0.003). Wintering birds preferentially occupied hypersaline lagoons with submerged aquatic vegetation (SAV) biomass > 500 g/m² (odds ratio = 3.7, 95% CI: 2.1–6.5), despite declining SAV coverage linked to coastal development. Breeding site fidelity was high (78% of individuals returned within 5 km of prior nests), but wetland drainage reduced available habitat by 12% annually in core breeding areas. Dynamic occupancy models identified water depth fluctuations as the primary driver of winter habitat suitability (ΔAIC = 15.7 vs. null model). Our results highlight the vulnerability of Redheads to synergistic effects of agricultural expansion and climate-mediated hydrologic shifts. Conservation strategies must prioritize wetland complexes ≥40 ha in the PPR and SAV restoration in Gulf Coast estuaries to mitigate carrying capacity declines. Future research should address carryover effects between seasonal habitats on reproductive success.

We conducted a 7-year demographic study (2015–2022) of Least Tern (Sternula antillarum) populations across 23 barrier island colonies in the northern Gulf of Mexico, analyzing survival rates, fecundity, and recruitment dynamics. Using capture-mark-recapture (CMR) data from 1,243 banded individuals and nest monitoring of 687 breeding pairs, we quantified a 62% decline in nesting pairs since 2003, with the steepest reductions occurring at mainland beach sites (78% loss) compared to dredge spoil islands (41% loss). Annual adult survival probability averaged 0.78 (±0.04 SE) based on Cormack-Jolly-Seber models, while first-year survival was critically low at 0.32 (±0.07 SE). Fledging success (0.8 chicks/pair) fell below estimated replacement thresholds (1.2 chicks/pair) in 80% of study colonies. Multivariate analysis identified tidal overwash events (β = -0.41, p < 0.001) and mammalian predator density (β = -0.33, p = 0.008) as primary drivers of nest failure. Experimental predator exclusion on five islands increased fledging success by 58% (p = 0.03), while colonies near active dredging sites exhibited 40% higher site fidelity (p = 0.02). Our matrix projection models indicate current demographic rates cannot sustain 72% of existing subpopulations without targeted management. These results underscore the urgent need for adaptive habitat creation strategies, particularly artificial sandbars engineered to reduce flood risk, which supported 37% higher chick survival in pilot interventions. This study provides critical baselines for assessing climate change impacts on beach-nesting seabirds and informs regional recovery plans under the U.S. Endangered Species Act.

We investigated predator-prey dynamics of Horned Grebes (*Podiceps auritus*) across 12 boreal wetland complexes in Alberta, Canada, from 2018 to 2021. Using GPS telemetry (n = 47 adults), fecal DNA metabarcoding, and nest camera traps, we quantified diet composition, predation rates, and habitat-mediated risk. Grebes exhibited a 68% reliance on larval odonates and trichopterans during pre-laying, shifting to small fish (36% of diet biomass) post-hatching. Nest survival probability (0.42 ± 0.07 SE) correlated negatively with water-level variability (β = -1.32, p = 0.003) and proximity to mammalian predator trails. American mink (*Neovison vison*) accounted for 58% of confirmed predation events (n = 31), with daily predation rates peaking during incubation (0.023 ± 0.005 SE). Generalized linear mixed models revealed a 3.2× increase in mink activity following seasonal drawdowns of reservoir-fed wetlands. Counterintuitively, grebes nesting in habitats with 15–30% submerged vegetation cover experienced 22% lower predation than more densely vegetated sites, suggesting trade-offs between concealment and predator ambush efficiency. Our results demonstrate how hydroperiod manipulation for waterfowl management inadvertently elevates predation pressure on Horned Grebes, highlighting the need for adaptive wetland stewardship balancing competing conservation priorities for diving birds.

We investigated the breeding biology of Swamp Sparrows (Melospiza georgiana) across 12 freshwater marshes in the Chesapeake Bay estuary from 2018–2020. Using systematic nest monitoring (n = 237 nests) and radio-telemetry (n = 58 adults), we quantified habitat selection, reproductive success, and renesting behavior. Nest survival analysis revealed a daily survival rate of 0.963 (95% CI: 0.952–0.972), yielding a 42% probability of survival from egg laying to fledging. Clutch size averaged 3.8 ± 0.2 eggs (range: 3–5), with significantly higher hatching success in nests constructed in sedge (Carex stricta)-dominated vegetation (78%) compared to mixed graminoid habitats (64%; p = 0.03). Nestling provisioning rates (5.2 ± 1.1 visits/hr) showed strong correlation with aquatic invertebrate biomass (r = 0.71, p < 0.001). Hydrologic regime emerged as a critical driver of breeding phenology, with a 15-day advancement in first egg dates during drought years (2018, 2020) compared to the flood year (2019). Restoration marshes (<10 years post-rehabilitation) exhibited 28% lower nest survival than reference sites due to reduced structural complexity (stem density: 143 ± 21 vs. 218 ± 34 stems/m²). Renesting intervals averaged 10.3 days post-failure, with 18% of females successfully producing double broods. Our results highlight the vulnerability of Swamp Sparrow populations to hydrological extremes and suboptimal habitat conditions in restored wetlands, emphasizing the need for marsh management strategies that maintain heterogeneous vegetation structure and stabilize water tables during critical nesting periods (May–July).

We investigated the daily energy expenditure (DEE) of breeding Forster's Terns (Sterna forsteri) in relation to wetland habitat changes and prey availability across five colonies in the Great Salt Lake ecosystem, Utah, USA. Using doubly labeled water (DLW) and accelerometry, we measured energy budgets of 40 adults during incubation and chick-rearing phases (June–July 2022). Results showed mean DEE of 2.8 ± 0.4 kJ g⁻¹ day⁻¹ during incubation, increasing to 4.1 ± 0.6 kJ g⁻¹ day⁻¹ during chick-rearing (p < 0.001). Birds in habitats with reduced aquatic invertebrate biomass (≤12 mg/m³) exhibited 18% higher foraging effort and 22% greater energy expenditure compared to sites with stable prey resources. Temperature-regulated thermoregulatory costs accounted for 15–28% of total DEE during peak afternoon heat (34–38°C). Terns commuting >6 km between nests and foraging sites showed 31% higher DEE than those with foraging ranges <2 km (F₁,₃₈ = 9.24, p = 0.004). Our isotopic analysis (δ¹⁵N, δ¹³C) revealed a 63% reduction in preferred fish prey consumption compared to pre-drought (2017) levels, correlating with increased time-activity budgets spent plunge-diving (42 vs. 28 min/hr). These findings suggest that cascading effects from the lake's 2021 megadrought and salinification crisis (24.5% salinity increase) have created an ecological trap, requiring terns to allocate 38% more energy to self-maintenance at the expense of chick provisioning. Conservation strategies must address hydrological connectivity and brine shrimp management to mitigate escalating energetic trade-offs in this climate-vulnerable species.

We investigated sex-specific parental care strategies in Caspian Terns (Hydroprogne caspia) across three breeding seasons (2018–2020) at a mixed-colony site on Gotland, Sweden. Using GPS loggers (n = 48 adults) and 1,240 hours of behavioral observations, we quantified nest attendance, provisioning rates, and chick growth outcomes relative to environmental variables (water temperature, herring abundance). Males delivered 73% of total prey items (x̄ = 4.2 ±1.1 fish/hr vs. females’ 1.6 ±0.7), while females spent 62% more time incubating and brooding (p <0.001). Chick survival to fledging varied significantly with parental coordination (r² = 0.41, p = 0.003), declining by 22% in years with low herring availability. Unexpectedly, 31% of males engaged in transient foraging excursions >50 km from the colony during chick-rearing, correlated with a 15% decrease in partner body condition (GLMM, β = -0.18, SE = 0.05). Stable isotope analysis revealed sex-based dietary partitioning (δ¹⁵N: males 12.3‰ vs. females 10.8‰), suggesting males target larger, offshore prey. Our results highlight vulnerability to asynchronous environmental pressures: declining Baltic Sea fish stocks disproportionately impact male foraging efficiency, while coastal development disrupts female nest site fidelity. Conservation strategies must address sex-specific resource requirements to mitigate reproductive failure in this declining seabird (IUCN Near Threatened).

We investigated the relationship between resource availability and parental care strategies in Canvasbacks (Aythya valisineria) across six breeding seasons (2018–2023) in the Prairie Pothole Region of North Dakota and Minnesota. Using radio telemetry (n = 78 females, 52 males) and 4,200 nest-hours of behavioral observation, we quantified brood attendance, provisioning rates, and habitat selection patterns. Females nesting in wetlands with ≥35% submerged aquatic invertebrate biomass exhibited 42% higher daily brood survival (Cox PH model: HR = 0.58, 95% CI 0.47–0.72) compared to those in resource-poor habitats. Isotopic analysis of eggshell membranes (δ15N, δ13C) revealed that females consuming amphipod-dominated diets produced ducklings with 28% faster growth rates (linear mixed model: β = 2.14, SE = 0.89, p = 0.003) than those relying on plant material. Contrary to predictions, male Canvasbacks showed no territorial defense or provisioning behavior post-hatching, with 93% departing brood-rearing wetlands within 72 hours. Drought conditions in 2021 reduced wetland invertebrate biomass by 61%, triggering a 400% increase in brood abandonment rates compared to wet years. Our results demonstrate that Canvasback parental investment is tightly coupled to protein availability, with implications for conservation strategies targeting wetland complexes that sustain high invertebrate productivity. Climate-driven hydrological variability and agricultural runoff pose critical threats to this trophic linkage, necessitating dynamic management of water-level regimes in key breeding areas.

We investigated juvenile survival rates in Herring Gulls (*Larus argentatus*) across a metapopulation in the East Frisian Islands, Germany, from 2018 to 2022. Using a combination of GPS tracking (n = 150 fledglings), mark-resight analyses, and environmental covariate modeling, we assessed how anthropogenic pressures and habitat selection influenced first-year survival. Individuals hatched in urban colonies exhibited significantly lower survival probabilities (62.3% ± 4.1 SE) compared to those from natural dune habitats (81.7% ± 3.6 SE; Cox PH model: HR = 2.41, p < 0.001). Mortality risks peaked during post-fledging dispersal, with 68% of deaths attributed to anthropogenic causes (vehicle collisions, plastic ingestion, and predation by invasive raccoons *Procyon lotor*). Resource selection functions revealed strong associations between survival and proximity to fishery waste sites (β = 0.87, 95% CI: 0.52–1.22), though gulls foraging >5 km from landfills showed higher blood lead concentrations (14.2 µg/dL vs. 8.7 µg/dL, p = 0.03). Contrary to expectations, winter severity (North Atlantic Oscillation index) had minimal influence on survival (ΔAICc < 2). Our findings highlight the ecological trap potential of urban nesting sites and demonstrate how marine resource subsidies buffer juvenile mortality in coastal populations. Management strategies prioritizing reduced anthropogenic food availability and invasive predator control could increase recruitment rates by 19–27%, critical for this declining subspecies (*L. a. argentatus*) facing a 5.8% annual population decrease. These results underscore the need to integrate terrestrial and marine conservation planning for coastal seabirds.

We investigated parental care dynamics in Northern Bobwhite (Colinus virginianus) across 12 sites in the Piedmont region of Georgia, USA, from 2018 to 2021, using a combination of radio-telemetry, nest cameras, and behavioral observations. Nest attendance patterns revealed biparental care in 68% of monitored nests (n = 75), with males contributing 43% of total incubation duties—significantly higher than previously reported for this species. Chick-rearing adults exhibited distinct spatial partitioning, with males preferentially using shrub-dominated habitats (χ² = 8.31, p = 0.004) while females occupied open grasslands. Survival analysis (Cox proportional hazards model) showed biparentally tended broods had 62% higher 21-day post-fledging survival compared to single-parent broods (HR = 0.38, 95% CI: 0.24–0.61). However, 22% of males abandoned broods during drought conditions (Palmer Drought Severity Index ≤ -3), disproportionately impacting populations in intensively farmed landscapes. Our GPS tracking data (n = 60 adults) demonstrated that successful co-parenting pairs maintained overlapping home ranges ≤15 ha, while failed pairs showed 83% greater spatial divergence. These findings challenge assumptions of female-dominated care in galliforms and highlight the ecological sensitivity of paternal investment. Conservation strategies for this declining species should prioritize habitat configurations that facilitate coordinated parental behavior, particularly maintaining shrub-grassland ecotones within 200 m of nest sites.

We conducted a 12-year demographic study (2010–2022) of Great Blue Heron (Ardea herodias) populations across 23 breeding colonies in the Pacific Northwest and Chesapeake Bay watersheds. Using a combination of mark-recapture (n = 1,243 individuals), nest monitoring (4,517 nests), and satellite tracking, we quantified age-specific survival rates, reproductive success, and dispersal patterns. Adult annual survival averaged 0.78 ± 0.04 SE, while first-year survival was significantly lower (0.32 ± 0.07 SE). Nest success declined by 18% over the study period, with daily survival rates negatively correlated with April precipitation (β = -0.21, p = 0.03) and bald eagle (Haliaeetus leucocephalus) attack frequency (β = -0.34, p = 0.01). Bayesian population projection models indicated a λ of 0.94 (95% CI: 0.89–0.98), suggesting regional declines. Dispersal distances averaged 42.3 km (range 3–278 km), with 14% of adults exhibiting inter-colony movements between breeding seasons. Surprisingly, urban-adjacent colonies showed 22% higher fledging success than remote sites, potentially linked to anthropogenic food subsidies. Tidal amplitude emerged as a significant predictor of nest survival in coastal colonies (β = 0.17, p = 0.04), highlighting vulnerability to sea-level rise. These results underscore the need for landscape-scale management of heronries, including buffer zone enforcement, predator population control, and climate resilience planning for low-lying coastal habitats.

We investigated sex-specific parental care strategies in Northern Harriers (Circus hudsonius) across 27 breeding pairs in prairie wetlands of North Dakota and Montana (2018-2020). Using GPS-GSM transmitters (n=54 adults) and nest cameras, we quantified prey delivery rates, nest attendance, and habitat use patterns relative to asynchronous hatching. Males delivered 82.3% of prey items (x̄ = 4.2 ± 1.1 deliveries/day) versus 17.7% by females (x̄ = 0.9 ± 0.3 deliveries/day; p<0.001), with delivery frequency positively correlated with brood size (R²=0.71). Females exhibited 93% nest attendance during early brood-rearing, allocating 47% of hunting time to within 1.2 km of nests compared to males' 12% (p=0.004). Sexual size dimorphism (females 22% heavier) significantly predicted differential prey selection: females captured larger prey (x̄=126g vs. males' 84g; p=0.03) despite lower capture rates. Energy expenditure modeling revealed males traveled 18.7 km/day versus females' 5.3 km/day (p<0.001), with males preferentially hunting over native grasslands versus females' use of agricultural margins (χ²=14.2, p=0.002). Reproductive success declined 38% in territories with >40% cultivated land, linked to reduced paternal provisioning capacity. Our findings demonstrate how sexual role specialization creates distinct conservation priorities, emphasizing the need to preserve large grassland tracts (>200 ha) to support male hunting efficiency while maintaining wetland buffers for female-centric nest protection.

We analyzed 12 years (2010–2022) of demographic data from a Bald Eagle (*Haliaeetus leucocephalus*) population nesting across the Chesapeake Bay watershed to quantify vital rates and identify drivers of regional population dynamics. Using mark-recapture (n = 417 banded individuals) and satellite telemetry (n = 32 adults), we estimated annual adult survival at 0.92 ± 0.03 SE, with anthropogenic mortality (electrocution, lead toxicity) accounting for 68% of adult fatalities. Nest monitoring at 127 territories revealed mean fledging success declined from 1.8 ± 0.2 to 1.3 ± 0.1 chicks per active nest following consecutive years of extreme precipitation events (Ψ = 0.89, p < 0.01), potentially linked to reduced prey availability. Dispersal patterns showed juveniles exhibited high philopatry, with 73% establishing territories within 50 km of natal sites, creating localized density-dependent effects on reproductive output (R² = 0.41). Blood lead concentrations ≥10 μg/dL were detected in 39% of sampled adults (n = 154), correlating with elevated overwinter mortality (HR = 2.4, 95% CI 1.6–3.5). Our matrix population model projected a 22% population decline by 2035 under current lead exposure rates, highlighting the critical need for regulations on lead ammunition and fishing tackle. These results demonstrate how localized contaminant exposure and climate-driven resource fluctuations can undermine long-term viability even in a federally delisted raptor species.

We investigated the effects of climate-driven hydrological changes on Horned Grebe (*Podiceps auritus*) breeding success across 17 boreal lakes in Alberta, Canada, from 1995–2022. Using demographic data from 2,347 nests and environmental variables (ice-out dates, seasonal precipitation, wetland area), we quantified population declines of 62% (95% CI: 54–69%) concurrent with a 3.2-day per decade advance in spring ice melt. Nest survival models revealed a critical threshold: when May temperatures exceeded 12.4°C (historical average: 8.7°C), daily predation rates increased by 38% due to phenological mismatches with amphibian prey abundance. Remote sensing showed a 21% reduction in stable wetland habitats since 2005, disproportionately affecting lakes with <2 m maximum depth. Drought frequency tripled over the study period, with grebes abandoning 73% of territories during extreme dry years (PDSI < -3). Counterintuitively, earlier ice clearance reduced chick survival by exposing juveniles to heightened bald eagle (*Haliaeetus leucocephalus*) predation during peak vulnerability periods. Our integrated population model (AICc weight = 0.89) identified wetland permanence and invertebrate biomass as stronger predictors of fecundity than temperature alone. These findings highlight the collapse of shallow aquatic ecosystems as a climate change multiplier, necessitating immediate protection of remaining glacial-fed lakes and artificial wetland creation to maintain >40% emergent vegetation cover for this IUCN Vulnerable species.

We investigated seasonal resource use and habitat selection in Eastern Wild Turkeys (Meleagris gallopavo silvestris) across a mixed-landscape gradient in the Appalachian foothills (Tennessee and Virginia, USA) using stable isotope analysis of δ13C and δ15N in claw keratin. Claw samples from 126 adults and 87 juveniles were collected during 2018–2021 alongside GPS tracking data from 58 individuals. Isotopic values revealed distinct seasonal shifts in foraging strategies: adults showed higher δ13C values (−23.1 ± 0.7‰) in spring, reflecting increased use of agricultural maize (C4 plants), while winter diets (−25.4 ± 0.9‰) emphasized forest-floor acorns (C3 plants). Juveniles exhibited elevated δ15N (8.2 ± 0.5‰) compared to adults (6.8 ± 0.4‰), indicating greater insect consumption during early growth stages. Spatial analysis demonstrated turkeys in fragmented landscapes utilized riparian corridors 37% more frequently than continuous forest populations, correlating with 15% lower body condition indices in fragmented habitats. Bayesian mixing models attributed 62% of annual dietary carbon to anthropogenic food sources in areas with >20% agricultural cover, raising concerns about dependency on human-modified landscapes. Our results emphasize the critical role of hardwood mast production in winter survival and highlight trade-offs between agricultural subsidy use and long-term population resilience. These findings directly inform habitat management plans aimed at balancing sustainable hunting practices with forest conservation in rapidly developing regions.

We investigated the impacts of recreational human activity on Caspian Tern (Hydroprogne caspia) breeding success in the Columbia River estuary, Oregon, USA, from 2018–2021. Using GPS tracking (n = 42 adults), behavioral observations (1,200 hrs), and nest monitoring (327 nests), we quantified responses to pedestrian traffic, watercraft proximity, and drone overflights within 300 m of nesting colonies. Nests in zones with >15 human disturbances/day showed 38% lower fledging success (0.8 chicks/nest) compared to low-disturbance zones (1.3 chicks/nest; GLMM: z = -4.21, p < 0.001). Adults in high-disturbance areas spent 32% less time brooding (ANOVA: F₁,₃₈ = 9.74, p = 0.003) and exhibited a 2.5× higher frequency of alarm calls during chick provisioning. Drone incursions <100 m altitude triggered colony-wide flush responses in 89% of events, leaving eggs/chicks vulnerable to thermal stress and gull predation. Multivariate analysis revealed pedestrian presence within 200 m as the strongest predictor of nest abandonment (OR = 4.7, 95% CI: 2.1–10.3). Our results demonstrate that current 100-m buffer zones fail to mitigate reproductive impacts in this state-threatened population. We recommend expanding seasonal closures to 200 m, restricting drones near colonies, and implementing real-time monitoring of visitor density during critical breeding phases (May–July). These measures could enhance conservation outcomes while balancing recreational use in this biologically critical estuary ecosystem.

We investigated the foraging ecology of Virginia Rails (Rallus limicola) across 14 freshwater marshes in the Great Lakes region (2018–2021) using radio-telemetry and systematic habitat surveys. By combining 3,427 GPS locations from 22 instrumented individuals with fecal DNA metabarcoding, we quantified habitat selection, foraging rates, and dietary composition relative to water depth, vegetation structure, and invertebrate prey availability. Individuals exhibited strong selection for shallow-water habitats (5–15 cm depth) dominated by dense stands of emergent vegetation (Typha spp., Schoenoplectus spp.), where foraging bouts (2.3 ± 0.7 pecks/min) were 68% more frequent than in adjacent sedge meadows (p < 0.001). Diet analysis revealed 94% occurrence of aquatic invertebrates (Diptera larvae, Coleoptera adults, Odonata nymphs), with amphipods (Hyalella azteca) disproportionately represented (>40% biomass) despite comprising only 12% of available prey biomass. Foraging efficiency declined significantly when water levels fluctuated >8 cm/week (r² = 0.76, p = 0.004), suggesting sensitivity to hydrological variability. Our results demonstrate that Virginia Rails function as obligate wet-soil predators, with narrow microhabitat requirements that may limit their resilience to climate-driven wetland drying. Conservation strategies targeting rail populations should prioritize maintaining stable hydroperiods and heterogeneous vegetation structure in marshes <2 ha, which supported 83% of observed foraging activity despite representing only 31% of surveyed wetland area.

We investigated stopover ecology of Virginia Rails (*Rallus limicola*) across a migratory network in the Great Lakes region from 2018-2022 using radio telemetry and habitat metrics. A total of 120 individuals were captured at 12 coastal wetlands in Michigan and Ontario, fitted with nanotag transmitters, and monitored via automated receiver arrays. Movement analysis revealed 78% of birds utilized ≥2 stopover sites (mean = 3.2 ± 1.1 sites) during migration, with average stop duration of 4.3 days (range 1-12) before resuming flight. Habitat selection models (AICc-weighted) identified water depth (30-50 cm; β = 2.1, 95% CI 1.7-2.5) and cattail (*Typha* spp.) stem density (15-25 stems/m²; β = 1.8, 95% CI 1.3-2.2) as primary predictors of site use. Sites with invasive phragmites (*Phragmites australis*) cover >25% showed 63% lower occupancy probability compared to native vegetation stands. Plasma metabolite profiling indicated significantly higher refueling rates (triglyceride:β-hydroxybutyrate ratio) at stopovers with active beaver (*Castor canadensis*) impoundments (t-test: t = 4.1, p < 0.001). Our mark-recapture data revealed 22% higher daily survival probability for birds using sites within 500 m of forest edge, potentially due to reduced avian predation pressure. These findings emphasize the critical role of heterogeneous wetland complexes with interspersed open water and emergent vegetation in supporting rail migration. Conservation strategies targeting single large wetlands may inadequately address the serial habitat requirements we document, particularly given projected hydroperiod alterations under climate change scenarios in this region.

We investigated the effects of coastal habitat degradation on Bald Eagle (*Haliaeetus leucocephalus*) populations in the Mississippi Sound, USA, from 2018 to 2023. Using satellite telemetry (n = 45 breeding pairs) and GIS-based land cover analysis, we quantified declines in nesting habitat availability and foraging efficiency associated with marsh fragmentation and shoreline urbanization. Nesting density decreased by 22% in areas with >15% coastal development, while fledgling survival rates in degraded zones (62 ± 8%) were significantly lower than in intact habitats (89 ± 5%; p < 0.01). Stable isotope analysis of blood samples revealed a 34% reduction in estuarine prey consumption in eagles from developed regions, correlating with a 40% loss of tidal marshes since 2005. Linear mixed-effects models identified proximity to boat traffic (β = -0.47, SE = 0.12) and impervious surface cover (β = -0.63, SE = 0.09) as primary predictors of nest abandonment. Our findings suggest current coastal management policies underestimate cumulative impacts on apex raptors, with marsh restoration efforts failing to offset urbanization-driven habitat compression. We recommend expanding protected buffer zones to 1.2 km inland from current shoreline reserves and prioritizing conservation of large-crowned trees for nesting. This study highlights the cascading consequences of coastal habitat loss on raptor population viability and nutrient transfer dynamics in nearshore ecosystems.

We investigated sex-specific parental care dynamics in Ospreys (*Pandion haliaetus*) across 12 breeding seasons (2010–2021) in the Chesapeake Bay estuary, USA, using motion-activated nest cameras and GPS telemetry. Adults (n = 48 pairs) exhibited significant division of labor, with males providing 87.3% of prey deliveries (mean = 4.2 ± 1.1 fish/day) and females performing 92% of nest defense against Bald Eagle (*Haliaeetus leucocephalus*) intrusions. Chick provisioning rates positively correlated with fledging success (R² = 0.68, p < 0.001), but excessive male foraging effort (>6 km from nest) increased nest abandonment risk by 40% during heatwaves (>32°C). Stable isotope analysis of blood samples (n = 217 nestlings) revealed that lipid-rich Menhaden (*Brevoortia tyrannus*) constituted 74% of diets in successful nests versus 38% in failed nests. Unexpectedly, 22% of females engaged in extra-pair copulations during mate foraging absences, though genetic analysis showed no resultant extra-pair paternity. These findings highlight climate-mediated trade-offs between provisioning and nest attendance, emphasizing the importance of conserving forage fish populations and minimizing thermal stress in tidal nesting habitats to support this sentinel raptor species.

We investigated juvenile survival and post-fledging ecology of Cooper's Hawks (Accipiter cooperii) across urban and exurban habitats in the Colorado Front Range from 2018–2022. Using radio-telemetry (n = 94 fledglings) and nest monitoring, we assessed survival rates, dispersal patterns, and mortality drivers during the critical 120-day period post-fledging. Cox proportional hazards models revealed significant spatial variation, with exurban juveniles exhibiting higher survival (62%, 95% CI: 54–69%) compared to urban conspecifics (38%, 95% CI: 29–47%). Predation accounted for 51% of mortalities (primarily by Great Horned Owls, Bubo virginianus), while anthropogenic factors caused 33% (vehicle collisions, window strikes). Dispersal distances differed markedly between sexes, with females traveling significantly farther (mean ± SE: 18.7 ± 2.1 km) than males (7.3 ± 1.4 km) by winter onset. Resource selection functions indicated strong avoidance of impervious surfaces (β = -1.72, p < 0.001) and preference for riparian corridors during dispersal. Survival probability increased with prey biomass (β = 0.41, p = 0.03) and decreased with proximity to major roads (β = -0.29, p = 0.01). These findings highlight urbanization's divergent impacts on juvenile raptor survival, suggesting exurban landscapes may act as population sources while urban areas function as ecological traps. Conservation strategies emphasizing retention of native vegetation buffers and mitigation of anthropogenic threats could enhance recruitment in rapidly developing regions.

We investigated morphological variation in Redhead (Aythya americana) populations across the Central Flyway to assess geographic differentiation and sex-based dimorphism. Morphometric measurements (culmen length, tarsus depth, wing chord, body mass) and plumage reflectance spectra were collected from 540 adult specimens (2018–2022) at key breeding (Prairie Pothole Region, Saskatchewan) and wintering sites (Laguna Madre, Texas; Cheyenne Bottoms, Kansas). Multivariate analysis revealed significant latitudinal clines in body size (wing chord: F = 8.3, p < 0.001; mass: F = 6.9, p = 0.009), with northern breeders averaging 5.2% larger than southern counterparts. Sexual dimorphism exceeded regional variation (MANOVA: Wilks' λ = 0.74, p < 0.001), with males displaying 12% greater culmen length and 7% higher UV plumage reflectance (340–400 nm). Unexpectedly, bill morphology covaried with wetland salinity gradients (R² = 0.38, p = 0.02), suggesting local adaptation to forage conditions. Cluster analysis identified three ecotypes differing in wing-to-body mass ratios, potentially linked to migratory strategies. These findings challenge assumptions of morphological homogeneity in this generalist diver and highlight vulnerability to climate-driven habitat desiccation, particularly for southern populations experiencing disproportionate wetland loss. Conservation strategies must account for cryptic regional adaptation in this IUCN Near Threatened species, as homogenization of wintering habitats may disrupt ecotype-specific resource partitioning.

We investigated the effects of wetland management practices on American Kestrel (Falco sparverius) breeding ecology across 27 managed wetlands in the Midwestern U.S. from 2018 to 2022. Using nest box occupancy surveys (n = 412 boxes), prey abundance transects, and drone-derived vegetation structure metrics, we assessed how water-level manipulation, invasive plant control, and prescribed burning influenced reproductive success. Nest occupancy declined by 32% in wetlands subjected to late-season drawdowns compared to early-season manipulations (β = -1.42, SE = 0.31, p < 0.001), coinciding with reduced small mammal prey availability during critical nestling periods. Multivariate analyses revealed that kestrels preferentially selected nest sites within 500 m of wetlands maintaining ≥40% native emergent vegetation cover (AICc weight = 0.87). Contrary to expectations, prescribed fire frequency showed a non-linear relationship with fledging success, peaking at biennial intervals (2.8 fledglings/nest) but declining by 45% in annually burned units. Radio-telemetry data from 47 adults demonstrated significant hunting habitat partitioning, with males preferentially foraging in moist soil units during peak orthopteran abundances (July-August). Our results challenge assumptions that wetland management optimized for waterfowl automatically benefits raptor communities. We propose staggered drawdown schedules and 10-30% riparian shrub retention as compensatory strategies to maintain prey resources for kestrels while achieving primary waterbird management objectives. These findings underscore the need for adaptive, multi-taxon approaches in wetland conservation planning.

We investigated the spatial and trophic interactions of Green Herons (Butorides virescens) within a mixed-species wading bird community in the freshwater marshes of Georgia's Altamaha River floodplain (31°58'N, 81°22'W) from 2018–2020. Using 127 nest observations and 482 foraging hours of behavioral data, we quantified overlap with syntopic species including Little Blue Herons (Egretta caerulea) and Great Egrets (Ardea alba). Green Herons exhibited significant vertical stratification in nesting preferences, selecting shrubs ≤3 m height (χ² = 17.3, p<0.001), while larger herons nested in taller trees (4–7 m). Foraging niche analysis revealed 78% dietary overlap with Snowy Egrets (Egretta thula) in crayfish consumption (Pianka index=0.65), but temporal partitioning minimized competition, with Green Herons preferentially feeding at crepuscular periods (GLMM: z=4.12, p<0.001). Nest survival rates (65%) were inversely correlated with proximity to Black-crowned Night-Heron (Nycticorax nycticorax) colonies (<200 m: 48% vs >500 m: 72%; Cox PH model: HR=2.1, p=0.03), suggesting predation or kleptoparasitism risks. Vegetation analysis identified buttonbush (Cephalanthus occidentalis) density as the strongest predictor of Green Heron occupancy (AUC=0.83). Our results demonstrate that this diminutive ardeid maintains coexistence through microhabitat specialization and temporal avoidance, but faces increasing pressure from habitat homogenization favoring larger competitors. Conservation strategies targeting understory riparian vegetation may buffer against competitive exclusion in anthropogenically altered wetlands.

We investigated population genetic structure and diversity of Brown Pelicans (*Pelecanus occidentalis*) across six breeding colonies in the Gulf of Mexico (Louisiana, Texas) and Pacific Coast (Baja California, Sonora) following decades of pesticide-driven population declines and post-DDT recovery. Using reduced-representation genomic sequencing (ddRAD) and mitochondrial DNA from 147 individuals, we identified significant divergence between Gulf and Pacific populations (FST = 0.137, p < 0.001) with asymmetric gene flow (m = 0.43 migrants/generation). Gulf colonies exhibited 18% lower nucleotide diversity (π = 0.0011 vs. 0.0017) and elevated inbreeding coefficients (FIS = 0.09 vs. 0.03), potentially reflecting lingering effects of the Deepwater Horizon oil spill that reduced Gulf populations by 40% in 2010. Effective population size estimates (Ne) remained below 500 in all Gulf colonies, contrasting with Ne > 1,200 in Pacific populations. Private alleles associated with cytochrome P450 genes were detected in Gulf populations, suggesting potential selection pressure from hydrocarbon exposure. These results highlight the vulnerability of genetically depauperate Gulf colonies to future environmental perturbations and underscore the need for targeted genetic monitoring integrated with habitat restoration efforts. We advocate for transnational management policies that address differential conservation risks across biogeographic populations while maintaining adaptive potential through ecological connectivity.

We investigated juvenile survival rates in Tricolored Herons (Egretta tricolor) across six breeding colonies in coastal Louisiana from 2018–2021. Using radio-telemetry (n = 120 fledglings) and mark-resight data, we estimated first-year survival at 0.58 ± 0.07 SE, with significant spatial variation linked to wetland fragmentation (Cox proportional hazards model: χ² = 9.3, p = 0.002). Survival probabilities declined by 32% in colonies adjacent to agricultural runoff zones compared to intact marsh habitats. Bayesian network analysis revealed prey density (primarily cyprinodontiform fishes) explained 41% of mortality risk, followed by nocturnal predation by raccoons (Procyon lotor) and great horned owls (Bubo virginianus). Juveniles in hydrologically managed impoundments exhibited 1.7× higher survival than those in unmanaged tidal creeks, mediated through enhanced foraging efficiency (GLMM: β = 0.83, p < 0.001). Unexpectedly, hurricanes during the study period caused only transient survival dips (<15% mortality), while chronic drought conditions reduced survival by 28% through prey scarcity. Our demographic modeling indicates that stabilizing Tricolored Heron populations requires maintaining ≥60% juvenile survival, achievable through watershed-scale management of freshwater inflow and predator exclusion around nursery marshes. These findings highlight the vulnerability of juvenile wading birds to anthropogenic hydrologic alterations, with direct implications for Everglades restoration targets and coastal wetland conservation strategies under climate change scenarios.

We investigated the trophic ecology and habitat use of Northern Bobwhite (Colinus virginianus) populations across a gradient of agricultural intensification in the southeastern United States using stable isotope analysis of δ¹³C and δ¹⁵N in breast muscle tissue (n = 147) and covert feathers (n = 203). Samples were collected from 15 study sites in Georgia between 2018-2021, representing native longleaf pine savannah, mixed forest-pasture, and intensive row-crop landscapes. Isotopic niche widths, calculated using SIBER models, revealed 32% narrower dietary breadth in agricultural areas (SEAc = 1.8‰²) compared to native habitats (SEAc = 2.7‰²). Bayesian mixing models indicated that birds in cultivated landscapes derived 58 ± 11% of their protein from maize-associated arthropods, versus 22 ± 9% in undisturbed habitats where native C3 plants dominated. Feather δ²H values demonstrated 18% lower site fidelity in fragmented agricultural regions (σ² = 4.3‰) relative to contiguous habitats (σ² = 3.5‰). Multivariate analysis of variance confirmed significant interactions between land use type and seasonal resource availability (F₆,₂₈₈ = 4.71, p < 0.001), with agricultural populations exhibiting 23% lower body condition indices during drought periods. These findings suggest that current agricultural subsidies promoting homogeneous crop cover reduce the species' adaptive capacity to climatic extremes. We recommend incorporating isotopic monitoring into adaptive management frameworks to evaluate the effectiveness of Working Lands for Wildlife program interventions targeting quail conservation.

We investigated population genetic structure and diversity of Snowy Egrets (Egretta thula) across their North American breeding range to assess anthropogenic impacts on metapopulation connectivity. Using microsatellite markers (n=15 loci) and mitochondrial DNA sequencing (control region), we analyzed 350 individuals from 15 colonies spanning the Gulf Coast (Texas to Florida), Atlantic Coast (Georgia to Maine), and interior wetlands (Mississippi River Valley). Bayesian clustering revealed moderate genetic structure (FST = 0.08, p < 0.001) with three distinct clusters corresponding to major hydrological basins. Coastal populations exhibited higher allelic richness (mean AR = 7.2 ± 0.4) compared to interior populations (AR = 5.1 ± 0.3), suggesting historical fragmentation of freshwater habitats. Landscape genetic analyses identified urbanization density (ρ = -0.43, p = 0.01) and dam presence (ρ = -0.37, p = 0.03) as significant barriers to contemporary gene flow. Effective population size estimates (Ne) ranged from 82 to 412 across colonies, with six populations falling below the IUCN threshold for genetic viability. Temporal comparisons using museum specimens (n=45) revealed a 22% decline in mitochondrial haplotype diversity since 1950. Our results highlight the urgent need for wetland corridor restoration and targeted genetic rescue efforts, particularly for isolated interior populations facing increased climate change vulnerability. These findings provide a framework for adaptive management of wading bird metapopulations in rapidly developing coastal ecosystems.

We investigated seasonal movement patterns and stopover-like site usage in a non-migratory population of Ruffed Grouse (*Bonasa umbellus*) in the Upper Peninsula of Michigan from 2018 to 2022. Using GPS telemetry data from 42 individuals, we identified 137 distinct stopover sites (mean duration: 3.2 ± 1.5 days) during autumn dispersal of juveniles (n = 28) and short-distance elevational movements of adults (n = 14). Stopover sites occurred at a mean elevation 85 m lower than origin locations (p < 0.001) and were disproportionately located in mixed deciduous forests with dense *Corylus americana* understory (χ² = 18.7, df = 3, p < 0.001), compared to random forest patches. Movement analysis revealed a mean daily displacement of 1.2 km during stopover periods versus 3.8 km during active movement phases (Welch's t-test: t = 5.43, p < 0.0001). Faecal glucocorticoid metabolite levels measured from 214 samples indicated significantly lower stress hormone concentrations at stopover sites compared to areas of active transit (ANOVA: F₁,₂₁₂ = 9.84, p = 0.002). Survival modeling demonstrated that stopover site selection influenced overwinter mortality, with individuals using sites containing >40% hazel cover experiencing 22% higher survival rates (Cox PH model: HR = 0.62, 95% CI 0.47-0.81). These findings challenge traditional definitions of stopover ecology by demonstrating that facultative site fidelity in non-migratory galliformes serves similar ecological functions to obligate migratory stopovers, emphasizing the importance of fine-scale habitat connectivity for forest-dependent species under climate change scenarios.
